Breaking: Pentagon tests pack hunting with autonomous war robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Pentagon has been testing packs of autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat situations.
  • In a recent development, “Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable upcoming warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA.
  • Recent findings suggest that during the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Pentagon has been testing packs of autonomous ground vehicles (UGVs) in simulated combat situations. In mid-October, at Fort Knox’s St. Vith Range in Kentucky, four UGVs “worked as a team, negotiating and surveilling the rolling landscape in search of enemy forces,” recalls a DARPA blog post. These UGVs are highly modular and can be kitted out with a wide range of tactical add-ons, but target engagement was controlled by a human operator. This latest exercise was prompted by the request of European allies.

In a recent development, “Out here at Fort Knox, we’re looking at how autonomous mobility technology can be paired with payloads to enable upcoming warfighter capabilities,” explained Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA. The blog notes that this location was also chosen as it represents a similar landscape to the European theater.

Recent findings suggest that during the demo an operator received a tip about a simulated threat alongside some satellite imagery. They then sent the pack of UGVs to the area to surveil the landscape and identify targets. Smartly, a sole UGV went ahead of the pack to scout, with the three others waiting behind. The scout UGV was equipped with a flying drone. In a real-world scenario this could have been flown for better visuals or to strike the targets from the sky. “Soldiers can mount anything and everything onto – 240 Bravos, drones, rockets,” remarked a technician attending the demo, as they are “super modular platforms.” The blog indicates three of the four UGVs in the exercise had drones.

Industry observers note that after the designated area was scouted by the leading autonomous ground vehicle, other UGVs followed on “to provide cover and support.” A simulated rocket was fired at a target identified about 300 yards from the robot pack. Finally, the last robot came out of cover, higher up over a ridge, to assess the field of conflict.

It was emphasized that during the exercise, a human operator was controlling any kinetic engagement. “All the mobility, all the movement, all the detections, all of that is autonomous,” explained Gregory. “But they don’t pull the trigger until a human says pull the trigger.”.

It has been revealed that this exercise was part of DARPA’s Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER program. Expertise required for RACER’s success includes vehicle design, algorithm technologies, super intelligence, and secure communications.

In a recent development, after five years of work, these UGVs can now be instructed to complete tasks on the battlefield, instead of being manually driven, notes Gregory. They roam off-road as fast as any human driver could manage, at a minimum.

In a recent development, testers reckon the UGV packs are ready for deployment and use in “a host of other missions, including food, ammunition and supply logistics and more,” according to the DARPA blog. More UGV pack hunting tests are scheduled for December, with a group of serving soldiers involved.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • はじめてDOOMで遊びます、自作のi486 PCで https://t.co/feosWgd6deNovember 9, 2026.
  • According to recent reports, this project’s first signs of life were seen towards the end of October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that an app engineer has showcased his homemade breadboard 486 DX2 PC running Doom. The intricate explosion-of-wires system build appears to have taken just 16 days, with the first appearance of the legendary Intel CPU on @nagakurage’s timeline on October 24, and a video demo of some fragging in Doom published on November 9. Moreover, the Tokyo-based app engineer behind the project also developed and made a bezelicious ‘CRT monitor’ to go with the homemade early-90s-era gaming beast.

はじめてDOOMで遊びます、自作のi486 PCで https://t.co/feosWgd6deNovember 9, 2026.

According to recent reports, this project’s first signs of life were seen towards the end of October. On October 24, @nagakurage showcased the legendary Intel i486 DX2 CPU that he had acquired. It was the sought-after DX2 66 model, which meant it ran at a blistering 66 MHz internally, and 33 MHz externally (2x multiplier). On the other side of this gray made-in-Malaysia chip, you can see its 168 pins, which look incredibly tree-trunk-like by today’s standards.

Recent findings suggest that the enthusiast next bought a Colorlight i9 v7.2 FPGA board to attach the CPU to and to cover chipset duties. We know this is a breadboard PC, but there are limits… Every pin of the 486 CPU appears to have been connected separately to an experimental ‘socket’ made using a baseboard.

i486 CPU実験用ソケット完成 低クロックで動かなければ基盤発注する https://t.co/cXCnvPtkQ5October 24, 2026.

Industry observers note that A significant milestone was reached on October 26, when the finished form of the breadboard system started to come into view, and the dev managed to get the CPU to blink an LED using x86 code. RAM was added on October 31, and tweaked to be error-free. Then, on November 3, the enthusiast managed to add microSD storage to the system. That same day @nagakurage enjoyed seeing the breadboard 486 boot FreeDOS 1.3 for the first time [machine translation].

The app developer then took a 3D printing diversion and used his Bambu Lab A1 mini to output the parts necessary for a custom CRT-style enclosure. This was designed by Claude and was assembled with a 5-inch 800×480 Elecrow Raspberry Pi panel inside.

In a recent development, finally, on November 9, @nagakurage showcased his breadboard PC and era-matching design beige-shelled monitor side-by-side and powered up. The seminal shooter looked smooth enough on the vintage 1992 silicon, as it should do.

Going forward, the enthusiast wants to refine this breadboard-based project and make it fully PC-98 compatible, in line with the dominant NEC PC-9800 series in Japan in the early 90s.

3D printing dev’s free tool unlocks curved printing along all three axes

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer.
  • Sources indicate that alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners.
  • Industry observers note that commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, alpaca Engineering posted a YouTube video yesterday showcasing his self-hostable non-planar slicer. He explains that most non-planar 3D printing — printing across all three axes, rather than in 2D horizontal layers — demonstrations are usually for research purposes, for demonstration and experimentation, with no easy way for most 3D printer owners to try out non-planar 3D printing. His project, named PancakeSlicer, aims to fix this by making his non-planar slicing algorithm as easy to implement as existing slicing workflows, even improving upon it with 3D printer management features.

Sources indicate that alpaca Engineering explains that every few months, a non-planar 3D printing demonstration goes viral, but is rarely adopted practically by most 3D printer owners. Most non-planar experiments are for research, with half-abandoned GitHub projects. He further explains that non-planar isn’t widely adopted not because there aren’t any general-purpose non-planar slicers, but because it’s not accessible and easily implemented in a familiar workflow, with 3D printer owners spoiled by modern workflows and not needing to manually run G-code directly from an SD card.

Industry observers note that commercially available 3D printers are also not optimized for non-planar 3D printing. The challenge with printing at various angles is the clearance angle needed to bring a print head up and down without crashing into its own print. The slicer uses 3D models of various print heads from different 3D printer models to know how to slice the object to avoid collisions, thus having limited support; but Alpaca Engineering has listed a large number of supported 3D printers from Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Voron, and many others. The varying shapes of the print heads also mean different printers will have different capabilities, with some managing less angle and curvature than others.

Alpaca Engineering also has great animations and practical demonstrations of the different slicing algorithms in the slicer, including how the algorithm slices the object for non-planar printing. We highly suggest you watch the video if you’re interested, as his animations explain non-planar slicing intuitively.

One of the best features of this slicer is its self-hosting features. Users can host the slicer from a desktop, NAS, or a home server and access it with a web UI, allowing multiple users to send print jobs from any device. It also has 3D printer management features, applying different profiles to different printer brands, unifying the experience without hopping from one slicer to another to operate multiple 3D printers — this is even available to Bambu Lab users, replacing Bambu Studio and Bambu Connect in LAN-only mode. The slicer can also manage two slice jobs at the same time in case other users happen to be slicing at the same time.

In a recent development, while PancakeSlicer isn’t the first to implement self-hosted 3D printer management features, it certainly levels up his initial goal of making non-planar slicing as easy to access as most modern workflows. We hope to see how more people can experiment with non-planar 3D printing, contribute their findings, and rapidly improve upon it as a genuinely practical slicing method.

Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed.
  • In a recent development, micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is.
  • The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed. According to the decision, the defendants’ argument that the legal action is just “a rerun” of the same antitrust case filed against the industry in 2018 was rejected as the plaintiffs have established that there’s some newly introduced evidence suggesting that there was collusion between the significant three memory chip manufacturers.

In a recent development, micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is. Judge Wise disagreed with this characterization, though, saying that what they are accused of goes beyond that. “Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation — an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”.

The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year. One of the events they cited included the “simultaneous DRAM production cuts” from October 2022 to April 2023, which was quickly followed by a “coordinated pivot to HBM.” They also stated that the three companies revealed the winding down of DDR4 production in a span of three months and have failed to expand the production capacity “despite these extraordinary prices — the single most powerful supply signal the DRAM industry has ever produced.”.

Other factors that the suing parties brought to the table include the introduction of stringent customer vetting procedures in response to the shortage, the refusal to sign long-term contracts for DRAM customers, Micron’s decision to shut down Crucial (its consumer memory brand), multiple statements projecting the shortage, as well as their involvement in previous price-fixing scandals.

The big three memory chip makers argued that all of these are logical business moves so that they can maximize their revenue during a period of great demand and that they are “consistent with [their own] independent self-interest.” They also said that they appear to have similar behaviors because they’re in a highly concentrated market, and that they’re all “reacting to the same market pressures,” thus it would make sense for them to have a similar response.

Despite their rebuttals, the judge decided that the case is plausible enough to move forward. This isn’t a judgment, though — both sides would still have to show their evidence and speak their arguments before the court before getting a decision. Because of this, the three companies are given until December 7 to respond to the original complaint with the case management conference, which will determine the administrative matters on the case, set for January 2027.

Industry News: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (476 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage.
  • Recent findings suggest that the tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running.
  • This is one of the concerns that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage. The establishment had a “maintenance safety system” for its sauna area that relied on sending emails to warn the operators if the chlorine level in the area was too high. Unfortunately, the service disruption meant that the system's messages could not be sent, leading to increased levels that precipitated human injuries, writes Notebookcheck. German emergency services had to deploy 40 first responders to the site, with local media reporting that four victims were taken to the hospital for treatment, with one remaining for further observation.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running. Although this Microsoft outage wasn’t as large as the CrowdStrike fiasco in 2024, which led to a massive service disruption to a good number of corporate computer systems and sent shockwaves across the world, this incident has caused injuries and could’ve even led to something more catastrophic if the concern wasn’t caught earlier.

This is one of the concerns that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety. Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline. More importantly, their people should know that they exist and be familiar with how they work. Alternatively, businesses can host their own servers, build their own automations, and run everything locally, although this would require a bit more involvement in building and programming the entire system. And there could be local infrastructure impacting issues like power cuts, still.

It has been revealed that aside from that, the Microsoft outage also highlights the corporate world’s increasing reliance on a few major tech companies. While tech giants like Microsoft, Google, and AWS have the advantage of economies of scale, allowing them to offer their services reliably and more affordably compared to smaller rivals or an in-house deployment, it also means that if they go down, they affect millions of businesses that rely on them and cause economic activity to grind to a halt.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal-clear, detailed die shots of 357 legendary and some lesser-known processors.
  • The unnamed collator of this gallery might not have contributed any die shots, but has still done an admirable job putting these macrographs and micrographs together in this way.
  • By default, the die shot gallery gives you the gallery view, ordered by the oldest silicon first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal-clear, detailed die shots of 357 legendary and some lesser-known processors. At sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies, you will find a sortable, searchable, and filterable gallery featuring the outstanding, freely shared die shots from the likes of Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz. Find one or two of your favorites, and peer into the details to enjoy a nostalgic technological trip down memory lane. That’s what I did.

The unnamed collator of this gallery might not have contributed any die shots, but has still done an admirable job putting these macrographs and micrographs together in this way. Beneath a brief introduction that credits the skilled photographers who share these images for free, you can glide through the 357-photo collection.

By default, the die shot gallery gives you the gallery view, ordered by the oldest silicon first. Those browsing the gallery can instantly switch to a True Scale gallery view, too, which provides some physical sizing context. The next view option for the gallery is a table, where you can see processor maker, year, die dimensions, and photo license at a glance, but it sacrifices visual impact by showing just tiny thumbnails.

It has been revealed that navigating the gallery is also quick and intuitive thanks to a built-in search function. Using this, it was easy to display only 486 CPUs, for example. For your information, there are 17 486 CPU variants in this gallery with samples produced by AMD, Cyrix, IBM, TI, UMC, VLSI, and Intel of course. You can click any of the thumbnails to jump to a larger view with notes of the design, as well as photographer details/credits. Though that click zooms in the image considerably, I found that a right-click – open image in newly introduced tab - was needed to enjoy the die shot’s full visual splendor.

It has been revealed that it would be great to see the database/gallery maintained with the latest shareable die shots from the various contributors. Also, it could be improved by fully populating details such as the die area, which is not always present. Some more searchable and sortable fields, such as transistor count, might also make this resource more satisfying.

It has been revealed that for my personal nostalgia, I enjoyed seeing CPUs like the Motorola 68000 and the AMD Athlon XP up close. Surprisingly, some eras, including the Intel Ivy Bridge and Haswell generations, seemed underrepresented, though.

FBI disrupts North Korean FaceStealer campaign behind $5 billion Binance hack

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The ongoing social-engineering campaign that's reportedly taken $400 million in cryptocurrency from victims and was behind the recent Binance heist now has a name: FaceStealer.
  • The DoJ's press release on the matter is blustery, but the FBI's detailed report contains the crucial details.
  • The campaign isn't likely to stop despite the setback, and has reportedly been running for at least 18 months, a timeline that matches up with documented instances of similar intrusion attempts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The ongoing social-engineering campaign that's reportedly taken $400 million in cryptocurrency from victims and was behind the recent Binance heist now has a name: FaceStealer. The moniker came from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ), who have unveiled a fight against this crime wave, starting with the seizure of associated cloud infrastructure. According to the DoJ, North Korea is behind these attacks, stealing cryptocurrency to fund its government.

The DoJ's press release on the matter is blustery, but the FBI's detailed report contains the crucial details. The agency's techs seized "cloud-based infrastructure," containing 900 videos of targeted victims. FaceStealer is an advanced form of spear-phishing, complete with AI deepfakes, usage of the victims' contact networks and personal information, and carefully orchestrated preparation — sometimes months in advance.

The campaign isn't likely to stop despite the setback, and has reportedly been running for at least 18 months, a timeline that matches up with documented instances of similar intrusion attempts. The largest heist attributed to FaceStealer is the recent Binance hack that saw thieves make out the proverbial door with over $5 billion (most of it thankfully frozen and/or recovered), but far from the only one.

According to recent reports, the FBI attributes about $400m in stolen cryptocurrency to the campaign, and importantly, also notes that the hackers have repeatedly tried to sneak into open-source software, chiefly Javascript/NPM modules and Rust crates. Despite not being mentioned by name, one example hack is almost certainly the Axios compromise from March 2026. The Node/Javascript library sees about 100 million downloads a week, and temporarily contained a remote-access tool — thankfully for only a few hours.

Jason Sayayman, the Axios developer in question, got hooked by an attacker posing as a legitimate tech giant interested in hiring him. The malfeasants replicated the CEO's persona, created a Slack workspace with legitimate-looking channels, then invited him to a Teams meeting with multiple "people.".

Industry observers note that this modus operandi is what the FBI warns about. According to the bureau, FaceStealers start by getting access to a person's communication application(s), then lifting all previous conversations, contact lists, and, most importantly, stealthily recording video of them and/or their contacts. The footage and information will then be used to catch the actual targeted victim, who'll often be sent offers for jobs or investment opportunities.

The victim will eventually be invited to a Zoom or Teams meeting that's actually hosted on an attacker-controlled server, with a typo-squatted domain like "uu01webzoom.us" or "teams.livemeet.us". The meeting will often have deepfaked AI participants and/or previous meeting recordings playing, granting the event an air of legitimacy — particularly because conversations leading up to this point will contain real information and context.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that at some point, though, there will be some sort of "technical problem," and the victim will be prompted to install an "enhancement" or software to fix the problem, which is loaded with malware. From there, the attackers have free rein over the victim's computer and data, and will siphon off browser sessions, CI/CD passwords, and all manners of access credentials to eventually get access to cryptocurrency wallets — or just use this information to find a juicier target, like the poor Binance developer through which Binance's hot wallets were broken into.

The FBI notes that the above scenario may play out in multiple cycles until the attackers reach their intended target, collecting loads of precious video and information along the way to make the final strike much more convincing.

Industry observers note that after rumors of Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards being withdrawn from the consumer retail channel, it is pleasing to see major U.S. e-tailers like Newegg stuffed with stock today. Checking out this popular online electronics retailer, we note that there are 21 RTX 5090 SKUs available, and 11 are sold by and shipped by Newegg. Sadly, pricing remains in 3x MSRP+ territory at the time of writing. Remember, you can sift through pricing trends in our comprehensive GPU price tracking 2026 feature to see that Nvidia's Blackwell flagship was once available at its fabled sub-$2,000 price.

Recent findings suggest that despite what looks on the surface like an ample supply (but there are order limits of one per customer), prices for RTX 5090s remain extremely high. The best prices we can see at Newegg are $6,599, but this price applies only to a water-cooled Aorus model and another sold inside a Gigabyte AI BOX eGPU. They might still appeal to you, depending on your setup, though.

It has been revealed that for a ‘standard’ air-cooled graphics card, albeit a very nice Aorus RTX 5090 Master, you’ll need to squeeze at least $6,659 out of your savings. A bonus with this card, alongside several others from the Gigabyte stables now purchasable from Newegg, is that it comes with a free motherboard. Many of these Gigabyte Aorus designs are being bundled with a full-ATX-sized X870 Aorus Elite WIFI7 AM5 motherboard, purportedly worth $319. Please note that the same motherboard is available to purchase outside this bundle for a more reasonable $249.

In a recent development, if you have money to burn, there are plenty of even more expensive SKUs to pick from. There are no opulent Golden Dhabab models on Newegg, sadly, but you’ll still be asked to part with $11,896 for the Asus ROG Astral GeForce RTX 5090 Edition 20 (sold by a Newegg marketplace partner). Perhaps surprisingly, given recent trending pricing news, that’s the only model above $10K, but there are still many models that are almost $10,000 from Asus, MSI, and Zotac. Even an Nvidia Founders Edition RTX 5090 refurb is priced at $8,899.

In context, these RTX 5090s are still at astronomical prices for consumer gaming PC add-in hardware. But they are now purchasable from a substantial retailer with fast delivery, rather than off a random scalper. It was only a month ago that rumors swirled about the RTX 5090 and the RTX 5080 being withdrawn from retail. That seemed to trigger crazy levels of price inflation, and reports of $10,000+ prices for the flagship card seemed to become the norm.

One can only hope that stock continues to flow to Newegg and other outlets, and RTX 5090 / RTX 5080 prices will settle lower as a result.

The CS 737X CDU (v2) brings an authentic, premium-build Boeing 737 Control Display Unit to the home cockpit, but its high price makes it a niche product for serious flight sim enthusiasts.

Accurate 1:1 replica of the real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits.

It has been revealed that cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the tech giant was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment.

Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024.

Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality.

Sources indicate that the CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight blueprint, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot.

The CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys.

Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The buttons are made of silicone rubber, which also closely replicates what we felt in our time on a 737 simulator.

Recent findings suggest that the display is where we noticed the biggest departure from the real 737 CDU. The real unit uses a thick, chemically strengthened, anti-glare optical glass cover, whereas the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a standard commercial display. As a result, there is some glare, although the display itself is excellent and offers very wide viewing angles. Despite this difference, the visual presentation is remarkably close to that of the real 737 CDU. The font styling, image sharpness, and color reproduction all closely match what you would see on the real flight deck.

The CS 737X CDU v2 also features a handle, which on the real aircraft is used for the maintenance crew to remove the CDU. This isn’t entirely necessary in a home setup, but it is a nice touch.

The unit can be easily placed on a desk using the included desktop stand, or integrated directly into a larger cockpit setup.

The weight, rigidity, and metallic construction closely replicate the feel of the CDU we experienced in a 737 simulator. The silicone buttons also require a firm, deliberate press to actuate, helping prevent accidental double-inputs during turbulence. This tactile resistance closely matches the experience of using the real unit. Manually entering a long route, rather than importing it from SimBrief, will give your fingers a workout – and will give you a newfound appreciation for the import button.

For our testing inside of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, we used the PMDG 737-800. We flew the following routes:.

This allowed us to examine how the CS 737X CDU v2 handles routes of various duration.

For hardware, the device only requires a USB connection. It also requires the CockpitSimulator Bridge, which needs to be left open throughout the flight. This can be downloaded from the official Cockpit-Simulator site.

Our flow was similar in each case:.

It has been revealed that the overall feel of the unit, combined with the firm, deliberate key presses, adds another layer of immersion. More importantly, having a physical CDU means we can operate it directly — rather than panning the camera toward the virtual CDU, zooming in, and navigating it with a mouse. This makes interacting with the FMS considerably faster and more intuitive.

This is particularly useful when ATC gives you a direct-to instruction shortly after takeoff, while you are still hand-flying the aircraft. Performing the direct-to operation on a physical CDU is much easier than interacting with the virtual CDU, as it allows you to make the necessary inputs without taking your eyes away from the Primary Flight Display.

In a recent development, one of the first things that stood out was the extremely low input latency. Our key presses were reflected almost instantly on both the unit’s physical display and the virtual CDU inside Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, making the two feel effectively synchronized.

We were also able to switch seamlessly between the various CDU pages, even with longer flight plans loaded into the unit. Everything shown on the virtual CDU was accurately reproduced on the hardware, including aircraft-specific options for the PMDG 737-800 we were flying. The information was presented with accurate fonts, colors, and formatting, making the physical CDU feel like a natural extension of the one inside the simulator.

Sources indicate that the CS 737X CDU v2 is the most premium and immersive Boeing 737 CDU we have tested. From the weight and feel of its metallic construction to the tactile resistance of the silicone keys and the accurate rendering of fonts and colors on the display, nearly every aspect of the unit contributes to an authentic experience. It's a fitting addition to any high-end home cockpit setup.

This level of construction and attention to detail comes at a price: the CS 737X CDU v2 retails for $799, which means it will likely be out of reach for many flight simmers. But if you're building a dedicated, high-end cockpit and looking for a CDU that closely replicates the experience of the real aircraft, it's an excellent addition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that just days after Jensen Huang suddenly resigned from his position at Nvidia, an Nvidia Robot Research Engineer mentioned that he would leave the tech giant as well. But more than just showing support for the former CEO with a generic “I stand with Jensen” message, Darrel Dai laid out several reasons for the decision on X.

I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say. As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the firm’s CEO. I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI. I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in. But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build. Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard. That is why this has been so disappointing. I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny. What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me. I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected. I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day. A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too. Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were vital reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close. I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me. These are my personal views.November 15, 2026.

“What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me,” the engineer posted. “I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.”.

It seems that Jensen Huang has gained the respect of the people working under him, with many calling for his reinstatement despite the many controversies he is currently facing. There’s also an online petition demanding that the Nvidia board “Bring Jensen Back,” with over 150,000 signatures at the time of writing.

Nvidia is centered around Jensen Huang, with the former chief executive reportedly having a small army of 60 people directly reporting to him. But despite his busy schedule and legendary persona, Dai noted that “Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly,” and that “It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.” Dai also pointed out that “employees’ trust and sense of belonging” are part of what makes a manufacturer great. More importantly, Nvidia is known as one of the tech companies with the most generous pay packages. Jensen was even quoted saying, “I pay my employees as much as I can.”.

It remains unclear what the former Nvidia CEO will do after all these complications. Elon Musk has already said on X that “it would be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang, especially as he’s embarking on his own ambitious chipmaking journey. As for the employees left behind at Nvidia, some are staying and have shown their full support to interim CEO Colette Kress, while many more want him back. However, there has also been talk that various Silicon Valley tech and semiconductor firms are aggressively attempting to poach Nvidians, although these are just rumors so far.

Developer creates a 100% valid ZIP file that doubles as a BIOS-bootable operating system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hacking stories these days mostly involve someone using an army of AI agents to find vulnerabilities in networks and software that were carefully hidden in plain sight.
  • You can unpack the ZIP file just like any other, boot it using Linux's GRUB, QEMU, or any other Multiboot-compatible loader (even if imaged to different media), or alternatively, perform the finest party trick: image-write it to a floppy and boot from it directly from BIOS on any compatible PC, without modification.
  • According to recent reports, much like me, that sequence of words may be triggering a head-tilt reminiscent of a confused puppy, so we'll explain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hacking stories these days mostly involve someone using an army of AI agents to find vulnerabilities in networks and software that were carefully hidden in plain sight. Today, for a change, we have a story about hacking in its original meaning — twisting computing artifacts into purposes not in their design spec. David Oberhollenzer, aka Goliath, a greybeard in spirit if not in shade, crafted a 100% valid ZIP file that's simultaneously an archive, BIOS-bootable, and a Multiboot-compatible OS image.

You can unpack the ZIP file just like any other, boot it using Linux's GRUB, QEMU, or any other Multiboot-compatible loader (even if imaged to different media), or alternatively, perform the finest party trick: image-write it to a floppy and boot from it directly from BIOS on any compatible PC, without modification.

According to recent reports, much like me, that sequence of words may be triggering a head-tilt reminiscent of a confused puppy, so we'll explain. The first thing you need to know is that unlike most file types, the metadata (in this case, file directory) of a ZIP is actually at the end of the archive. Up to that point, the data is comprised of every compressed file in sequence.

According to recent reports, the file packs all have a predictable structure: "PK" followed by bytes 03 04, metadata (including name), some extra/comment fields, and then the file's contents. Notably, any file can be stored uncompressed, and Goliath made use of that for the very first file, called ZIPHEAD.COM — remember, this is the start of the ZIP archive.

Recent findings suggest that goliath stated that it was "easy" to make the ZIP file a valid Multiboot system image. A valid image only needs to contain bytes 0x1BADB002 in the first 8 KiB, followed by some flags and a checksum. It was trivial to place that datum in ZIPHEAD's data, along with the location of where the bootloader lies.

Grub or QEMU don't care about anything else in the image, as once they have the initialization information, from that point it's the bootloader's problem. The actual bootloader, predictably, is in ZIPHEAD's uncompressed data, and the image will happily boot directly, or, say, from a floppy.

It has been revealed that making the same exact archive bootable via a standard PC BIOS took a little more work and some clever shenanigans. Making a disk bootable is simple enough: the BIOS reads the first exact 512 bytes of the disk's contents, and if they end with bytes 0x55AA, then it's bootable, and the BIOS starts executing whatever code is the first byte.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, placing 0x55AA precisely at position 510 of the ZIP, already in ZIPHEAD's contents, is once again simple, and won't corrupt the Multiboot image, as if you'll recall, the Multiboot spec is flexible with data locations. But you may wonder: once the BIOS runs code in sequence starting from the ZIP's first byte, then ZIPHEAD's header ("PK" + 0x0304, plus all metadata) surely is garbage for practical purposes, and not proper code? Well, yes, but actually no.

Sources indicate that the first four bytes represent CPU instructions that don't write anything to memory, so they're harmless, other than a push-to-stack. The next few belong to ZIPHEAD's metadata, and Goliath massaged those values to represent instructions that would either be innocuous or perform operations he could use, namely using the modification time bytes as instructions to jump further down the data.

According to recent reports, sounds simple, but the actual process of choosing bytes that represent (1) non-crashy CPU instructions, (2) useful code for setting up the boot process, and (3) still represent a valid file header in a ZIP archive is far trickier than the above. Do go and check out the full blog post if you want all the details.

Hacker gets Doom running on a USB flash drive's built-in LCD, played by copying files

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Doom now runs on a USB flash drive’s built-in LCD and is played by copying files to and from it, as hardware hacker Aaron Christophel showed in a teardown video.
  • Industry observers note that the off-the-shelf drive, the MOVESPEED MSSU10, has USB-A on one end and USB-C on the other, and the 128GB model, the smallest capacity in the range, cost him about 50 euros.
  • The main flash controller is the Silicon Motion SM2320G, one we have reviewed in portable SSDs like the Kingston XS2000 and Lexar SL660 Blaze, with a separate C*Core CCM4101 microcontroller — which has 2MB of flash and a small amount of RAM to itself — for the 428 x 142 color LCD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Doom now runs on a USB flash drive’s built-in LCD and is played by copying files to and from it, as hardware hacker Aaron Christophel showed in a teardown video. The marking on the drive’s display chip had been removed, but an open debug port let him extract its firmware, which enabled identification. He was then able to use AI to reverse-engineer the hardware and get the game running on the drive’s screen.

Industry observers note that the off-the-shelf drive, the MOVESPEED MSSU10, has USB-A on one end and USB-C on the other, and the 128GB model, the smallest capacity in the range, cost him about 50 euros. Its screen normally shows status data such as transfer speed, how full the drive is, and its temperature.

The main flash controller is the Silicon Motion SM2320G, one we have reviewed in portable SSDs like the Kingston XS2000 and Lexar SL660 Blaze, with a separate C*Core CCM4101 microcontroller — which has 2MB of flash and a small amount of RAM to itself — for the 428 x 142 color LCD. The NAND carries SanDisk markings. All of this is fairly standard portable SSD hardware, aside from the display.

The drive’s metal body uses heavily glued plastic end pieces but, past that, the display lifts off first and unplugs. The board slides out after the USB-C end cap is removed, in this case with minor cosmetic damage inflicted. The display chip’s marking is scrubbed, most likely with a laser, by the hacker’s reckoning, which can hinder identification and tinkering. Luckily, a probe on the debug pads, ground, and a 3.3V pin connected on the first try, and memory was immediately readable.

According to recent reports, the bootloader returned a version string dated 2023, followed by the full firmware, which helped greatly with identification. He says the chip is marketed as one for security — for fingerprint readers and access control, for example — but no related features were found to be enabled for this drive. He also discovered that, although the data sheet and stock firmware declare a 200 MHz operating clock frequency, it measured 40.2 MHz. This is unexplained.

One critical problem is immediately apparent: how do you play on a drive with no buttons? The display chip has no USB connection of its own and, from the connected PC or host, it only sees the storage controller’s activity, which it uses to gauge transfer speed. The primary storage controller has read and write counters, and the chip pulls these every 50 ms over I2C. Christophel says this is far easier than relying on a single physical button, as he did on a previous power bank mod.

The solution, then, is a PC script, doomctl.py, which turns key presses into small, timed transfers in each direction. The commands are simply encoded as transfer rates, at five levels per direction, and each read/write pair can map to a certain button combination. Arrow keys are for movement and turning, Space or Ctrl for firing and opening doors, and M for the menu, keeping it simple. Ordinary copying, without the script, can still steer, but the control scheme is much nicer.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that performance is…well, not really playable at about 13 frames per second, although the game logic runs at Doom’s normal 35 ticks per second. This is why he names the chip’s clock as the biggest potential performance gain. The game itself is built on DMC100-DOOM, Artur Bieniek’s port for very small microcontrollers. Only the first map, E1M1, fits in the chip’s flash, and no sound is produced as the drive lacks a buzzer. Christophel did play the level end to end, noting the low resolution.

AI did the heavy lifting: the reverse engineering as well as the port, and Christophel stated, “I would not be able to do such a thing in a few hours.”.

In a recent development, the open-source project, with its code and prebuilt firmware published, is likely to draw attention and may spawn similar hacks. The tools required are relatively minimal, mainly a debug probe, and he does suggest backing up the stock firmware before trying. For his own unit, he put it back together to use as a normal drive, but one that can still play Doom, if so desired.

Subway is celebrating the launch of GTA 6 with a latest Vice City Cubano sandwich, but fans hoping to try it will need to be in Miami to get their hands on one.

With Grand Theft Auto 6 finally launching on November 19, 2026, fast food chains are getting in on the excitement with special promotions inspired by Rockstar’s highly anticipated game.

Popeyes has already announced its Spice City Sandwich, featuring two crispy chicken fillets, while KFC in Australia is hosting a fake funeral to give fans an excuse to take the day off work.

Now, Subway is joining the celebrations with a sandwich inspired by Vice City, although there’s a catch.

According to an announcement shared with Dexerto, Subway has given its existing Cubano Pulled Pork Melt a GTA 6-inspired makeover, renaming it the Vice City Cubano.

The sandwich features hardwood-smoked pulled pork, Black Forest ham, melted provolone cheese, pickles, and mustard, all served on freshly baked artisan Italian bread.

It’s available in both six-inch and footlong sizes, but there’s one major restriction: you can only get it in Miami.

The Vice City Cubano is exclusive to the Florida city that inspired GTA 6‘s fictional setting, meaning fans elsewhere in the US won’t be able to order one under the promotional branding.

Those lucky enough to be in Miami can purchase the sandwich in-store, online, or through the Subway app, with delivery available for players who don’t want to put their controllers down.

Subway also indicated off the sandwich in an Instagram post, adding to the growing number of food promotions surrounding the game’s release.

In October, Rockstar brought GTA’s iconic Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell restaurants to life at the Kaseya Center, complete with themed packaging and actual food.

The limited-edition merchandise proved so popular that fans began reselling items for hundreds of dollars.

Unlike Popeyes’ nationwide sandwich promotion, Subway’s Vice City Cubano is keeping things local, giving Miami residents another way to celebrate GTA 6’s long-awaited arrival.

Without a doubt, Nvidia's dominance in the AI hardware market stems not only from the capabilities of its AI accelerators and its vast software ecosystem, but also from its aggressive procurement strategy that effectively denies its rivals access to sufficient production capacity at TSMC and other contractors. The result of his deals is that supply and capacity commitments rose by almost a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter, primarily due to memory procurement, according to SemiAnalysis. However, even Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang had apparently begun to question the sustainability of this strategy before his departure, based on reports from The Wall Street Journal and SemiAnalysis.

Industry observers note that over the past several years, Nvidia has not only captured the vast majority of the AI accelerator market, but has also secured a substantial proportion of the world's production capacity for advanced logic, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and various other components required to build AI accelerators and systems, which has limited the ability of its competitors to ramp up shipments of their processors. To support the deals, Jensen Huang personally negotiated agreements with major suppliers in Taiwan and South Korea.

It has been revealed that the massive scale of Nvidia's procurement commitments also enabled the company to secure more favorable quotes than its rivals. SemiAnalysis estimates that SK hynix could charge Nvidia between $3.00 and $3.30 per gigabit of HBM4 memory in 2027, whereas other first-tier customers, such as AMD, Amazon, Broadcom, and Google, would pay between $3.70 and $4.10 per gigabit. The analysts believe that as part of an informal arrangement between the two companies, Nvidia gives SK Group preferential access to its AI GPUs.

It has been revealed that while Nvidia's ability to secure vast production capacities has been instrumental in its success, such commitments also carry considerable risks. At a meeting with senior executives in August, Huang reportedly expressed concerns about the massive volumes of wafers and memory that Nvidia had committed to purchase as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on the company's hardware in favor of alternative AI accelerator platforms, according to The Wall Street Journal.

In a bid to diversify its customer base and create additional demand for its products, Nvidia offered financial guarantees to emerging cloud service providers and data center developers that otherwise could not afford to procure its hardware at scale. As of the end of its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia had $530 billion in gross off-balance-sheet guarantees, up from $184 billion a quarter earlier, as well as $99 billion worth of equity investments, according to SemiAnalysis. In a recent development, the scale of such commitments raised concerns even within Nvidia. Then-CFO Colette Kress questioned the criteria used to select recipients of financial support and the potential returns on such arrangements. She also reportedly reduced Nvidia's initial financial commitment to OpenAI's massive data center project in Ohio by half before the two companies signed an agreement on August 17. The facility is expected to house some $300 billion worth of Nvidia processors.

At some point, Huang himself began to question the merits of Nvidia's aggressive financing strategy in the event of his departure, essentially calling the current interim CEO, Colette Kress, a mere 'reporting CFO' rather than an executive capable of making strategic decisions. He also expressed concerns about massive wafer and memory procurement commitments as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on Nvidia’s GPUs.

Despite questionable commitments, without Huang and his personal relationships with executives at major semiconductor companies, Nvidia may find it harder to secure preferential treatment from its suppliers. SemiAnalysis believes that customers other than Nvidia could account for over 70% of TSMC production capacity in 2028. While this could enable Nvidia’s competitors to significantly increase shipments of their AI processors, it could also affect the willingness of Taiwanese and South Korean suppliers to invest aggressively in additional production capacity without the kind of assurances that Huang used to provide.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • YouTube is changing its public view counts so that one person hitting play on a TV can count as several views.
  • If you’ve ever put a YouTube video on for everyone in the living room, you’ve probably given the creator one view, even if the whole room was watching.
  • Now, YouTube wants the number under the video to do a better job of reflecting how many people may have actually seen it, by incorporating “estimated co-views” into the public video view counts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

YouTube is changing its public view counts so that one person hitting play on a TV can count as several views.

If you’ve ever put a YouTube video on for everyone in the living room, you’ve probably given the creator one view, even if the whole room was watching.

Now, YouTube wants the number under the video to do a better job of reflecting how many people may have actually seen it, by incorporating “estimated co-views” into the public video view counts.

If it estimates that three people watched a video together on a TV, that single play can count as three views. On phones, tablets, and PCs, one play still counts as one view.

To predict the size of the audience, YouTube looks at things like what’s playing, when it’s playing, and patterns in who tends to watch.

“YouTube never uses cameras, microphones, or device sensors to measure co-views,” the organization said in an announcement.

YouTube already gave creators a private estimate of how often people watched together. Now those extra views are being added to the public total.

It’s a change that matters more as people spend more time watching YouTube on the big screen. TVs are its fastest-growing method of watching, with viewers watching more than a billion hours on them every day.

“Until now, one TV playback has only counted as a single public view, even if several people watched together on the same living room screen,” the announcement continues, explaining the change.

YouTube rolls out massive changes for watching videos on your TV.

YouTube is making a major change to how long-form video views are counted.

YouTube will let other creators react live to your videos and keep the live ad revenue.

“By updating public view counts to include co-views, we’re solving this measurement gap, better aligning with long-standing TV industry standards, and telling a more accurate story of how viewers watch your content.”.

YouTube states creators can use that information to show potential sponsors how many people their videos reach more accurately. The public count is separate from how it calculates creator pay and who qualifies for its Partner Program.

This comes after YouTube unveiled a change to how long-form videos are counted, with a view now registering as soon as it’s played.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both owners and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5.
  • Recent findings suggest that the demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load.
  • In a recent development, building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both owners and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5. Perhaps as practical proof of that claim, front-end developer Maksymilian Dendura took inspiration from the demoscene and had Fable roll his own virtual underwater world, Abyssal Garden, in only 96 KB of Javascript/HTML — you can check it out here.

Recent findings suggest that the demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load. Using actual meshes and images for textures would otherwise take up a significant amount of space.

In a recent development, building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly. Some games employ this technique for repeated elements like trees and grass.

Likewise, all the visual effects and even some texturing are done with shaders, which are small programs that change how a mesh or texture appears — for example, to make parts of an object shiny. Games use them extensively, as many players are aware, thanks to endless "loading shaders" screens or Unreal Engine's st-tu-tutering.

Sources indicate that the result is definitely impressive, especially but not only as it's purely browser-based, relying on WebGPU and WebGL. Both are rarely-mentioned technologies that have actually existed for a long while now. As their names imply, they let developers render 2D and 3D graphics in a manner similar to that of OpenGL, but in a browser, using JavaScript as the base language.

The demo's most impressive fact is the simplicity of the prompt that got Fable 5.2 to build it. It's only about 40 lines long with word wrapping, and clearly illustrates the degree of autonomy that contemporary agentic AI has when given a specific, yet exceedingly open-ended task like this one. It's reasonable enough to assume the author did a few rounds of tweaking (and he has excellent artistic taste too), but the agent's acumen is nevertheless impressive.

Comparing this demo to an actual game is inevitable, but the reality is that demos have but an atom-sized fraction of the content of a full game, and are limited to little or no interaction, logic, or physics.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that performance is decent for what is a great-looking but otherwise tiny and almost featureless space. The author states that he's getting 180 FPS at 1440p on an RTX 5070 Ti. Likewise, having this world in 97 KB sounds impressive, but it's actually gigantic for this type of demo, even if an X user further optimized it for 52 KB.

Regular computing customers, including AI neophytes and acolytes, may not be aware that this kind of space-optimized programming for the purposes of visual/aural demonstrations is a discipline and art form that harkens back to the 1980s when 16-bit computers appeared — called the "demoscene.".

According to recent reports, by no means discounting the extraordinary fact that Fable did this nearly all by itself — which is the actual achievement here — code wizards have pulled off nearly impossible feats decades ago, including in browsers. The 2009 demo Elevatedn (17 years ago) has a comparable aesthetic, and includes music, in just under 4 KB (yes, four). There's even a browser version of it, taking up all of 4,777 bytes.

Recent findings suggest that hartverdrahtet (2012 — 14 years ago) has a highly complex 3D space, again in 4 KB. And old-timers in the audience will remember ".kkrieger", an FPS game prototype that fit in all of 96 KB, including meshes, textures, music, and sound effects... back in 2004.

Melbourne Cup horse So You Are has been found dumped in a Sydney skip following his death, leaving fans and his trainer demanding answers over how the racehorse’s remains were handled.

So You Are finished eighth in Australia’s most famous horse race on November 3, but his racing days sadly came to an end when he developed severe colic. Despite emergency treatment, trainer Bjorn Baker confirmed the beloved racehorse’s death on November 16.

However, a video uploaded to social media appeared to show the body of So You Are lying in a skip. The footage has since gone viral, with both horse fans and trainer Bjorn devastated by the lack of proper burial and the state in which the racehorse was left.

In his initial statement on X, Baker paid tribute to So You Are and those who had cared for him. “Beyond his achievements on the track, So You Are was a much-loved horse, and his loss will be deeply felt by everyone who knew and cared for him,” Baker wrote.

However, following the discovery of the horse’s body in a skip, Baker called for an explanation from the veterinary hospital that treated So You Are before his death.

According to recent reports, “Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are’s remains. He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death,” he said in his November 17 statement.

Sources indicate that “I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred. My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family, and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss.”.

In a recent development, in a statement shared to news.com.au, REC Equine Specialists managing partner Dr Jonathan Lumsden has since apologized for the handling of So You Are’s remains. He explained that the horse had been humanely euthanized under anesthesia after emergency treatment for severe colic, but admitted he should have received a proper burial.

“After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried. What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry,” Lumsden said.

Although the hospital did not carry out the burial itself, Lumsden acknowledged its responsibility for choosing the contractor and making the arrangements.

Sources indicate that “We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.”.

Industry observers note that REC said it had stopped using the service provider and was reviewing how its contractors handle horses after death, from collection through to burial. It is also working with the facility operators and the state’s horse racing authority to establish what happened.

“No owner should have to go through what So You Are’s connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again. Out of respect for So You Are and those who loved him, we ask that the footage not be shared further.”.

Huang's resignation from his Nvidia post came after he released a statement confirming his affair, one which could have repercussions far beyond Nvidia itself. U.S. intelligence was reported to believe that the woman involved in an affair with Jensen Huang, Alice Huang (no relation), is a spy working for the Chinese Ministry of State Security, or MSS. Ms. Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, an AI firm accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of AI chips into China via a subsidiary called Speedmatrix. Since Jensen Huang admitted to his adultery, it was further alleged that he had a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. That alone would potentially constitute a violation of Nvidia's own code of conduct. But the affair with an alleged Chinese spy is likely to be the most troublesome for the former-but-potentially-returning CEO.

Now, an open letter sent to Nvidia's board by Huang's allies has urged them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” The open letter was penned by Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker, both shareholders.

@yunta_tsai A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it tooNovember 13, 2026.

In a recent development, however, Nvidia has already started looking elsewhere. After placing chief financial officer Colette Kress in charge on an interim basis, it's believed the company has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential Huang successor. Haas spent around seven years at Nvidia before leaving in 2013, but no official confirmation has been declared, nor is it likely to be until a decision is made.

It has been revealed that it's possible that Huang can expect a vote of confidence from U.S. President Donald Trump, with the pair having a good relationship to date. But Trump recently called for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to take over at Nvidia.

Outside of the White House, Huang has other concerns to deal with. Congress has summoned him to appear before a Select Committee over his affair with the suspected Chinese spy, threatening to subpoena him if necessary.

Intel sued by shareholders for misleading investors after stock plunges 29%

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the organization of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters.
  • The proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California.
  • "Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the organization of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters.

The proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California. The lawsuit alleges that Intel failed to inform investors in a timely manner about the extent to which slow demand for consumer processors and excessive inventories would affect its sales. In particular, the plaintiffs argue that the negative impact of the PC market downturn on Intel's business was greater than the benefits the manufacturer enjoyed from the unprecedented buildout of AI data center infrastructure and other AI-related opportunities.

"Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads.

While Intel, like many other major technology companies, has invested heavily in its manufacturing capabilities, supply constraints have prevented the chipmaker from fully capitalizing on strong demand for data center processors. Meanwhile, a severe shortage of memory has driven up DRAM prices and, consequently, the cost of PCs, which has affected demand for consumer systems. As a result, Intel could not sell enough CPUs in the third quarter, which dramatically affected the manufacturer's stock price in October.

Sources indicate that intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan expressed disappointment with the supply constraints, the extraordinary situation in the memory market, and the subsequent weakness of the PC business during the firm's earnings call. Yet, the plaintiff believes that the company should have warned about the turmoil situation on the client PC market earlier. In fact, back in the early 2000s, when Intel was led by Craig Barrett, the company routinely issued mid-quarter business updates to inform investors about changes in its financial outlook. In fact, in September 2004, Intel used such an update to cut its third-quarter revenue and gross margin projections due to weaker-than-expected demand for its processors and inventory adjustments by its customers, which were very similar circumstances that the company faced in the third quarter of 2026.

A similar revision could have alerted Intel's shareholders to the challenges the chipmaker faced well ahead of its quarterly earnings release. Unfortunately, Intel abandoned the practice of mid-quarter updates in January 2006 under Paul Otellini, though it occasionally revised its guidance between quarterly earnings releases thereafter, particularly during the global financial crisis of 2008 – 2010.

Industry observers note that intel's shareholders also allege that the tech giant had a financial incentive to withhold information about the state of its business as it raised $23 billion through a stock offering at $95 per share in mid-August, roughly halfway through its third quarter. Intel secured the additional capital as it planned to expand its semiconductor production capacity.

In a recent development, intel’s stock price dropped by 28.6% on October 30, erasing around $140 billion of the manufacturer's market capitalization, after the chipmaker issued Q4 revenue and earnings projections that fell short of expectations and warned that the PC market downturn would persist. Meanwhile, despite the massive sell-off, Intel's shares have gained 62% since the beginning of the year.

Industry observers note that the lawsuit seeks unspecified damages on behalf of Intel investors who purchased the manufacturer's shares between July 23 and October 29, 2026. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner are also named as defendants.

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Jailbroken PS4 runs 9-billion-parameter AI model at up to 43 tokens per second

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Developer Leonardo Alegría’s open-source project Garlic LLM lets a jailbroken PS4 run the 9-billion-parameter Qwen3.5-9B AI model offline on the console’s 2013-era GPU.
  • It has been revealed that the project, named after the memory the GPU reads directly — its sibling memory type is “Onion” — relies on a PS4 running GoldHEN, which is a homebrew enabler for exploited consoles.
  • Sources indicate that it’s capable of voice conversation, with spoken replies in seven languages through the Chatterbox speech model and the chat model running at about 22 tokens per second.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developer Leonardo Alegría’s open-source project Garlic LLM lets a jailbroken PS4 run the 9-billion-parameter Qwen3.5-9B AI model offline on the console’s 2013-era GPU. The app talks to the GPU directly, and the model is shrunk to about 4.5GiB to fit in the console’s memory, running at 31 to 39 tokens per second.

It has been revealed that the project, named after the memory the GPU reads directly — its sibling memory type is “Onion” — relies on a PS4 running GoldHEN, which is a homebrew enabler for exploited consoles. Garlic LLM is a free, single 5.66GB download, available on Hugging Face and installable through the PS4’s Package Installer, with about 6GB free needed, or 12GB if the package is first copied to the console’s internal disk. The developer tested it on a base/Slim PS4 on firmware 11.52.

Sources indicate that it’s capable of voice conversation, with spoken replies in seven languages through the Chatterbox speech model and the chat model running at about 22 tokens per second. A held controller button also lets it take dictation with Nvidia’s Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 speech-to-text model, which supports 25 European languages. Parakeet models also power local transcription and dictation apps such as Meetily and Hex. The main model is Alibaba’s small open-weight Qwen3.5-9B, which, at the claimed 31 to 39 tokens per second in text chat — the prompt and test method are not given — is usable on the console.

According to recent reports, the closest comparison is the PS5LM fork, which runs llama.cpp as a native app on the PS5 and reaches the console’s AMD GPU through PS5_Vulkan, a port of the RADV driver. The open-source llama.cpp is a widely used program for running language models locally, and RADV is the open-source driver that lets AMD GPUs run Vulkan, the graphics and compute API. On the PS4 there is no such driver layer for homebrew; Garlic LLM uses neither llama.cpp nor a Vulkan port, or so it would appear.

The model’s operations, such as matrix multiplies over 4-bit weights, are compute kernels written in OpenCL C and compiled with LLVM for AMD’s Graphics Core Next (GCN) architecture. The weights are kept in that “Garlic” memory, while the CPU side, in plain C, handles the tokenizer, the interface, text rendering, and audio. The pipeline runs from the prompt to the CPU tokenizer, then, for each token, a PM4 command buffer — the low-level commands a graphics driver would normally generate, which, in this case, the app builds itself — and the GCN kernels, before the token is displayed or spoken. The whole thing is built with the open-source OpenOrbis PS4 toolchain.

According to recent reports, one immediate question is how you fit a 9-billion-parameter model in the console’s 8GB of memory, which the CPU and GPU share. At 8 bits per weight, you have one byte per parameter, meaning you’d need at least 9GB, with typically more than that required overall. Part of the answer is 4-bit (“Q4”) weights, which take half as much, although 3-bit (“Q3”) weights, at about 3.5 bits with scales, are used for the two largest matrices in each layer.

Sources indicate that using the combination gets you to about 4.5GiB, versus about 4.9GiB if it were all 4-bit. The attention, or KV, cache is also 4-bit, which lets a 16K-token context fit, in comparison to the model’s native 256K. The Parakeet dictation model adds 0.33GiB and the Chatterbox voice models 0.29GiB and 0.09GiB, for a grand total of 5.23GiB, or 5.62GB, which closely matches the 5.66GB package size.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The next question is performance. Qwen3.5 comes with a multi-token prediction (MTP) head, and Garlic LLM uses it to draft up to two tokens ahead, with the full model verifying. This matches what the model was trained for, and the vLLM instructions on Alibaba’s model card use two speculative tokens. The project credits this for its chat speed on 2013 hardware.

According to recent reports, code also comes out faster with this setup, at up to 43 tokens per second. Also detailed is the default temperature, or model variability, which is 0.7 — Alibaba recommends 0.7 for general tasks with thinking off and 1.0 with it on — although the demo video uses 0, so it is predictable. At 35 tokens per second, the middle of the reported performance range, a 300-token answer takes under nine seconds. As a comparison, the PS5 ran the three-times-larger Qwen3.8-27B at about 20 tokens per second and the smaller Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B at 61 and 124, respectively, which is potentially quicker.

Sources indicate that the PS4 Pro is “not tested yet,” but the developer is asking owners for reports on GitHub. The PS5 is not supported as the app is written specifically for the PS4’s GPU and system software. The app itself contains no exploit, but GoldHEN is installed at the user’s own risk.
