Intel bets on Classiq acquisition to turn Quantum efforts into commercially viable business

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2268 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After having spent more than a decade pursuing quantum computing research, Intel is making its first real push at commercializing its efforts.
  • The key ingredient of that strategy is the pending acquisition of Classiq, which offers a hardware-agnostic quantum software development platform that enables engineers to design, synthesize, optimize, simulate, and execute quantum algorithms using high-level programming tools and AI-assisted automation, essentially untying software design from the complexity of quantum hardware.
  • In a recent development, intel has spent more than a decade developing quantum computing technologies, including silicon spin-qubit processors, cryogenic control electronics, and software for hybrid quantum-classical computing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After having spent more than a decade pursuing quantum computing research, Intel is making its first real push at commercializing its efforts. First, with the pending acquisition of quantum computing manufacturer Classiq, which has an existing list of enterprise customers. Intel says it'll be the only company that can produce qubit chips and cryogenic control electronics at scale; the deal would give it a complete top-to-bottom hardware-to-software stack, and Intel will also gain the chance to become a leading vendor of quantum computing products. Intel's acquisition of Classiq is expected to complete in the first half of 2027.

The key ingredient of that strategy is the pending acquisition of Classiq, which offers a hardware-agnostic quantum software development platform that enables engineers to design, synthesize, optimize, simulate, and execute quantum algorithms using high-level programming tools and AI-assisted automation, essentially untying software design from the complexity of quantum hardware. Meanwhile, Intel also plans to manufacture quantum processors using specialized versions of its 18A process technology, offer foundry services, and eventually sell complete quantum computers. Although the manufacturer expects its quantum business to become profitable, it acknowledges that commercial success will take time.

In a recent development, intel has spent more than a decade developing quantum computing technologies, including silicon spin-qubit processors, cryogenic control electronics, and software for hybrid quantum-classical computing. However, the tech giant has largely treated these activities as research and development projects rather than an actual business. The acquisition of Classiq, which Intel expects to complete in the first half of 2027, marks a shift toward commercialization as Classiq already has many clients and established revenue streams.

"Up until now […] our quantum computing group for the last ten years was […] purely a research and development project," said Pushkar Ranade, chief technology officer at Intel, during a media briefing. "It was not really viewed as a commercial activity.".

Industry observers note that intel's quantum computing journey kicked off in 2015 with a research collaboration with QuTech — the quantum research institute of TU Delft and TNO — to develop quantum computing technologies, including silicon spin qubits. The idea was to leverage Intel's extensive expertise in silicon transistor development and its high-volume semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure to produce quantum processors in the same fabs that make conventional CPUs, overcoming the manufacturing scalability challenges alternative quantum computing architectures faced at the time. Intel subsequently developed Horse Ridge, a cryogenic control SoC manufactured using a 22nm process technology in 2020. Three years later, the firm introduced Tunnel Falls, a 12-qubit silicon spin processor manufactured on a 300mm wafer.

Industry observers note that intel's quantum computing effort focuses on silicon spin qubits, which use spin states of individual electrons to store and manipulate quantum information. The organization chose this approach partly because silicon spin qubits can be manufactured using equipment and processes similar to those employed for conventional semiconductor devices. This compatibility enables Intel to re-use most of its existing manufacturing infrastructure and expertise rather than build dedicated semiconductor fabrication facilities for quantum processors that yet have to become commercial products.

Recent findings suggest that despite the recent cuts at Intel, the manufacturer sustained its quantum computing project. Intel has developed two specialized versions of its 18A manufacturing technology for quantum computing: 18A-Q for silicon spin-qubit processors and 18A-CC for cryogenic control and readout electronics. To define/build 18A-Q, Intel has collaborated with Hitachi, AIST, and NEDO (three major supporters of quantum computing from Japan), and there appears to be a design kit intended to support large quantum computing systems. Without a doubt, 18A-Q and 18A-CC put Intel on the map of quantum computing chips in a massive way. A couple of things should be kept in mind, though.

According to recent reports, "The underlying device that we use, underlying process that we use to make the actual qubit device is a unique process, but it fits into those design rules," Ranade explained. "We can make these chips […] in the same fab that we use to make our CPUs.".

Sources indicate that although Intel 18AQ uses BEOL interconnect geometry and design rules derived from Intel 18A, its underlying qubit devices require a different manufacturing process. According to Ranade, the technology requires a specialized thin-film stack and several additional manufacturing tools. Nevertheless, more than 90% of the manufacturing equipment is identical to that used for conventional semiconductor production, according to Intel.

According to recent reports, "Intel 18A-CC, meanwhile, uses 18A-based geometry but requires additional characterization for operation at cryogenic temperatures," Ranade said. "Crucially, Intel can manufacture quantum processors alongside conventional CPUs in existing semiconductor fabs, which could reduce the capital expenditure required to scale production. […] More than 90% of the process equipment is exactly the same.".

For conventional x86 architectures and IA-64 (while it was active), Intel has historically offered compilers that made software run better on its hardware (and sometimes on AMD hardware too). By contrast, with its quantum computing efforts, Intel has generally focused on hardware and while it has its own Quantum SDK that includes a compiler, this is not enough in the quantum computing realm as Classiq's offering operates at a higher abstraction level. With the acquisition of Classiq, the company intends to fill that gap.

Classiq develops a hardware-agnostic quantum software platform that applies electronic design automation (EDA) principles to quantum programming, which lets developers design, synthesize, and optimize quantum algorithms without manually constructing circuits from individual quantum gates. The firm's software provides high-level modeling, automated algorithm synthesis, optimization, debugging, and execution capabilities across different quantum computing architectures, which somewhat resembles Intel's approach to its x86 compilers, albeit working at a different level.

Recent findings suggest that intel already has its Quantum SDK, which includes a C++-based compiler, runtime environment, and simulator for hybrid quantum-classical applications. Classiq's platform will sit above these tools and provide an application-development environment for programmers who lack extensive expertise in quantum computing.

Intel compares the potential significance of Classiq's software layer to Microsoft's MS-DOS, which helped establish the personal computer software ecosystem; Nvidia's CUDA, which enabled developers to exploit GPUs for general-purpose accelerated computing; and EDA tools, which abstracted high-level design descriptions from the complexities of transistor-level integrated circuit implementation and essentially set the stage for the multi-billion foundry industry today.

Furthermore, unlike Intel's quantum hardware business, Classiq already has commercial customers and generates revenue. The tech giant employs approximately 130 people and serves more than 50 enterprise customers, including BMW, Comcast, Lufthansa, Rolls-Royce, and Toshiba. It also participates in more than 10 national quantum computing programs and supports over 50 quantum processors and simulators.

Industry observers note that as existing quantum processors remain insufficient for many practical applications, companies can develop and optimize software ahead of hardware availability. As a result, these customers primarily use Classiq products to develop quantum algorithms, train engineers, and create intellectual property in preparation for commercially useful quantum computers.

Intel's CTO described Classiq's revenue and anticipated growth as healthy, but did not disclose actual financial figures.

Sources indicate that "They have a very healthy revenue this year and a very healthy revenue CAGR over the coming years," Ranade remarked. "We hope that… we want that to continue.".

It is necessary to note that Intel intends to preserve Classiq's hardware-agnostic approach, which means allowing the firm to continue supporting quantum processors and simulators from competing vendors. This is essential to maintain Classiq's existing customer relationships and expand its revenue opportunities, as its clients can/will be able to develop quantum applications without committing to a particular hardware architecture. Obviously, Intel can generate software revenue regardless of which quantum computing technologies ultimately become commercially successful.

"We very much want to maintain that hardware-agnostic platform that they have developed to attract more and more customers," Ranade said.

According to recent reports, when it comes to quantum computing, Intel's ambitions extend beyond manufacturing silicon spin-qubit processors. The tech giant intends to become a supplier of complete quantum computing systems, which would combine quantum processors, cryogenic control electronics, classical computing resources, and software. For now, Intel has most of the building blocks required to develop complete quantum computing systems, but it still has to demonstrate that it can integrate them into commercially viable quantum computing at scale.

"We want to be in the business of building quantum foundry components, but also complete quantum systems," mentioned Pushkar Ranade, chief technology officer at Intel.

Intel is also considering opportunities to provide quantum foundry services to other hardware developers. While its internal processor development will remain focused on silicon spin qubits, the manufacturer is open to manufacturing components for alternative quantum computing technologies, which somewhat resembles its approach to its x86 CPU and foundry businesses.

Recent findings suggest that "We are committed to spin qubits," Ranade said. "But we are also open to providing foundry services to other modalities.".

Intel believes that its capabilities in photonics, advanced packaging, and semiconductor manufacturing could become commercially relevant even to companies developing quantum processors based on different physical principles than silicon qubits.

Sources indicate that intel's decision to expand its quantum computing activities with the takeover of Classiq comes as chief executive Lip-Bu Tan emphasized profitability, financial discipline, and high-margin products across the company’s established businesses. Given that Intel's quantum computing initiative barely generates any revenue, let alone profits, the CEO stance raises questions about the viability of quantum computing for Intel, especially in a situation where the industry has yet to demonstrate widespread practical applications that justify the cost of large-scale quantum hardware.

When asked how Intel’s quantum computing strategy fits Tan's profitability requirements, Ranade explained that the manufacturer's immediate financial priorities primarily concern its established client and server processor businesses. Nevertheless, Intel must continue investing in emerging technologies that could shape future computing markets.

According to recent reports, "This is really a bet on the future," Ranade mentioned. "This is something we also have to do in addition to our mainstream businesses today.".

Recent findings suggest that the Intel CTO acknowledged that quantum computing is not set to become a high-margin business in the near future. Meanwhile, the acquisition of Classiq gives Intel an established commercial software operation and revenue stream here and now, as well as an opportunity to expand customer relationships well before its own quantum processors reach commercial maturity. Intel also hopes that combining its hardware and software capabilities (probably including Classiq) will attract customers interested in complete quantum computing solutions.

When asked whether vertical integration would make Intel's quantum computing operations profitable, Ranade acknowledged that he could not predict gross margins of the quantum computing business because the industry is still in its infancy. Nevertheless, he expressed confidence in the commercial prospects of Intel's quantum hardware and software.

"I expect it to become a profitable business very swiftly on the hardware side, but too early to tell," Ranade stated.

According to recent reports, even though quantum processors evolve at a rapid pace, the technology is unlikely to replace existing CPUs and GPUs for conventional computing any time soon. Instead, Intel expects quantum computing systems to operate alongside the usual processors in data centers and supercomputing environments.

Sources indicate that classiq's software platform will provide high-level quantum algorithm development capabilities, while Intel Quantum SDK will handle compilation, simulation, and hybrid quantum-classical execution. This approach differs from Nvidia's CUDA-Q, which is designed to integrate quantum computing workflows with existing accelerated computing infrastructure. According to Classiq chief executive Nir Minerbi, Classiq operates at a higher level of abstraction and can complement CUDA-Q rather than compete with it.

"CUDA Q is very much low-level; it is gate-level. It is a good platform, by the way, but it is very low-level," said Minerbi. "The reason companies like Rolls-Royce and BMW and others use the Classiq platform on top of CUDA Q is due to the level of abstraction. It is much, much easier to develop quantum programs with Classiq and then to simulate it with CUDA Q rather than only with CUDA Q.".

In a recent development, meanwhile, commercial success of quantum computing still depends on substantial advances in quantum hardware, including qubit scalability, error correction, control electronics, and system integration. For now, many Classiq customers are developing applications for quantum computers that have yet to reach the scale required for commercially valuable workloads.

Intel expects to complete its acquisition of Classiq in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. The company has not disclosed the purchase price or other financial terms.

Industry observers note that the transaction will bring Classiq's software development capabilities and established customer relationships into Intel's quantum computing organization, but will preserve the platform's compatibility with competing hardware technologies. For Intel, the acquisition represents an opportunity to turn more than a decade of quantum computing research into a commercial business unit as it will have all the building blocks required to create quantum systems. Furthermore, Intel's quantum computing business will be open to third parties in the sense that Intel will be able to build quantum processors for partners using its 18AQ and 18ACC process technologies.

Whether Intel's quantum computing business eventually delivers the high margins Intel seeks will depend not only on Intel's ability to build systems, produce quantum chips for others, or Classiq's software revenue, but also on the industry's ability to develop quantum processors and systems capable of solving real-world problems that people are willing to pay for.

In a Facebook post titled “WANTED: ONE MORE DAY OF PATIENCE,” the school urged students to treat attending classes as their final side quest before GTA 6 arrives.

“We know many of our students will be counting down the days until the highly anticipated release of the GTA video game on Thursday,” the school wrote.

Instead, it declared a special one-day attendance challenge, with every student who attends and completes the school day entered into a draw for a £65 (around $85 USD) Amazon voucher.

“That’s the equivalent value of a copy of GTA… just for turning up to school and completing your Thursday mission,” the school explained.

“No cheats. No shortcuts. No skipping cut-scenes. Just one day of attendance for a chance to win.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the battery on the Pixel Tag is rated for about a year, but what happens when you need to replace it? Here’s how to replace it.

Due to the shape and design of the Pixel Tag, you might have a bit of difficulty getting the backplate off swiftly to throw in a new battery when it’s time.

Having had a few problems myself (yes, a me problem most likely) due to the slick, smooth shape, I figured that, even though it might insult the intelligence of many, the process was at least documented so that anyone having problems has a reference to come to if they’re struggling to get that backplate off.

You will have difficulty if you try to do this one-handed. Instead, clasp the Pixel Tag with one thumb at the base or midframe, then with your other thumb twist anticlockwise until the backplate comes loose and the battery will drop out.

The first time you do this, it will be harder due to the tight factory seal. However, once it’s open, the process gets easier to replicate. Here’s a little demonstration of how to get it off without it slipping and being flung into the ether:.

Be aware that you may need to open and reseat the battery if Find Hub does not recognize the Pixel Tag again when you’ve done this. Even with the factory-supplied battery, it can misalign if you don’t place it in the correct position and fully close the door when reassembling.

If you’re wondering what type of battery you need, CR2032 are the standard for watches and most Android trackers. They’re super cheap with a 10-pack of Amazon Basics batteries for just $10, Duracell offers a 4-pack for under $7 but you can even get unbranded 20-packs for around $9. All fairly cheap at various points in the quality spectrum.

Sources indicate that it can’t hurt to have some on hand when you do eventually need to replace the battery in your Pixel Tag. You can get the tracker from Amazon and the Google Store right now.

According to recent reports, with 250+ client engagements across both agency and embedded in-house roles, Vitalii Khomenko has seen product teams from the inside in a way few designers have. Here he makes the case for a new kind of design workflow built for the AI era, and explains why the window to adapt is narrower than most founders think.

For the last decade, every startup conversation about speed eventually became a conversation about engineering. Hiring more developers, cutting scope, choosing a simpler stack, it was almost always a dev-side problem. Vitalii Khomenko, Principal Designer at Orizon Design and founder of Fluente LLC, argues that's no longer true. And he has a specific view on what teams should do instead.

What makes Khomenko's perspective worth taking seriously isn't just seniority. It's the specific shape of his experience. Over a career spanning 250+ client engagements, he has worked both as an external specialist brought in to deliver and as an embedded designer who became the single connective thread between product, brand, and execution. That dual vantage point is rare. Most designers live on one side of that line. Khomenko has operated extensively on both, which gives him an unusually clear read on where friction actually originates inside product teams, and where it doesn't.

It has been revealed that his work spans early-stage startups finding their first visual language and established brands managing complex, multi-disciplinary design systems. Across that range, certain patterns repeat. And the pattern that started becoming impossible to ignore this year pointed him toward a conclusion that is reshaping how he thinks a modern design workflow should actually be structured.

The bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved. And the workflow needs to move with it.

When shipping code was slow, the existing design workflow made sense. Multiple rounds of revision, user testing, iteration, all of that fit naturally into the window while engineering caught up. That window is now gone, and most design workflows were never updated to reflect it.

Sources indicate that "Founders are asking design teams to move at the same speed as an AI-assisted dev pipeline, and design doesn't compress the same way code does," Khomenko notes. The result is a workflow that was built around a constraint that no longer exists, applied to a pipeline that has fundamentally changed around it.

The forced choice between polish and speed that product teams are now navigating isn't fresh as a concept. What's new is how stark it has become, and how directly it traces back to a workflow problem rather than a people problem. "Because development is cheap and fast now, there's constant pressure to ship the next thing immediately," he explains. "But the products that actually retain people are still the ones where the details were considered carefully. Fewer revision rounds isn't a process improvement if it means shipping avoidable friction.".

In a recent development, khomenko has watched this play out across enough teams, at enough stages, to be specific about where the existing workflow breaks down. The problem isn't design judgment. It's where that judgment sits in the process, and what format it's expected to produce at the end.

To understand Khomenko's proposed fix, it helps to understand exactly where the current workflow stalls. For most product teams, the end of the design process looks like this: a designer produces polished, dev-ready screens inside Figma, and hands that file to engineering. Engineering then interprets those screens, translates the visual decisions into code, and builds from there.

Sources indicate that that translation step, Figma file to working code, is where the pipeline now breaks down. AI-assisted engineering has made the building part dramatically faster. But the translation step hasn't changed. An engineer still has to read a Figma file, interpret spacing, extract assets, make judgment calls about component structure, and write the implementation from scratch. That process takes the same amount of time it always did.

"The manual workflow inside Figma simply isn't keeping up with AI-boosted engineering," Khomenko says. "The design handoff is quietly becoming the thing everyone is waiting on.".

It has been revealed that the result is a pipeline where everything around the handoff has accelerated, and the handoff itself has become the single point of drag. Figma, in other words, was built for a world where engineering was the slow part. It wasn't designed to feed a pipeline where engineering moves at AI speed.

This is the core of what Khomenko is proposing, and it's a more significant structural shift than it might first appear.

In his workflow, Figma doesn't disappear. It moves. Rather than serving as both the exploration environment and the final delivery artifact, Figma becomes the visual exploration layer exclusively: the place where brand identity is established, layout logic is worked through, and design direction is validated. It remains the right tool for figuring out what something should look and feel like.

Recent findings suggest that but the final delivery, the artifact that actually goes to engineering, is code. Specifically, components built into prepared libraries that engineering can work from and scale directly, without any translation step in between.

Sources indicate that the difference in implementation speed is the point. When a designer delivers a coded component library rather than a Figma file, engineering doesn't need to interpret anything. The decisions are already expressed in the language they're building in. What previously required an engineer to read, interpret, and re-create from a visual reference now arrives ready to use. In a pipeline running on AI-assisted development, that difference compounds fast.

Sources indicate that "Figma is still the right place to explore what something should look and feel like," Khomenko notes. "But handing over a Figma file and asking engineering to implement it is now the slow path. Delivering in code is the fast path. That's the shift.".

Executing this workflow requires a different kind of designer, and Khomenko is direct about that. The UI/UX designer becoming a Design Engineer is, in his assessment, not a distant possibility. It is a matter of time, and the teams treating it as a future consideration rather than a present reality are the ones most likely to find themselves stuck at the handoff.

But Khomenko is equally clear about what this shift doesn't mean. Delivering in code is one part of the role, not the whole of it. The full design cycle isn't going anywhere. Applying branding to imagery, producing animations, building marketing materials, these remain essential creative tasks that require a broad and varied toolkit well beyond code. "The designer of the near future isn't just generating code," he says. "They're moving across the full cycle, brand, motion, marketing, product, with design engineering as an key and growing part of that stack, not a replacement for it.".

Industry observers note that what changes is that code-ready delivery becomes a core expectation within that stack. The designer who can move fluidly from visual exploration in Figma to component delivery in code, while also carrying the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level consumers actually experience, is the profile that the newly introduced workflow demands.

It has been revealed that khomenko is candid that no single version of this workflow has fully standardized yet. Every team is figuring it out differently. The tools are evolving, the handoff expectations are shifting, and the processes teams are building around all of it vary considerably. There is no off-the-shelf playbook.

But this is precisely where his 250+ engagements become more than a credential. They're a dataset. Having watched enough teams, at enough stages, through enough cycles of tooling change, Khomenko can see through the noise of individual variation and identify what's directionally true even when the specifics are still in flux. "Each team's workflow is really custom at this stage," he claims. "But some general patterns of how this is going to look in the near future are already visible.".

According to recent reports, those patterns consistently point in the same direction: design judgment moving earlier, final delivery moving into code, and the designer's role expanding in technical range while staying broad in creative scope. The exact tools and sequences will keep shifting. The underlying logic of the workflow Khomenko is describing is already taking shape in the teams paying closest attention.

For founders and product leads, the workflow Khomenko is describing has direct implications for how teams are staffed, budgeted, and structured.

Industry observers note that front-load design judgment. The biggest leverage in the new workflow isn't faster execution, it's better problem definition before generation starts. Bring senior design thinking in earlier, when it can shape what gets built rather than polish what's already done.

According to recent reports, separate exploration from delivery. Figma and the visual exploration phase serve a distinct purpose from the final delivery layer. Treat them as separate stages with separate expectations, rather than collapsing them into a single step expected to produce everything.

Recent findings suggest that shift the delivery expectation to code. Whether that means hiring for Design Engineer range, developing it internally, or restructuring handoffs, the end of the design pipeline needs to arrive in a form engineering can work from directly. The translation step is where time goes to die, and it's now the most avoidable part of the process.

Protect the full creative stack. Design engineering matters more than it ever has. It is not, however, the whole job. Teams that reduce design to code generation will lose the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level customers actually experience.

According to recent reports, stay flexible. The workflow is still forming. Teams that build rigidity into their process now will find themselves redoing that work within a year. The teams getting this right are the ones building enough adaptability into their structures to absorb what's still coming.

"The Figma handoff made sense when engineering was the slow part," Khomenko says. "Engineering isn't the slow part anymore. Delivering in code isn't the future of design workflow. For the teams paying attention, it's already the present.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Supercomputing 2026 conference is under way, and despite continuing turmoil elsewhere in the company, Nvidia has lots to reveal at the show.
  • To accelerate those most demanding workloads, Nvidia states Rubin HPC has the highest number of CUDA cores on any of its GPUs - "more than 50,000" - which might imply that this chip uses a configuration similar to the four-die Rubin Ultra GPU, which links those dies together using NVLink-C2C.
  • Today's Rubin GPU has 224 SMs and 28,672 CUDA cores, so scaling compute resources to the degree Rubin HPC does would necessarily require more dies on a package.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Supercomputing 2026 conference is under way, and despite continuing turmoil elsewhere in the company, Nvidia has lots to reveal at the show. Foremost among its announcements today, Nvidia took the wraps off a new member of the Rubin GPU family called Rubin HPC, a chip that the company says is meant to accelerate agentic workflows and simulation for scientists, engineers, and analysts working with large data sets.

To accelerate those most demanding workloads, Nvidia states Rubin HPC has the highest number of CUDA cores on any of its GPUs - "more than 50,000" - which might imply that this chip uses a configuration similar to the four-die Rubin Ultra GPU, which links those dies together using NVLink-C2C.

Today's Rubin GPU has 224 SMs and 28,672 CUDA cores, so scaling compute resources to the degree Rubin HPC does would necessarily require more dies on a package. Nvidia didn't reveal more details of the chip's physical layout alongside the announcement. (The representative image shared by the manufacturer wouldn't appear to take this into account.).

To keep data moving between Rubin HPC GPUs, Nvidia will use its NVLink 7 interconnect. The company didn't share any new details of the bandwidth or physical layer of this interconnect within the rack, but past disclosures about the tech have indicated that it retains the 3.6 TB/s of per-GPU bandwidth that NVLink 6 delivers while enlarging the size of its scale-up domain.

Nvidia didn't share any details of the Rubin HPC GPU's HBM capacity or bandwidth, and it also didn't share whether this part includes a rebalancing of compute resources towards native FP64, as AMD and Intel are touting at the conference with their own GPUs this week.

Nvidia instead touts the suitability of this chip for scientists and engineers using agentic workflows, for which the manufacturer expects faster simulation performance and therefore faster opportunities for discovery in those fields thanks to better agent performance in those domains.

In fields like climate research, genomic analysis, and financial simulation, Nvidia indicates the Rubin HPC GPU's "balanced design," with both higher compute resources and (presumably) faster data movement between nodes, will help feed the chip with the massive data sets typical of those workloads, minimizing idle compute resources and achieving better utilization.

Researchers, engineers, and analysts marshaling agent swarms to explore the problem spaces in their domains will also be able to take advantage of Nvidia's CUDA-X domain-specific libraries to boost performance on Rubin HPC, tightening the reasoning loop from hypothesis to simulation to refinement and hastening the pursuit of the most promising results.

Nvidia says Rubin HPC will arrive sometime in 2028.

Sources indicate that as the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

Shark Tank investor and businessman Kevin O’Leary is at odds with Gen Z, who say building wealth and success is harder for their generation than it was for his. In Jubilee Media’s latest Surrounded video—an online series where a single public figure faces 25 individuals with opposing viewpoints—O’Leary, known as “Mr. Wonderful,” takes on a slate of questions regarding success and wealth. But it’s one particular conversation in the nearly two-hour-long video that has gained traction on social media. When the discussion turned to O’Leary’s assertion that “if you want to be successful, work-life balance comes second,” one participant pushed back on how realistic that advice is today. “We used to have work-life balance—we don’t have that anymore,” one of the participants told O’Leary. “My question to you is, how do you believe that our generation is supposed to be successful and have a work-life balance if we can’t even afford what success would look like, which is owning a home and not being straddled by student loans and medical debt.” O’Leary rapidly replied, “Every single generation has had whiners like you in it. Each generation is surprised to find out things change in the economy all the time.” Twenty years ago, O’Leary continued, a liberal arts or humanities degree could be considered an “economic disaster,” whereas today, videographers and storytellers are “making anywhere from $200,000 to $400,000 working for corporations.” ‘The kids . . . have totally given up’ As the clip made the rounds on social media, some agreed with O’Leary’s stance on the matter, echoing the age-old claim that younger generations are less willing to work than their older counterparts. “Not a huge Kevin O’Leary guy, but the kids he’s speaking with have totally given up. They need to keep pushing, they break through or change careers,” one user said on X. But for most, Mr. Wonderful’s comments came across as disconnected from reality. “With a straight face, Kevin said “photographers, videographers are making $200-$400k a year.” Out of touch doesn’t even begin to describe this guy’s ignorance,” one user replied on YouTube. “Kevin O’Leary needs to go walk in the shoes of a middle-class American for a week. He has no idea what he’s talking about,” another added on X. For others, the conversation further highlighted the tensions between generations. A user on X added: “Kevin’s generation got theirs, bought houses cheap, got money to build businesses, got cheap college, then changed the rules to fuck every other generation after them.” The video and the discourse surrounding it also pointed to a larger problem: Neither side can reach consensus. A user added: “Problem is, the truth is somewhere in the middle of both tales being told, and nobody wants to acknowledge that their respective sides are both overstating the opposing ends of the equation.”.

Grindr boss George Arison has defended the platform’s $120 premium subscription tier, noting it is only aimed at a “small” portion of their consumers.

At this point, pretty much every dating app offers a premium subscription for people who are struggling to find love. These bonuses come at a cost, typically giving you unlimited swipes and better matches along the way.

In a recent development, however, Edge rapidly came under fire online after users of the world’s biggest LGBTQ dating app noted that it could cost up to $6,000 to use it for the year. Some screenshots indicated the price ranging from $80 to $499.99 per month.

Speaking to the BBC, Grindr’s George Arison noted that the premium AI-powered subscription was aimed at a “very small community of users” to offer them a “very different” experience on the app.

“I think we’re a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not,” the Grindr CEO added.

The price of the subscription has settled at $120 per month, but Arison noted that it could increase in the future. He told the BBC that Edge users “being willing to pay more for that set of features will result in us being able to subsidise the product for everybody else. It’s a choice that people make on whether they want to be on it.”.

Industry observers note that as noted, other apps have expensive premium services too. Tinder debuted a $499 subscription of its own called Tinder Select back in 2023.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it might finally be happening. A new Google Voice patch plants seeds of RCS support, though the exact details remain unclear.

It has been revealed that about APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.

Google Voice is an invaluable tool for accessing one phone number across a host of different devices, but to say it’s becoming less impactful without support for RCS is a bit of an understatement. Now that virtually every Android phone and iPhone supports the latest messaging experience, Google Voice is less useful both for business and consumer users.

Google Voice for Android version 2026.11.01.1014278023 doesn’t enable RCS, but it does, for the first time, actually hint that the functionality might be on its way. In a teardown of the app, one simple string stands out:.

That points to a latest send button used for RCS messages rather than SMS. Google Messages similarly changes its send button to differentiate between the two standards.

This is great news. I can have both options now to text friends and businesses with RCS as a fallback option on Google Voice because I don't want to give out my Google messages number.

This upgrade contains a host of other fresh strings around images, videos, and more, but none of them are directly tied to RCS support.

The folks over at Android Authority dug up some other tidbits about RCS including an “RCS chat preference” toggle and various RCS actions and messages. But, again, nothing is live just yet, and there’s no word on when it might arrive, if ever.

Google has been championing RCS support for over a decade now, so it’s long past due for Voice, a long-running Google product, to get on board. While the tidbits in this update don’t serve as any confirmation RCS if coming to Voice, it’s the most exciting update on the matter in years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the coming of SC26, also comes a fresh edition of the TOP500 list, which ranks the world's most powerful supercomputers. The newly released list illustrates that AMD powers 40% of the list, up 14% compared to 2025. AMD-powered systems now tally up to 202 on the list, up from 177 last year. New to the list is Lux, a “SI + HPC supercomputer” developed by AMD and the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), which debuted at position 14.

Sources indicate that AMD’s representation in the top 10 is familiar. After debuting in June, China’s LineShine remains in the top slot. El Capitan, powered by AMD chips, is in the second slot, followed by Frontier in third, HPC7 in sixth, and HPC6 in eighth, the same as the most recent TOP500 list.

Lux was declared a little over a year ago in a $1 billion deal between the DOE and AMD to develop two supercomputers. This is the first of the two, and the first time it’s been on the TOP500. The system was built by HPE and developed by AMD and DOE as part of the U.S. government’s Genesis Mission. The machine is housed in Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF), alongside machines like Frontier.

According to recent reports, lux relies on over 4,000 Instinct MI355X GPUs separated into over 500 nodes. For HPC workloads using FP64, the machine is capable of 317 PetaFLOPS. For AI training, the machine peaks at 20 ExaFLOPS of FP8, and for inference, 40 ExaFLOPS of FP4. With 288 GB of HBM3E per GPU, the entire system has access to 1.1 PB.

The machine uses AMD EPYC host CPUs — we weren’t able to find details on the specific generation— and AMD’s Pensando networking, with nodes built inside HPE’s ProLiant Compute XD685.

LingKun, LX2 304C 1.55GHz, LingQi, Kylin OS.

HPE Cray EX255a, AMD 4th Gen EPYC 24C 1.8GHz, AMD Instinct MI300A, Slingshot-11, TOSS.

HPE Cray EX235a, AMD Optimized 3rd Generation EPYC 64C 2GHz, AMD Instinct MI250X, Slingshot-11, HPE Cray OS.

HPE Cray EX - Intel Exascale Compute Blade, Xeon CPU Max 9470 52C 2.4GHz, Intel Data Center GPU Max, Slingshot-11.

BullSequana XH3000, GH Superchip 72C 3GHz, NVIDIA GH200 Superchip, Quad-Rail NVIDIA InfiniBand NDR200, RedHat Enterprise Linux.

HPE Cray EX255a, AMD 4th Gen EPYC 24C 1.8GHz, AMD Instinct MI300A, Slingshot-11, RHEL 9.

Microsoft NDv5, Xeon Platinum 8480C 48C 2GHz, NVIDIA H100, NVIDIA Infiniband NDR.

HPE Cray EX235a, AMD Optimized 3rd Generation EPYC 64C 2GHz, AMD Instinct MI250X, Slingshot-11, RHEL 8.9.

Supercomputer Fugaku, A64FX 48C 2.2GHz, Tofu interconnect D.

HPE Cray EX254n, NVIDIA Grace 72C 3.1GHz, NVIDIA GH200 Superchip, Slingshot-11, HPE Cray OS.

The machine has 3.5 million node-hours (one node running for one hour) per year, half of which are reserved for Genesis Mission research. Genesis Mission was established through an executive order in November 2025 with the stated goal of creating a “dedicated, coordinated national effort to unleash a latest age of AI‑accelerated innovation and discovery that can solve the most challenging problems of this century.”.

More specifically, the order lays out training scientific foundation models on Federal datasets, and creating “AI agents to test new hypotheses, automate research workflows, and accelerate scientific breakthroughs.” Lux is the first dedicated supercomputer for the Genesis Mission, but it joins existing machines that have been at least partially dedicated to research, including the Intel-powered Aurora at Argonne National Laboratory, which arrived fourth in the most recent TOP500.

Lux is built primarily for AI research, not as a successor to Frontier. Discovery is on track to debut as a next-gen flagship exascale supercomputer in 2028, also developed jointly by the DOE, AMD, and HPE.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

The FAA’s ground stop has a simple culprit. Its causes may not

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Friday afternoon, L3Harris Technologies was doing what it has done at Federal Aviation Administration facilities month after month: moving a communications line off decades-old copper and onto fiber, work that federal auditors count as part of a $12.5 billion overhaul of the country’s air traffic control system.
  • On Friday afternoon, L3Harris Technologies was doing what it has done at Federal Aviation Administration facilities month after month: moving a communications line off decades-old copper and onto fiber, work that federal auditors count as part of a $12.5 billion overhaul of the country’s air traffic control system.
  • Shortly after a technician installed a latest router at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, the device began pumping out data—so much that the flood disrupted communications at 17 of the 22 so-called en route centers that handle high-altitude traffic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Friday afternoon, L3Harris Technologies was doing what it has done at Federal Aviation Administration facilities month after month: moving a communications line off decades-old copper and onto fiber, work that federal auditors count as part of a $12.5 billion overhaul of the country’s air traffic control system. Shortly after a technician installed a new router at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, the device began pumping out data—so much that the flood disrupted communications at 17 of the 22 so-called en route centers that handle high-altitude traffic. At 3:36 p.m. Eastern, with about 3,500 planes in the air, the FAA held all departures nationwide. The stop lasted more than four hours, until 8:15 p.m. Airlines canceled more than 5,000 flights by Saturday and about 1,500 more on Sunday as they repositioned crews and aircraft. It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the system that sends safety notices to pilots failed. “We haven’t determined what the fault was,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy mentioned at a Saturday news conference. Investigators are trying to establish whether L3Harris installed or configured the router incorrectly, or whether the equipment itself was at fault. Adam Bauer, a spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns router maker Juniper Networks, told Fast Company its devices appeared to have worked as intended. “Based on what we know and have been told by others, our equipment was working as configured.” But the failure exposed weaknesses the FAA has been warned about for years: a contractor that has run the FAA’s network since 2002 and has a record of outages, an integrator the agency’s own staff rated a financial risk, a technician workforce the FAA admits is understaffed, and a $12.5 billion overhaul that auditors say is racing ahead without a master schedule. There is no evidence yet that any of them caused Friday’s failure. Still, some critics see Friday’s chaos as years of warnings come true. “The sad fact is this has happened before,” Mary Schiavo, a former Transportation Department inspector general, told NPR’s Weekend Edition. The sprawling network of copper and fiber that carries the country’s air traffic communications across roughly 4,400 FAA sites still runs largely on technology that dates back decades. Some older equipment, including radar, requires replacement parts that can only be obtained through online auction websites or made with 3D printers. In 2023, an FAA-commissioned panel of outside experts warned that the condition of the agency’s facilities and equipment was “elevating system risk to unsustainable levels.” The agency under President Joe Biden had commissioned another group of aviation experts to examine air traffic control in October 2024, but weeks after Trump took office, the group learned it was being disbanded, The Washington Post reported. Last May, Duffy said the FAA was speeding up its overhaul of the system under a program called BNATCS, or the Brand New Air Traffic Control System. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the effort, which aims to modernize the telecom network by the end of 2028, before the end of Trump’s term, and 21 months ahead of an earlier September 2030 target. In September, the Government Accountability Office released its latest report on the overhaul. The FAA was moving at an unprecedented speed, auditors said, but without a reliable lifecycle cost estimate or an integrated master schedule. Instead, auditors counted 11,389 separate project schedules that had not been coordinated, so different programs were booked to visit the same sites repeatedly or in ways that risk “excessive disruptions to air traffic control operations” and could jeopardize the FAA’s “aggressive deployment schedule.” Delays, in turn, could leave controllers reliant on outdated systems that are prone to failure, and “lead to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, and safety incidents.” The GAO auditors also found the agency had exempted the effort from nearly all of its standard acquisition rules. Schedule pressure on federal programs can lead teams to skip or compress testing, they warned. “In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions,” the GAO wrote. The incident has also drawn attention to Peraton, the Herndon, Va.-based defense contractor hired last December to manage the broader overhaul, under a contract with a $1.5 billion ceiling. Politico reported in June that one lobbyist—a former Duffy spokesperson who sits on the board of a nonprofit linked to the Transportation Secretary—lobbied for Peraton in the period when it won its FAA contract. (The FAA has said that Duffy played no role in the company’s selection.) By August, FAA officials were frustrated with Peraton’s performance, according to a September Politico report, citing people familiar with the matter who described slipping schedules and a contractor that was not managing the project. Peraton was “not sophisticated with how the FAA works” and was being asked to sprint from the start, one person told Politico. The same person said the FAA was partly to blame, accusing the agency of blocking Peraton’s efforts to work with its own staff. As the FAA began its investigation into the cause of the router concerns on Saturday, Schiavo told NPR that uncoordinated schedules and a rush to patch the system had made such a failure predictable. “What did the GAO conclude? That it will result in air traffic outages and disruptions. And there we are.” The FAA and L3Harris take different approaches to scheduling  The trouble first showed up as interruptions at the FAA’s Indianapolis center, as a surge of data flooded the network’s older routers. A flurry of erratic radar feeds and communication drop-offs with aircraft led officials to order a ground stop. Soon troubleshooters traced the glitch to the El Dorado router and to a second one at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas; when both were cut off from the network, the problems stopped. Officials have zeroed in on a feature on the new Juniper routers that broadcast data more widely than necessary. The FAA has since switched the feature off on all of its Juniper routers. The two suspect routers are being tested in Florida with help from Juniper and Cisco engineers, L3Harris and the FBI. “Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration?” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford asked on Saturday, adding that the agency would have to rethink how it carries out upgrades. Asked why the work was done on a busy Friday afternoon, Duffy cited the urgency of the upgrades and said the site was far from major flight corridors. But he added: “there will be a reevaluation of when we do this work.”  The timing contrasts with how L3Harris describes its own method. In an interview published in March, Chris Collings, the L3Harris vice president who runs the business, said the company never switches network segments off. At critical sites with two paths, he said, crews upgrade one path, validate it, then upgrade the other, during low-traffic windows. The network is designed to contain a local fault, so why one remote radio site could disrupt most of the country’s en route centers remains unexplained. Duffy repeatedly blamed the contractor. “We’re going to hold people accountable,” he said, adding that many contractors “take our money and provide really poor service.” He also told reporters he was “stuck with L3Harris.”  In a statement, L3Harris said it was supporting the agency’s investigation, and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” The FAA said that one of its representatives helped an L3Harris technician gain access to an agency site on Friday. The union for FAA technicians, however, said its members had no part in the work. Historically, it said in a statement Saturday, contractors have relied on FAA employees to assess risk and coordinate maintenance, but its “technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.”  The FAA has acknowledged that its technician workforce is understaffed and released a workforce plan in May 2026 calling for an increase of at least 750 more certified technicians by 2030. “However, little progress has been made on hiring those new technicians,” the union said. The FAA and L3Harris did not respond to a series of emailed questions for this story. A push to shift from L3Harris to AT&T L3Harris, based in Melbourne, Fla., specializes in defense, but it has run the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network, known as FTI, since its predecessor Harris Corp. won the contract in 2002. The company notes it has already converted 70% of the copper-to-fiber conversion. The agency has had warnings about the network for years, including a failure strikingly like Friday’s. On Nov. 19, 2009, an FTI outage hit 129 air traffic facilities. The inspector general concluded that configuration and procedural errors by Harris caused the outage and delayed restoring service. A Harris engineer had put a new router into service in Los Angeles that carried a configuration error. Even after fixes, the inspector general noted, FAA and Harris officials acknowledged a continuing risk of critical outages. The FAA has since faulted the company publicly. After a September 2025 telecom outage at the Dallas approach-control facility halted flights at both of the city’s major airports for hours, the agency blamed failures in service from local carrier Frontier Communications. It added: “Oversight by L3Harris, an FAA contractor, failed to ensure that redundancies in the system functioned properly.” L3Harris responded that it and the carriers had warned the FAA for years that the circuits needed replacing, but the money never came. This September, a primary circuit serving the Philadelphia approach-control facility failed, and after L3Harris advised switching to a backup fiber line, which turned out to have been cut by a construction crew in New Jersey. About 9,500 U.S. flights were delayed or canceled. “When it fails, we just don’t have the redundancy” of a modern architecture, Bedford said at the time. The FAA is already moving to replace FTI. In August, using waiver authority tied to the modernization program, it made a single, undefinitized award to AT&T to lead the FAA Enterprise Network Services program, FTI’s successor. The award started with a $74.3 million task order for what the FAA expects to be a multibillion-dollar contract lasting up to 15 years. In September, Bedford called for an additional $10.5 billion from Congress for the project. On Saturday, Duffy said that Verizon and Lumen were also “ready to go” on the upgrade. Until that transition is done, L3Harris remains the operator, and the contractor converting the FAA’s copper lines. The FAA network is a small part of a company that has become more central to the administration’s priorities. L3Harris, which reported $21.9 billion in revenue last year, converted a Boeing 747 donated by Qatar into an interim Air Force One this year. It worked against a July 4 deadline that, Democratic senators say, forced it to scale back the usual upgrade package. (The Air Force has said the work would cost less than $400 million; the contract is classified.)  In January, the Pentagon agreed to invest $1 billion in L3Harris’s missile business, which the company aims to spin off—a rare direct federal stake in a major defense supplier. And in July, the Space Force awarded L3Harris up to $955 million to build 18 missile-defense satellites for the Golden Dome shield, bringing its orders for U.S. missile-tracking and defense satellites to at least 70. What the GAO found about the FAA upgrade The GAO’s September report examined the FAA’s upgrade. Of the $12.5 billion Congress allocated, $9 billion is for systems modernization. Telecommunications is one of 13 programs in the overhaul’s first phase: replacing 5,170 copper lines with fiber and moving nearly 30,000 services to Internet Protocol. GAO figures show the program’s estimated cost rising from about $4.75 billion to about $5.91 billion. The auditors’ main findings: There’s no reliable cost estimate. In June the FAA put phase one’s systems work at $10.6 billion, but officials could not produce the analysis behind the figure, telling auditors it would take a tremendous effort to find. The estimate omits government costs, most operating and maintenance costs and all of phase two. The FAA says it needs another $10.8 billion. There’s no master schedule. Peraton, the prime systems integrator, delivered a preliminary integrated master schedule in April. As of May, though, the 11,389 project schedules had not been integrated, which risked inefficiencies and conflicts with airport operations. Officials said loading them all into their scheduling tool “would not be useful or helpful.” The FAA planned to use an artificial intelligence tool to flag conflicts, but as of May it was still being tested and rules for using it had not been set. Rules were waived. In August 2025, Bedford issued a blanket waiver exempting the program from nearly all of the FAA’s acquisition management requirements, including the one that would require a lifecycle cost estimate. The GAO called that a key reason no such estimate exists. The Transportation Department partly agreed with the GAO’s two recommendations: build a reliable lifecycle cost estimate and a detailed integrated master schedule. In its reply, the department said 12 of 13 workstreams, covering over 95 percent of project tasks, were on plan as of July. According to the FAA’s public Modern Skies dashboard, 11 out of 12 programs are at or ahead of plan. The exception is the replacement of analog protocol converters, devices that turn analog signals into digital ones, which stands at 8 percent complete, with just 45 of 69 planned sites completed in the most recent month recorded. The FAA has said it will answer the GAO’s September recommendations in detail within 180 days of the report, a deadline that falls in March. Whose upgrade was it? Bedford tried to separate Friday’s failure from the modernization program. “We’re conflating modernization with this upgrade at this particular facility. We spend $1 billion a year maintaining and sustaining the existing 1980s [legacy] telco network,” Bedford said. “This is not part of the Peraton-FAA $12.5 billion modernization effort.” That contrasts with the GAO’s account, which lists the copper-to-fiber program as part of phase one of the modernization. And according to the GAO, existing program contracts were modified to give Peraton authority to manage the other contractors on the FAA’s behalf. “Peraton, think of them as an extension of me,” Bedford said in April. Peraton was seen as an underdog for the FAA job, in part because it had little prior experience working with the agency. The company itself grew out of the government IT services unit of Harris Corp., L3Harris’ predecessor, which private equity firm Veritas Capital bought and rebranded as Peraton in 2017. Before the FAA award, agency staff had rated the company a high risk for financial instability in an October 2025 presentation to Duffy, Bloomberg reported in September. When agency staff evaluated the bids last year, they graded Peraton and Parsons, which bid alongside IBM, on four technical criteria, according to the presentation. Parsons rated better on three and the same on the fourth. Staff wrote that Peraton’s answers to use cases and direct questions “often focused on matters irrelevant to the discussion topic.” Peraton scored better on past performance, helped by a positive review from NASA. The FAA told Bloomberg that strong ratings from Peraton’s customers, including NASA, were among its reasons for the choice, along with what it called the company’s significant telecommunications experience. The presentation also showed that Peraton sought a higher award fee than Parsons; it is unclear whether that changed later in the process. Politico reported in June that a former Duffy spokesperson, Mark Bednar, who now sits on the board of the nonprofit that paid for Duffy’s road-trip video series, Great American Road Trip Inc., had lobbied for Peraton in the period when it won its FAA contract. At a December 2025 congressional hearing, Bedford said career FAA staff ran the selection without interference from Duffy or Trump. The recommendation went from Bedford to Duffy and then to the president, he said, and Trump demanded a $200 million cut in the fee. Concerns about Peraton’s work have since dogged the program. A few months ago, the FAA called Peraton in and told it to improve its performance, and the company blamed the agency in return, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The FAA has said it hasn’t penalized Peraton or issued the company a formal warning about poor performance. A Peraton spokesperson told Bloomberg in August that the program is on track. But the company said the schedule is among the largest and most complex in government history, covering 330,000 independent projects and half a million dependencies. Peraton did not respond to an inquiry for this story. Duffy used the outage to renew and even scale up his call for Congress to fund the larger telecom modernization effort, arguing the $12.5 billion already allocated is not enough. For weeks, he has been calling for $30 billion in additional funds—with only about $10 billion of that request specifically for air traffic modernization—but during the outage he raised the demand to $50 billion. Bedford said the FAA would review its upgrade protocols. Neither said whether copper-to-fiber cutovers would be paused while investigators work out why and how one router could halt the country’s air traffic. Representative James Walkinshaw (D-Va.), a member of the House Oversight Committee, said on Saturday that Duffy must be questioned by Congress, including about why the work was being conducted “on a busy travel day, as opposed to in the middle of the night where a disruption wouldn’t have been so damaging because they’re rushing.”.

The GAO’s September report examined the FAA’s upgrade. Of the $12.5 billion Congress allocated, $9 billion is for systems modernization. Telecommunications is one of 13 programs in the overhaul’s first phase: replacing 5,170 copper lines with fiber and moving nearly 30,000 services to Internet Protocol. GAO figures show the program’s estimated cost rising from about $4.75 billion to about $5.91 billion.

The auditors’ main findings:.

The Transportation Department partly agreed with the GAO’s two recommendations: build a reliable lifecycle cost estimate and a detailed integrated master schedule. In its reply, the department said 12 of 13 workstreams, covering over 95 percent of project tasks, were on plan as of July. According to the FAA’s public Modern Skies dashboard, 11 out of 12 programs are at or ahead of plan. The exception is the replacement of analog protocol converters, devices that turn analog signals into digital ones, which stands at 8 percent complete, with just 45 of 69 planned sites completed in the most recent month recorded.

The FAA has said it will answer the GAO’s September recommendations in detail within 180 days of the report, a deadline that falls in March.

Bedford tried to separate Friday’s failure from the modernization program. “We’re conflating modernization with this upgrade at this particular facility. We spend $1 billion a year maintaining and sustaining the existing 1980s [legacy] telco network,” Bedford noted. “This is not part of the Peraton-FAA $12.5 billion modernization effort.”.

That contrasts with the GAO’s account, which lists the copper-to-fiber program as part of phase one of the modernization. And according to the GAO, existing program contracts were modified to give Peraton authority to manage the other contractors on the FAA’s behalf. “Peraton, think of them as an extension of me,” Bedford mentioned in April.

Peraton was seen as an underdog for the FAA job, in part because it had little prior experience working with the agency. The company itself grew out of the government IT services unit of Harris Corp., L3Harris’ predecessor, which private equity firm Veritas Capital bought and rebranded as Peraton in 2017.

Before the FAA award, agency staff had rated the company a high risk for financial instability in an October 2025 presentation to Duffy, Bloomberg reported in September. When agency staff evaluated the bids last year, they graded Peraton and Parsons, which bid alongside IBM, on four technical criteria, according to the presentation. Parsons rated better on three and the same on the fourth. Staff wrote that Peraton’s answers to use cases and direct questions “often focused on matters irrelevant to the discussion topic.”.

Peraton scored better on past performance, helped by a positive review from NASA. The FAA told Bloomberg that strong ratings from Peraton’s customers, including NASA, were among its reasons for the choice, along with what it called the tech giant’s significant telecommunications experience. The presentation also showed that Peraton sought a higher award fee than Parsons; it is unclear whether that changed later in the process.

Politico reported in June that a former Duffy spokesperson, Mark Bednar, who now sits on the board of the nonprofit that paid for Duffy’s road-trip video series, Great American Road Trip Inc., had lobbied for Peraton in the period when it won its FAA contract. At a December 2025 congressional hearing, Bedford said career FAA staff ran the selection without interference from Duffy or Trump. The recommendation went from Bedford to Duffy and then to the president, he said, and Trump demanded a $200 million cut in the fee.

It has been revealed that concerns about Peraton’s work have since dogged the program. A few months ago, the FAA called Peraton in and told it to improve its performance, and the company blamed the agency in return, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The FAA has remarked it hasn’t penalized Peraton or issued the company a formal warning about poor performance.

A Peraton spokesperson told Bloomberg in August that the program is on track. But the firm stated the schedule is among the largest and most complex in government history, covering 330,000 independent projects and half a million dependencies. Peraton did not respond to an inquiry for this story.

Recent findings suggest that duffy used the outage to renew and even scale up his call for Congress to fund the larger telecom modernization effort, arguing the $12.5 billion already allocated is not enough. For weeks, he has been calling for $30 billion in additional funds—with only about $10 billion of that request specifically for air traffic modernization—but during the outage he raised the demand to $50 billion. Bedford mentioned the FAA would review its upgrade protocols. Neither said whether copper-to-fiber cutovers would be paused while investigators work out why and how one router could halt the country’s air traffic.

Representative James Walkinshaw (D-Va.), a member of the House Oversight Committee, said on Saturday that Duffy must be questioned by Congress, including about why the work was being conducted “on a busy travel day, as opposed to in the middle of the night where a disruption wouldn’t have been so damaging because they’re rushing.”.

#23624. Today’s leaders. Tomorrow’s bad role models?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Today’s leaders. Tomorrow’s bad role models?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there is a rising generation of students in high school and college who are forming beliefs about how to lead.
  • According to recent reports, there is a rising generation of students in high school and college who are forming beliefs about how to lead.
  • In a recent development, role models are an important part of the way we learn how a complex task should be handled.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there is a rising generation of students in high school and college who are forming beliefs about how to lead. The most prominent examples of leaders in politics, business, and education make me concerned about the future. Role models are an important part of the way we learn how a complex task should be handled. We may adopt the behaviors of role models or react against them, but we internalize a lot of the prominent people around us. I’ll highlight a few of the problems I see and explore some potential solutions. The negative role models Politics has been the source of negative role models for future leaders for a long time. For decades, politicians being interviewed on television repeated talking points that were only vaguely related to the questions they were asked. The support of leaders for complications often depended more on party affiliation than on whether the position would lead to a meaningful benefit. And over the past 10 years, there has been a rise in true mean-spirited rhetoric that has devolved into name calling and insults rather than reasoned discussions of the issues of the day. The last decade has had few inspiring business leaders either. Prominent news stories focus on billionaires who are chasing additional profits while currying favor with leaders who have political power. The heads of AI companies forge ahead with the development of models that require resource-intensive data centers without letting concerns about the economic, social, and environmental costs of the work influence the pace of development of fresh models. University leaders have generally been no better. Many universities around the country have become highly politicized. Some university leaders are so paralyzed by the politics around them that they refuse to make any changes at all. Others push forward changes without bringing the community along with them to achieve their ends and alienate their students, staff, and faculty in the process. None of these are examples of healthy leadership. What is healthy leadership? Ultimately, good leadership involves three key components. Leaders must establish a vision for the future that brings people along with them and inspires them to engage to create that future. Leaders must grapple with the complexity of the world and work to develop solutions to significant problems that chart a course through competing priorities. Finally, leaders must meet the moment in a principled way in which they communicate clearly about the factors that drive the path forward. In politics, one of the differences between campaigning and governing is that campaigns can be one based on emphasizing the negatives of an opponent, while governing requires supporting a course of action that addresses key problems. In an era of perpetual campaigning, it can be difficult to find people who actually embrace a position and see it through. In all aspects of life, there are rarely courses of action that are good for everyone all the time. Instead, everything has tradeoffs. Great leaders recognize those tradeoffs, find a reasonable compromise among them, and then help the people they lead to recognize the value of that particular path. They are also committed to continuous improvement of outcomes even after they implement a change. The path forward To ensure that we have great leaders in the future, we have to acknowledge the absence of great role models at present. Then, there are two significant things we must do. First, we must hold our leaders accountable to be better role models. That should start with our university leaders who are all educators at heart. They must take a step back from the local politics of their position and remember that their actions are being watched and may ultimately be emulated by others. We should also remind our business and political leaders that winning is important, but how you win also matters. Encourage them to do things that send the right message to the people learning from their example. And those of us who teach and write about leadership must also provide a counterweight to the existing role models. If there are key skills that leaders should have that are not easily found among role models, then we must use them as examples of what not to do. We must point out ways that the short-term benefits of poor leadership have long-term negative consequences. As complex as the current moment may seem, the world of the future will be more complicated as the influences of climate change, globalization, artificial intelligence (and a host of other issues) affect the world. We will need leaders who unite us around a vision and take a far different approach than the leaders who dominate the news cycle right now.

#23622. Researchers ‘recognize that AI will never replace HPC,’ notes AMD executive — high-precision workloads will ‘exist for a very long time’ even as AI usage expands
