Researchers ‘recognize that AI will never replace HPC,’ notes AMD executive — high-precision workloads will ‘exist for a very long time’ even as AI usage expands

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, while AI continues to reshape industries across science and mathematics, traditional supercomputing has seemingly taken a back seat.
  • A heterogeneous compute stack brings together quantum, HPC, and AI under one roof, a fleet that AMD is helping pilot at Oak Ridge National Laboratory alongside IBM.
  • FP64 is key for HPC workloads because of its precision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, while AI continues to reshape industries across science and mathematics, traditional supercomputing has seemingly taken a back seat. However, AMD's Scott Tease told Tom's Hardware Premium that most HPC sites “recognize that AI will never replace HPC,” and suggests that building a heterogeneous compute stack is the best path forward to tackle bleeding-edge research, despite Nvidia pushing performance on lower-precision data types higher for AI workloads at the cost of native performance for the vital double-precision FP64 format that’s critical for HPC workloads.

A heterogeneous compute stack brings together quantum, HPC, and AI under one roof, a fleet that AMD is helping pilot at Oak Ridge National Laboratory alongside IBM. Tease is AMD’s corporate vice president of HPC and sovereign AI, who joined the firm earlier this year after more than a decade at Lenovo (and, before that, another 13 years at IBM). We spoke with Tease ahead of SC26 to get a read on the state of HPC, how it intersects with AI, and what’s actually driving the research community in a time when computer chips are driving headlines about international espionage plots.

FP64 is key for HPC workloads because of its precision. FP64 is a hot-button problem, largely due to how Nvidia’s GPUs have progressed over the past two generations. Or rather, how they haven't progressed. Nvidia’s latest Rubin GPU has 33 TFLOPs of FP64 compute, which is lower than the four-year-old H100’s 34 TFLOPs of FP64. For context, AMD’s year-old Instinct MI355X peaks at 78.6 TFLOPs of FP64 compute, while its upcoming HPC-angled MI430X peaks at 288 TFLOPs.

Nvidia has leaned on emulation to drive FP64 performance higher, a tactic that AMD is now pushing back on, but regardless, it’s easy to see why the HPC world could feel left behind in this new AI era. AI is defined by fuzzy, low-precision data formats, which is diametrically opposed to the accuracy of high-precision FP64. And, over the last generations of hardware from the massive green giant that is Nvidia, FP64 performance has seemingly stalled in favor of driving low-precision data formats for AI workloads.

Sources indicate that “Maybe a few years ago, people in HPC might have felt a little threatened by AI because it was taking some of the limelight,” Tease told Tom’s Hardware Premium. “But I think now they’ve come to realize that AI is an essential part of scientific discovery today. It’s just, how are you going to deploy it?”.

It has been revealed that that central question recontextualizes the apparent conflict between AI compute and HPC compute. Tease pointed to researchers spawning dozens of agents to explore viable paths for a given intent, while still leaving the complex simulations for a traditional FP64-driven HPC fleet. “...to try to do that with old approaches where you have islands of CPUs or islands of GPUs or something like that, and they're very different. They're not interconnected. It's just not going to be able to keep up,” Tease stated.

It has been revealed that one of the challenges right now is actually connecting those systems, which is an area AMD is exploring with its recent collaboration with IBM and Oak Ridge National Laboratory to deploy AMD’s “classical” computing stack in the Umbra HPC system alongside IBM’s 129-qubit Quantum Nighthawk quantum computer. The systems will connect to the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, allowing researchers to “explore how integrated quantum, AI, and scientific computing can accelerate scientific discoveries and national security.”.

If the HPC crowd felt slighted by AI, you can imagine how quantum researchers probably feel.

In a recent development, regardless, Tease notes the future of scientific computing looks like a unified fleet that brings together AI, HPC, and quantum. “There [are] going to be a lot of problems where quantum will not be the be-all, end-all. There are some problems like human health, chemistry, where quantum’s going to allow us to do things we really can’t do with classical computing today. So having those things coexist, having them in a single workload, is where we want to get to.”.

Industry observers note that scheduling workloads for HPC is a solved game, with open-source schedulers like Slurm driving much of the TOP500 to properly schedule workloads on supercomputers. Tease described something that goes deeper to connect these systems. “What we want to be able to do is not only do those kinds of ‘where should it go, here or there’ for HPC, we want to figure out when AI could be applied to it, when [GPU acceleration is] appropriate… and also when is it best to go in a quantum environment?”.

The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility is a test bed for figuring out how to hook these systems together properly. The press release explicitly states that it’s a “shared environment to evaluate the architectures, software, and workflows that future hybrid quantum systems will require.” The system is a co-design initiative with IBM, bringing together quantum and classical computing into one system.

With the system, researchers are exploring how to accelerate quantum error correction with classical systems, a critical step in quantum computing to weed out environmental influences. The goal is ultimately to accelerate quantum systems in the Quantum Genesis Q competition, an initiative launched by the U.S. Department of Energy that will provide up to $215 million in funding for quantum research.

It has been revealed that by late 2028, the competition calls for quantum computers “with at least 100 logical qubits that are capable of performing hundreds of millions [of] fault-tolerant operations.” IBM describes the error correction research that will be performed at Oak Ridge as a “key component” in driving toward that goal. Separately, AMD announced last week an investment in quantum outfit PsiQuantum to provide CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs to drive the company’s first fault-tolerant quantum system.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

Industry News: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is GTA 5 without the finesse - so why is the 2004 classic such a strange delight to return to?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a place in Whitewood Estates where a promising stretch of blacktop suddenly gives way to the desert.
  • Sources indicate that it's fitting I guess that GTA San Andreas is such a strange delight to return to.
  • I mainly think of San Andreas these days through the lens of GTA 5, which gives you LA and its surroundings but lets the single city serve as the star.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a place in Whitewood Estates where a promising stretch of blacktop suddenly gives way to the desert. It feels like the road has been erased, a sentence left unfinished. It's quietly strange, a weird bit of urban wrongfooting. But I guess it makes some kind of sense. California, after all, is home to California City, a town that was planned and then never really built. It sits out there now, north of Los Angeles, streets laid out but slowly being eaten by the sand and dirt. Still, 14,000 people lived there as of 2018. Design limitation or something stranger, this digital dead end is a reminder that all of this land, so modern, so ancient - all of this is spook country.

Sources indicate that it's fitting I guess that GTA San Andreas is such a strange delight to return to. As I've waited, like everyone else, for GTA 6, I've been back here in the GTA games of the past, via the slightly dodgy remasters from a few years ago. And what's come through for me, spending a few idle mornings messing around in San Andreas, a game I thought I knew pretty well, is how beautifully odd everything is now. The best part of 20 years have given a game that once strained against its host technology a genuine aesthetic. Surprisingly sparse in detailing, as angular and sheer as dream architecture, in love with expanses, San Andreas is perfectly placed, it seems to me, to capture just how weird California can be.

California and Nevada. This is the part I always forget. I mainly think of San Andreas these days through the lens of GTA 5, which gives you LA and its surroundings but lets the single city serve as the star. It has a bigger footprint than the earlier game, sure, but it uses that space to go deep on the detailing and the sense of a singular, fiercely specific place. San Andreas meanwhile offers three cities - and one of them isn't actually in California. Alongside spins on LA and San Francisco, you get a version of Las Vegas. It's quite neat really: the three points of some arcane spiritual triangle. The kind of thing Marvel Whiteside Parsons, aerospace engineer and Actual Wizard, might have scratched in the dust of his backyard to help him control the weather. He lived - and died - in Pasadena, so all this would have been familiar anyway.

In a recent development, there is a classic moment in every GTA. A moment where the map opens up in the early games, or when you explore enough in the later games, and simply get to understand the audacity of what is being attempted here. In San Andreas, and this feels apt, the best way to have this moment is to break the rules, sneaking into the open map before the game is fully ready for you. An early mission allows you to step away from the critical path, as it were, and peg it to the airport in Los Santos, where a plane is waiting to be pinched. Taxi, feel the thrust, and you're off. LA beneath you - sorry, Los Santos - and on the horizon a dinkytown version of the Golden Gate Bridge and the MGM Grand.

Recent findings suggest that dinkytown is the word. From the sky, the huge map of San Andreas, which still feels like an incredible piece of work - such ambition! - can look like toys laid out on a duvet in the remasters. Coming back from GTA 5, a masterpiece of texture, the cities of San Andreas in particular feel very weird - cramped and condensed and wonderfully stagey, arranged the way a kid might jury-rig them together from shoeboxes and stray cardboard. On your way out of Grove Street early on you pass the Los Santos equivalent of the Hollywood sign, looming so close the way it does in the movies but not in the actual city and you feel you could touch it. Downtown is reduced to a handful of the best buildings - it's always pleasing to see the one from the brilliant first act of Speed made the cut - but still manages to capture the important stuff too, which in this case is the way that modern LA looms somewhat cruelly over the old city, captured with a strange sepulchral dignity in the form of the City Hall, so easy to spot but now so small!

Elsewhere, the ersatz Las Vega Strip looks like a drawing based on memory - a few of the classic shapes are there, but it's a sketch of a place. In this way, I guess, it captures a truth about Las Vegas. Also, perhaps, it's an admission that this is a town comfortably out of the reach of satire. As for San Francisco, it's a 60s cop movie delight to fishtail around. It nails the hills and what more do you need for a game with cars in it?

Taken as a whole these cities feel mesmerising now. And it's the limitations that make them sing, I think: those sheer granite canyons of downtown LA with its towering blocks of architecture and surprisingly thin traffic, with only the very faintest of ambient soundtracks that ensures any gunfire will pop and clap and shake you out of your seat. (Remember, I am playing the remasters and sound effects may be missing.) This is the LA of Repo Man rather than Heat - an otherland where the buildings feel alien, even the air feels alien. At night, palm trees stand out against a sky that glows a deep, clean red. GTA 5 would finesse all of this, the skyboxes and whatnot, but perhaps in that finessing something is lost. (Both games, incidentally, have such a talent for capturing California's kitsch excess that they perhaps miss some of the sweeter truths, such as the astonishing diversity of cultures a city like Los Angeles finds homes for. But how could any game do that justice?).

Dinkytowns aside, what San Andreas does better than GTA 5 is space - the peculiar flat spaces of Southern California in particular, a state in which you can never quite tell where the wilderness ends and the landscaping begins, and where the ancient rocks that announce the horizon can look upcoming, like stage settings, while the freeways feel truly ancient, concrete lizards sleeping on the dirt, bleached by the easy sun. I can lose hours out here. I have had to double- and triple-check that GTA 5 is the bigger game, in fact, because San Andreas still feels absolutely enormous, a trick that works even when you can see the not-Golden Gate Bridge seconds after taking off from not-LAX. Grab a bike and you can spend an absolute age exploring the between-spaces which video game California and real California are both so good at conjuring, stumbling on little towns you will never stumble on again, passing commercial follies, listening as the radio pumps out "All My Exes Live in Texas".

Recent findings suggest that and, paradoxically, the more I play the more I realise San Andreas is very good at the little things in its own odd way. GTA 5 is an astonishing feat of seeing and transposing, but I don't think it has anything across its acres to match the sense of place offered by San Andreas' take on Grove Street, where the story begins. It's just a neighborhood, but as you cross its small space and recross it in the game's opening hours, learning how to eat food and buy clothes and get a haircut and spray paint on walls and all that jazz, the sense that this is your home is grooved and regrooved into the experience. Maybe this is why it's such a thrill to return to this earlier pass at Los Santos. Because this one is where you truly live.

3 ways to calm your critical inner voice

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that my ride to work used to be a big red London bus.
  • My ride to work used to be a significant red London bus.
  • Sources indicate that she would pipe up: “Oh, off to Broadcasting House, are you?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that my ride to work used to be a big red London bus. I’d hop on and head to Broadcasting House, the BBC headquarters near Oxford Circus. Along for the ride was my invisible companion: Negative Nancy. She would pipe up: “Oh, off to Broadcasting House, are you? What are you going in there for? You don’t belong there.” By this point I’d worked my way from a secretarial job to producer on a national personal finance show. I had every right to be proud of my success, but Nancy wouldn’t shut up. She followed me into the office: “You look like you know what you’re doing, but you don’t.” Then into the studio, where I’d be interviewing a politician: “Your questions aren’t very good.” Thanks, Nancy. Any other helpful observations? I was doing the job, but that commentary made it hard to enjoy anything I’d achieved. We all have an inner voice. It’s the running conversation we have with ourselves, helping us make sense of the world without saying everything out loud. “It looks cold. Better take a coat.” Useful. “You’re going to make a fool of yourself in that meeting.” Less useful. When that voice turns negative, it can take up enormous headspace. Mine invalidated my hard work and success. It also thwarted my thoughts about career progression. At work, it can persuade perfectly capable people to keep an idea to themselves, avoid a difficult conversation, or let an opportunity pass. Self-doubt becomes the name of the game. If you lead or support colleagues, you’ll recognize some of those behaviors. You may recognize the voice yourself. ACE your self talk  I use a simple acronym to help: ACE. Acknowledge, Choose, and Evidence. Three ways to turn down that negative commentary and make room for confident supporting voices. 1. Acknowledge the voice First, I had to acknowledge there was in fact a voice inside my head. And acknowledge that the commentary, although familiar, wasn’t always factually accurate. Giving it a name helped me catch it in the act. “Oh, hello, Negative Nancy. You again.” You might have a Bring-Me-Down Brian or a Run-Me-Around Rita. Name yours whatever you like. The point is to recognize when that voice starts chipping away at your confidence. Notice when it gets chatty, too. Before a meeting? When you’re trying something new? When an email from your boss arrives and you immediately think, “What have I done wrong?” Once you are aware of it, you can start questioning it. 2. Choose not to listen Nancy had plenty of opinions about my career, but I didn’t have to let her make the decisions. “Thanks, Nancy, but I’m going into work now. I’ve got a show to produce. Get off the bus!” It sounds a little ridiculous, having an argument with an imaginary passenger. But answering back helped me interrupt the commentary rather than let it run all day. You can hear a doubtful thought and still choose to speak in the meeting, put yourself forward, or have that conversation. You don’t have to wait for Nancy’s permission. And if the voice pops back up? Recognize it and choose to ignore it again. This takes practice. 3. Evidence: Remind yourself of the facts Negative Nancy has a very selective memory. That awkward comment from five years ago? Perfect recall. All the good feedback since? Apparently, the files have gone missing. So gather some evidence. What have you achieved? What have people trusted you to do? What experience are you bringing to this situation? In my case, I’d worked my way up to producing a national radio show. I hadn’t wandered into Broadcasting House and found an unattended desk. People had employed me to do that job. Keep a “brag book,” a notebook or folder where you save positive feedback, successful projects, and things you’re proud of. When your inner voice starts dismissing your ability, you’ll have something concrete to refer to. You can help colleagues do this too. Remind them specifically what they did well and the difference it made. Give them something their Nancy will struggle to argue with. Keep fighting the voice I’m sorry to tell you this, but there’s no way to completely get rid of your mean inner monologue. Negative Nancy’s voice still occasionally pipes up for me—and I coach people on workplace confidence! It’s in our nature. It kept us safe when we were cave dwellers (“Don’t leave the cave! There’s a saber-toothed tiger outside, you idiot!”) so it’s always going to be ready to pop up when we least want it to. But the more conscious we are of our pesky critical inner voice, the more we talk openly about it with our colleagues, the easier it becomes to question and quiet it.

Industry observers note that in an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads. But direct routing is not automatically the right choice.

Industry observers note that the decision depends on what the organization controls and what it needs from the network. A team that owns the physical fabric, has enough address space, and is comfortable operating BGP may benefit from making pod networks directly routable. A smaller environment, a team without control of the underlay, or a cluster that benefits from network abstraction may be better served by NAT or an overlay.

In a recent development, kubernetes is also changing the ground under these decisions: kube-proxy is set to drop IPVS support starting with version 1.43, with nftables as the replacement. For on-prem teams already reviewing their service data path, it is a good moment to ask whether NAT still belongs in it.

So the useful question is not how to eliminate NAT, but when the operational benefits of doing so justify the additional routing responsibility.

NAT solves a real problem. It allows an internal network to use its own address space without requiring the surrounding infrastructure to know how to reach every endpoint inside it. This is especially useful when you don’t control the underlying network.

However, an on-premises data center is different. When you control both the Kubernetes cluster and the surrounding physical network, you can make Kubernetes networks directly routable.

Recent findings suggest that in our case, removing NAT had practical and architectural benefits. It improved network performance, reduced CPU load on the nodes, and removed the risk of conntrack tables filling up on Kubernetes hosts. A directly routed L3 model also works well for traffic balancing when a node has two uplinks.

This does not mean eliminating NAT from the data center entirely. NAT can remain at the boundary of the on-premises network, for example on hardware firewalls. Inside the data center, however, Kubernetes networks can be directly routable, allowing the physical network to reach workloads using the same routing mechanisms it already uses elsewhere.

It has been revealed that in our implementation, BGP connects the Kubernetes network to the data center fabric: BIRD runs on the nodes and advertises pod CIDRs and selected service addresses, while kube-router manages Kubernetes networking. We described this implementation in more detail in our earlier article on building a routable on-prem.

It has been revealed that kubernetes cluster with BGP and ECMP. The important point for this decision is not the particular stack, but the requirement it creates: the surrounding network must be able to accept and route Kubernetes prefixes safely. If the organization cannot or does not want to make the cluster part of its routing domain, keeping NAT or an overlay is usually the simpler choice.

According to recent reports, removing NAT alone does not make a network resilient. If every node still depends on one switch, one NIC, or one uplink, direct routing simply exposes the same physical single point of failure more clearly.

Sources indicate that the resilience benefit appears when the physical topology supports multiple independent paths. In our setup, nodes connect to independent data center switches and ECMP can use equivalent routes across those paths. If one path disappears, traffic can continue over the other.

Recent findings suggest that that distinction matters when deciding whether direct routing is worth the effort. Organizations with redundant uplinks and switches can integrate Kubernetes into an already resilient routed fabric. If the underlay itself has no path redundancy, removing NAT should not be presented as a high-availability improvement: the physical failure domain still dominates the design.

Recent findings suggest that our stack is one example of how direct routing can be implemented, not a default recommendation for clusters that remove NAT. We chose kube-router because it supports a minimal installation as a binary and systemd service and covers the networking functions we need for this L3 design. BIRD handles route advertisements to the surrounding network.

Other environments may reasonably choose Calico for conventional L3 routing or Cilium when an eBPF-based dataplane and its additional capabilities are useful. The choice of CNI and routing daemon is secondary to the architectural decision: first decide whether exposing Kubernetes prefixes to the physical network makes operational sense, then choose the implementation that fits the team’s requirements.

In a recent development, A directly routed Kubernetes network is not automatically better than an overlay or NAT-based architecture. Each model solves a different operational problem.

Recent findings suggest that NAT is a reasonable choice when the cluster needs to remain isolated from the surrounding address strategy, when pod addresses cannot be routed through the data center, or when the infrastructure team does not control the upstream network. It also keeps Kubernetes-specific prefixes out of the physical routing domain, which can be valuable for smaller environments where direct visibility into every pod is not vital.

In a recent development, an overlay is useful when portability and abstraction matter more than exposing the physical packet path. It lets Kubernetes networking remain largely independent of the underlay and can simplify deployment across heterogeneous infrastructure. The tradeoff is another layer to inspect during troubleshooting and, depending on the implementation, encapsulation overhead.

Sources indicate that direct routing makes the most sense when the organization owns the physical network, has address space available for pod CIDRs, and has operators comfortable with BGP and route filtering. It becomes more attractive when preserving source addresses, using standard network troubleshooting tools, predictable performance, or integrating the cluster with redundant data center paths are key. At a larger scale, those operational benefits can justify the extra coordination between Kubernetes and network teams.

The broader lesson is not that every Kubernetes cluster needs BGP or that NAT should disappear everywhere. It is that Kubernetes has matured enough that we should stop automatically treating its network as a black box.

As more production and AI workloads move onto Kubernetes, network architecture becomes part of application reliability. In an on-premises data center, BGP and ECMP give us the option to use the resilience already available in the physical network rather than building another isolated networking layer on top of it.

Sometimes the best way to make Kubernetes networking more robust is not to add another abstraction, but to remove one. But only when the surrounding infrastructure and the team operating it are ready to take responsibility for the routing that abstraction previously hid.

According to recent reports, if most of those answers are yes, direct routing is worth serious consideration. If not, NAT or an overlay may be the more resilient operational choice—not because it is technically more advanced, but because it better matches the environment.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that escape Academy 2: Back 2 School, a first-person puzzle adventure with a popular predecessor, was originally set to launch this September, but like many games this year saw its release date moved.
  • Escape Academy 2's original release date might have kept it away from Grand Theft Auto 6, but it would have instead faced a potential "bloodbath" of competition from the likes of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Blood of the Dawnwalker, Control Resonant, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6. It's got cool cars, crime, a big newly introduced city to explore, and the potential to hoover up so much player time that many developers have chosen to give it the widest berth possible. It's led to an October uncommonly packed with big-hitters, and a November - ordinarily one of gaming's biggest months - that's near-barren. But not every developer is steering clear. Despite the potential risks, a select few have looked at GTA 6 and seen not a threat but an opportunity, so what's driving these brave souls?

It has been revealed that escape Academy 2: Back 2 School, a first-person puzzle adventure with a popular predecessor, was originally set to launch this September, but like many games this year saw its release date moved. However, its developer bucked the industry trend, shifting its sequel not away from GTA 6's orbit, but closer. "The thing that scares me more than this monocultural event - GTA 6 - is releasing in a week when there are like 15 good games rather than one significant one", Coin Crew Games co-founder Wyatt Bushnell tells me when I ask about the studio's decision.

Escape Academy 2's original release date might have kept it away from Grand Theft Auto 6, but it would have instead faced a potential "bloodbath" of competition from the likes of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Blood of the Dawnwalker, Control Resonant, and more. "That was our rationale," Bushnell indicates. "We can still cut into the GTA stuff, but it would have been a lot harder in September and October.".

Industry observers note that it helps, notes Bushnell, that Escape Academy 2 and Grand Theft Auto 6 - one a contemplative puzzle game, the other a blockbuster action spectacle - are serving very different crowds. That's a sentiment echoed by David Lowey, Atari's senior director of sales and marketing. Atari has similarly bucked industry trends and is releasing two games - Godzilla Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered and Barbie Rewind - in the now largely vacant November window.

According to recent reports, when we speak, Lowey states there's a clear logic to smaller companies "sneaking" into spots that bigger-budget games can't risk filling, especially if their games differ greatly from Grand Theft Auto 6. "Look at Barbie Rewind coming out on the 12th," he elaborates. "It's a retro game, so it'll pull in people who grew up with these games [and] there's the cosy dreamhouse design at the core ... which is a vastly different game type to GTA 6 and plenty of other games.

In a recent development, "It's not an FPS, not a high-octane action game, there's not a lot of combat," Lowey continues. "It's designed to be the exact opposite. It's a game you're meant to curl up in a chair and play." And while he acknowledges the "reality of modern gaming" means there'll be some audience overlap between Barbie Rewind and GTA 6 players - "These sort of older ideas of what people play by gender and age have been smashed", he says - it "won't be the biggest overlap in the world". That, then, makes going toe-to-toe an easier bet.

But for Bushnell and Escape Academy, there's another consideration making GTA 6's launch window feel less of a risk: longer-tail sales. "The traditional thinking is that you have this massive release and make all of your money in those first two weeks," he explains. "I don't think that holds a tonne of water anymore. The vast majority of sales for Escape Academy were made well after its release. The reality is with digital distribution, discounting, and the fact there is this shelf of games, we're in a world where games last far longer than their initial launch." That means it's less of a concern if GTA 6 sucks up everyone's attention for a few weeks.

Recent findings suggest that and for Atari's David Lowey, Godzilla Destroy All Monsters and Barbie Rewind's proximity to GTA 6 has brought added benefits, enabling both games to capitalise on the hype around Rockstar's open-world epic in their own way. "One of the most rewarding things has been the fascination we've seen online around the proximity of Godzilla, Barbie, and GTA," he says.

The community has found it easy to root for games releasing in the behemoth shadow of GTA 6. Godzilla Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered - an updated version of the 2002 GameCube party fighting game, which released on 3rd November - has been jokingly dubbed the "GTA killer" by fans, while others have joked that Rockstar is "running scared" from Barbie Rewind. "There's no question that this buzz based on the closeness has created player interest," adds Lowey. "In retrospect the timing worked well for us.".

There's one game, though, that isn't just orbiting GTA 6, it's facing the triple-A juggernaut head-on. Edmund McMillen, Tyler Glaiel, and publisher Nicalis are bringing The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ to Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, and Switch 2 on 19th November, the same day GTA 6 arrives. "That was [Nicalis'] idea," McMillen laughs when we speak. "'Wouldn't it be funny if...?' I was like, whatever, that's funny ... We're done, so we've got to release this month ... It's a fun experiment.".

"There's a possibility [Repentance+'s release date] wasn't that stupid an idea," McMillen adds, "and if it was a stupid idea, it's a funny stupid idea." He also hints there's a "funny stupid" thing awaiting players who do a Repentance+ daily run on any platform during GTA 6's launch...

Industry observers note that mcMillen is, though, all too aware of the impact major releases can have on other games. "My heart claims it doesn't matter, but my brain has shown me it does," he explains. "When Mewgenics came out it blew up; we went past two million sales almost right off the bat. It was such a blasting, skyrocketing thing for like three weeks. Then Slay the Spire 2 came out, and it sucked everybody out. The same players who liked Mewgenics, they were Slay The Spire players. So they all went woosh and right over ... When a new thing comes out, people all move to the new thing ... You can see numbers go from astronomical to very small, and then if the game is good, it'll trickle back in.".

The way McMillen sees it, though, GTA 6 isn't immune to this natural ebb of flow of player interest either, and its pull might not be as long-lasting as some fear. "I know a lot of people buy Grand Theft Auto. I don't know how many people play Grand Theft Auto," he explains. "I don't know how many people are going to be sucked into this game and stay the whole time." And for McMillen, the fact GTA 6 is putting so many players in front of consoles is a positive.

"I think the people who like Isaac are going to play the game regardless," he claims. "[But] logically, there's a record number of people who are going to be on the console the game is on at launch [because of GTA 6] ... They might be like me, play [GTA 6] for a while, and say okay I have a console with one game, what am I going to play next? Then, you know, a rising tide will raise all ships. I think Grand Theft Auto will bring people back to consoles, because consoles are abysmal right now. Sales are bad and no one is playing anything. People own next-gen consoles and they're just sitting there...".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home.
  • According to recent reports, after adding a home key to Google Wallet, you can Tap to Unlock with your phone.
  • Industry observers note that there’s also support for Unlock on Approach with an Aliro Ultra Wideband (UWB)-compatible Android phone (see below) and an Aliro UWB-compatible lock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home.

According to recent reports, after adding a home key to Google Wallet, you can Tap to Unlock with your phone. This leverages NFC and “works even when your phone screen is locked” by default. However, you can adjust verification settings in the Google Wallet app to require screen lock or biometric authentication. This requires Android 9+.

Industry observers note that there’s also support for Unlock on Approach with an Aliro Ultra Wideband (UWB)-compatible Android phone (see below) and an Aliro UWB-compatible lock. Wear OS watches are not supported at launch.

Behind the scenes, the digital key is linked to the Google Home app rather than a single lock. As such, “each of your compatible Aliro locks will work with a single key in your Google Wallet.” Keys are added to Google Wallet using the Home app, which will prompt you to save after setup. You can also go to Home settings > Google Wallet key.

Sources indicate that crazy to me that Google's own smart lock with Yale doesn't have this functionality. Seems like a huge miss for them to not be forward looking with their own hardware here.

Afterward, your key “automatically syncs across compatible Android phones signed into your Google Wallet account.”.

The card in Google Wallet features a simple Google Home logo with your home’s name in the top-right corner.

Recent findings suggest that the following locks are supported at launch: Aqara u400 (UWB and NFC), Schlage Sense Pro (NFC at launch and UWB to follow), and Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Support for more models is coming.

Additionally, support is rolling out first to the Google Home Public Preview before coming to all customers “over the coming weeks.”.

It has been revealed that FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Tech Report: Latest US rules aim to restrict Chinese firms’ remote access to AI servers and infrastructure

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that new steps have been taken to ensure that countries and companies that are not on whitelists that would allow them to import advanced AI hardware cannot use cloud-based workarounds.
  • Industry observers note that nvidia, for example, is only allowed to export its high-performance AI chips to companies that are on a whitelist.
  • Sources indicate that but while blocking the sale of physical goods is one thing, the cloud-based workaround is another entirely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that new steps have been taken to ensure that countries and companies that are not on whitelists that would allow them to import advanced AI hardware cannot use cloud-based workarounds. The U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has today unveiled an interim final rule, or IFR, in collaboration with the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council, aimed at backing up existing limitations on the export of hardware built by companies like Nvidia to non-whitelisted companies based in countries such as China. "The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements" using data centers in third-party countries, a statement explains.

Industry observers note that nvidia, for example, is only allowed to export its high-performance AI chips to companies that are on a whitelist. But amid ongoing claims of black market GPU sales and a recent crackdown on overseas AI GPU rentals from China, it has become clear that these restrictions perhaps aren't as robust as they were intended to be. Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs were even recently discovered in a data center used by China Telecom.

Sources indicate that but while blocking the sale of physical goods is one thing, the cloud-based workaround is another entirely. Nvidia itself told data center operators earlier this month that they must limit remote access to their services — 51% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. But, again, it's unclear how effective that approach has been in ensuring access to powerful AI capabilities doesn't fall into the wrong hands, even if they're accessed remotely rather than in person.

The new BIS rule means that overseas data centers will be required to do more to limit access to their services where U.S-based technology is being used. Restrictions will also be placed on data centers that supply remote access to companies whose headquarters are deemed to be in higher-risk countries, such as China, Russia, and Iran. A license will also be required for anyone trying to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil. The new requirements will officially go into effect in 90 days.

It has been revealed that this latest rule comes against a backdrop of ongoing uncertainty over America's AI crown jewel, Nvidia. Jensen Huang, the tech giant's CEO, resigned after confirming an affair, but is now potentially in line for a quick-fire comeback, despite the fact that the woman involved in the affair is an alleged Chinese spy.

Holiday gift guide 2026: 20 thoughtfully curated tech gifts that will charm and delight everyone on your list

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the world obsesses over AI and conventional tech products balloon in price, the thought of buying gadgets for anyone this holiday season might feel a little intimidating.
  • In a recent development, as the world obsesses over AI and conventional tech products balloon in price, the thought of buying gadgets for anyone this holiday season might feel a little intimidating.
  • In a recent development, my selection process for this gift guide was entirely subjective.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the world obsesses over AI and conventional tech products balloon in price, the thought of buying gadgets for anyone this holiday season might feel a little intimidating. But that’s not to say that there aren’t options out there. I often find that the best gifts are charming, focused devices with a touch of style. My selection process for this gift guide was entirely subjective. Almost everything on it is a gadget or design object with an element of tactile satisfaction for how it handles an everyday task. You won’t find a boring black rectangle anywhere on the list, and you shouldn’t have to think too hard about the soaring cost of memory. Apple: The First 50 Years by David Pogue Published to mark Apple’s half-century this year, veteran tech journalist David Pogue has marked the occasion with a hefty tome that serves as a biography of the company itself. Pogue conducted 150 interviews for the book, including figures like Jony Ive and Steve Wozniak, and the presentation benefits from hundreds of photos throughout. This is a book that’s worth owning in print. Twelve South Airfly SE Some airplane seatback screens support Bluetooth, but it’s not something you can always rely on when boarding a long-haul flight, as many screens still won’t connect to noise-canceling headphones. Twelve South’s AirFly SE is an inexpensive dongle that plugs into your seat’s headphone jack and transmits the audio to your cans. You’ll never need to use airline earbuds again. Sharge Flow Mini Go Sharge’s whole thing is designing utilitarian gadgets with a stylish twist, and the Flow Mini Go is one I can recommend to anyone who ever finds themselves running low on a charge. It has a 5,800-milliampere-hour (mAh) battery, 22.5-watt charging and a built-in cable, as well as an option to attach it directly to your phone’s USB-C port. Just as importantly, it’s only about as massive as a lipstick tube. Nothing Ear (a) At $79, Nothing’s Ear (a) model is my pick for affordable wireless earbuds. They sound great and look even better, especially if you opt for the construction-equipment-yellow pair. Even the charging case is cool, with a design inspired by medicinal blister packs. Logitech MX Master 4 Developer Edition If you know someone who uses a mouse all day but has never really thought about the actual mouse they’re using, the MX Master 4 might just change their life. The MX Master series has long been considered the leading productivity mouse due to its unique free-spinning scroll wheel, and the latest model adds a customizable haptic thumb panel that buzzes to confirm a shortcut. The fresh Developer Edition adds a “Hello, World” prompt and a reference to the Linux kernel’s release date. BOOX Palma 3 The Boox Palma 3 is an E Ink reader the size and shape of a smartphone, offering a convenient antidote to doomscrolling that you can take anywhere. Because it runs on Android, you can easily add your Kindle and Kobo libraries straight from the Google Play store. This latest version features a streamlined aluminum design and stylus support. 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard 8BitDo is best known for its excellent range of gaming controllers, and its first mechanical keyboard turned out to be just as haptically satisfying. Rolled out in versions that evoked the Nintendo Entertainment System and the Famicom, the lineup now includes models inspired by the Commodore 64 and the IBM Model M.. Each comes with enormous programmable buttons you can place next to the keyboard, making copying and pasting feel like a session at the arcade. Balmuda The Lantern Balmuda is a hip Japanese appliance maker best known for its minimalist steam toaster, but its equally obsessive take on the camping lantern may be a more practical gift. It has a single rotary dial that takes you from a warm, flickering candle-style effect at the low end to a brighter reading light when you turn it up. The light is diffused through a pipe for a soft glow, and its rechargeable battery means you can use it anywhere from the bedroom to the balcony. Analogue Pocket The Analogue Pocket feels like it came from an alternate universe where Apple designed the Game Boy. It has a gorgeous stripped-down design, an amazing high-resolution screen, and programmable hardware that has been tuned to provide the most authentic reproduction possible of Game Boy and Game Boy Advance games. The newer Analogue 3D does much the same thing for the Nintendo 64, if your gift recipient is more of a couch potato. Lego Game Boy Lego’s Game Boy is another meticulous reproduction of the Game Boy, but from a totally different angle. This kit is incredibly fun to build, making you build up the hardware from the circuit board level and work on the mechanisms of the satisfyingly squishy buttons and D-pad. As a display piece, you can swap out cartridges and lenticular screen inserts for Super Mario Land and The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening. Backbone One The BackBone One has been around for a while, but together with its Pro version, it still remains the top name in smartphone game controllers. And the proposition is more compelling than it used to be, with modern phones now powerful enough to run solid versions of high-end console games like Assassin’s Creed Mirage and Death Stranding. Backbone offers models with both PlayStation and Xbox controller layouts, depending on your preference. Aura Carver Mat Digital photo frames have been a clichéd throwaway gift for a long time, which is why Aura’s products stand out. The Carver Mat is a landscape, color-calibrated matte screen with a paper-textured border that automatically dims its lighting to match the ambient surroundings, making it feel much more natural than other digital frames. It can display two portrait photos side-by-side and even supports Live Photos from an iPhone. Kodak Charmera The Kodak Charmera hits on two recent trends: Labubu-style blind-box collectibles and the throwback use of lo-fi digicams. Each $35 box contains one of seven retro designs, and the tiny camera itself has several filters and frames. The image quality is not great, of course, but the Charmera is well-designed and well-named—it’s the perfect stocking stuffer. Fujifilm Instax Pal 2 If you like the idea of a tiny pocket camera but want the results to be a little more usable, Fujifilm has you covered with the $169 Instax Pal 2. It’s shaped like a vintage range finder, like many of Fujifilm’s more advanced mirrorless cameras—but even though it fits in the palm of your hand, it makes room for an optical viewfinder, a 1-inch display, a command dial for color effects, and a lever to swap between aspect ratios. Photos can be transferred directly to your phone or to an Instax Link printer. Peak Design Mobile Tripod The biggest problem with tripods is finding a way to take them with you. But here’s one you won’t even notice in your jeans pocket. Peak Design’s take on the mobile tripod folds three legs and a full-on ball head into a package that’s about 5 millimeters thick. It snaps onto your MagSafe-compatible phone with minimal obtrusion, and unfolds into a stand you can angle for group shots, video calls, or hyper-lapses. Native Union Pop cables and phone I’ve long been a fan of Paris-based Native Union, which puts out some of the most thoughtfully designed tech accessories around. Its coiled Pop Cables are particularly great, avoiding tangles and saving desk space—and now the company has revived its original Pop Phone, giving you an old-school handset to conduct your Zoom calls like you’re in an episode of Mad Men. There’s even a hang-up button. Xiaomi Portable Electric Air Compressor If you know anyone who rides a bicycle and plays basketball, this gadget might just change their life. For everyone else, it’s still worth keeping around—I’ve recommended it to countless friends. This USB-C-powered air compressor has modes tailored to all sorts of devices and displays the real-time pressure rating on its LCD screen. Nintendo Sound Clock: Alarmo Trust Nintendo to come up with a bizarrely useful take on something as mundane as the alarm clock. Anyone who shares a bed with a partner may consider it a hard sell to start each morning with sounds from Mario Kart or The Legend of Zelda. But the motion-sensing feature alone is a game changer for the groggy moments before getting up; the screen stays switched off until you turn your head to check the time. Teenage Engineering Pocket Operator Swedish design company Teenage Engineering first made its name through its iconoclastic synthesizers, and it sounds like the company might be moving on from that heritage. If that’s the case, now could be a good time to stock up on its $99 Pocket Operator series. It’s a range of exposed circuit boards with clicky switches, rotary dials, and monochrome LCD panels, all amounting to remarkably capable instruments. Yukai Engineering Nekojita FuFu In Japan, if you’re sensitive to hot food or liquids, you’re noted to have a nekojita—in other words, a cat’s tongue. Yukai Engineering is attempting to solve this condition with a tiny, rechargeable cat that attaches to the rim of your coffee cup or ramen bowl. Its internal fan drops the liquid’s temperature to a drinkable level in just a few minutes, and the cat looks cute in the process.

#23614. The probable future is bleak. It’s time for improbable futures

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2676 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

The probable future is bleak. It’s time for improbable futures

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain.
  • Massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain.
  • Sources indicate that this is Paris in March 1883, and it bears striking similarities to Paris in October 2026, when grievance became a national movement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain. A crowd marches on the Interior Ministry and is driven back with bayonets. Students tear their school apart and barricade the doors; after hours of fighting with police, the army is called in. This is Paris in March 1883, and it bears striking similarities to Paris in October 2026, when grievance became a national movement. Then, it was about bread and work; today, the cost of living and declining public services. Then, the industrial revolution added a backdrop of anxiety; today, another revolution in technology. Then, as now, students rebelled against the schools meant to form them. France is an extreme case of a global mood. Across the 30 countries tracked by Ipsos, the public opinion research firm, 62% say their country is on the wrong track. In the U.S., the figure is 73%; in France, it’s 89%. Edelman, a communications consultancy, finds in its annual trust survey that only 32% of people across 28 countries expect the next generation to be better off. In the U.S., it’s 21%, and in France it’s just 6%. These numbers are so bad that the social contract, that bedrock of civil society, is at risk. The problem isn’t a lack of change. It’s that the change underway isn’t the change people want. If the probable future is bleak, the most pragmatic thing to do is to take seriously the quest for improbable futures. Unfortunately, that is not a muscle most political or business leaders have built, trained as they are in playing the present game, not inventing entirely new forms of social and financial value. The case study method of business schools entrenches lessons from the past, not from the future; being trained in the logic of the law and finance does not naturally foster the kind of empathetic creativity that designs for what people want next. #23613. Latest Update: China retains fastest supercomputer in the world crown as AI data centers soak up fresh hardware

Latest Update: China retains fastest supercomputer in the world crown as AI data centers soak up fresh hardware

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China's LineShine remains the world's highest-performing supercomputer, according to the 68th edition of the Top500 list published at SC26 in Chicago on Monday.
  • China's LineShine, installed at the National Supercomputer Center in Shenzhen, offers sustained FP64 compute performance of 2.198 FP64 ExaFLOPS in the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark at 42.22 MW.
  • Sources indicate that america's most powerful El Capitan supercomputer at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory relies on AMD's Instinct MI300A accelerated processing units (APUs), and the HPE Cray EX255a platform delivers 1.809 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 29.69 MW, which makes it significantly more power-efficient than its rival from China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China's LineShine remains the world's highest-performing supercomputer, according to the 68th edition of the Top500 list published at SC26 in Chicago on Monday. For the first time in decades, the supercomputer ranking saw exceptionally few additions despite unprecedented demand for high-performance computing hardware, as the vast amounts of compute resources deployed these days are destined for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers rather than traditional supercomputers.

China's LineShine, installed at the National Supercomputer Center in Shenzhen, offers sustained FP64 compute performance of 2.198 FP64 ExaFLOPS in the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark at 42.22 MW. The machine relies on the homegrown LingKun platform with 304-core Armx9-based LX2 processors clocked at 1.55 GHz (13,789,440 cores in total) and the proprietary LingQi interconnect. Unlike the other four exascale-class supercomputers, LineShine does not use any compute accelerators and exclusively relies on CPUs, which is largely why it only gains 3.6X performance when moving from FP64 to mixed-precision data, which is lower than systems that use low-precision accelerators.

Sources indicate that america's most powerful El Capitan supercomputer at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory relies on AMD's Instinct MI300A accelerated processing units (APUs), and the HPE Cray EX255a platform delivers 1.809 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 29.69 MW, which makes it significantly more power-efficient than its rival from China. The Frontier supercomputer at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, based on AMD's 3rd Generation EPYC processors and Instinct MI250X compute GPUs, achieves 1.353 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 24.61 MW. Meanwhile, Aurora at the Argonne National Laboratory, which uses Intel's Xeon CPU Max 9470 processors and Data Center GPU Max accelerators, offers 1.012 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 38.70 MW.

All three American exascale supercomputers use HPE’s Cray EX platforms and Slingshot-11 interconnect.

Germany’s Jupiter Booster at the Jülich Supercomputing Center, which employs Nvidia’s GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips, the BullSequana XH3000 platform, and Nvidia’s quad-rail InfiniBand NDR200 interconnect, delivers 1.0 FP64 ExaFLOPS at 15.79 MW and remains the most energy-efficient exascale supercomputer on the list.

Remarkably, neither the 10 highest-performing supercomputers nor the 10 most energy-efficient machines have changed their positions since June.

Only 27 new supercomputers (5.4% of all machines on the list) made it to the November edition of the Top 500, the lowest number since the project was founded in 1993. The most powerful newcomer is South Korea's Hanggang at the KISTI Supercomputing Center, which occupies the 12th position with 342.6 FP64 PFLOPS. The machine uses Nvidia's GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips and HPE's Cray EX254n platform. Hanggang also ranks eighth in the HPCG benchmark with 4.29 HPCG PFLOPS.

Recent findings suggest that the aggregate HPL performance of the world's 500 highest-performing supercomputers increased by a modest 4.4% over the past six months to 19.57 FP64 ExaFLOPS. Nonetheless, it now takes a machine with 2.857 PFLOPS of sustained FP64 performance to qualify for the TOP500, up 7.3% from 2.662 PFLOPS in June. The performance of the systems ranked 50th and 100th rose from 49.85 PFLOPS to 55.81 PFLOPS (12%) and from 21.85 PFLOPS to 22.74 PFLOPS, respectively. Also, there are now 27 machines that deliver at least 100 PFLOPS of FP64 performance, up from 25 in June, whereas the number of supercomputers equipped with compute accelerators increased from 275 to 291 (58.2%).

The historically low number of new entrants to the Top 500 is particularly noteworthy given the unprecedented scale of investments in advanced computing infrastructure these days. According to estimates by Epoch AI cited by the Top 500 authors, the amount of AI compute capacity added globally every quarter has increased by 2.5X per year. Essentially, the industry's priorities have shifted from construction of machines capable of solving exceptionally complex scientific problems to deployment of vast amounts of compute capacity for commercial AI workloads.

In fact, the world's installed AI compute capacity already exceeds the equivalent of 15 million Nvidia H100 GPUs, according to Epoch AI. Furthermore, as of the fourth quarter of 2025, five major American hyperscalers accounted for an estimated 71% of the world's AI compute resources, much of which was deployed in massive clusters. While demand for advanced computing hardware is at an all-time high, it appears that the vast majority of upcoming hardware never makes it to the world's most known supercomputer ranking.

#23612. FEMA has a cord-cutting problem

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1551 w)

FEMA has a cord-cutting problem

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Tuesday, countless TV viewers will find their favorite highlights interrupted for a one-minute test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Emergency Alert System (EAS).
  • In a recent development, on Tuesday, countless TV viewers will find their favorite highlights interrupted for a one-minute test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Emergency Alert System (EAS).
  • It has been revealed that that’s bad news, especially when the next real emergency happens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday, countless TV viewers will find their favorite highlights interrupted for a one-minute test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Emergency Alert System (EAS). The test will cut into live broadcasts and cable reruns alike, and also be heard on radio stations across the country. However, anyone getting their TV fix from Netflix, Disney+, or any other streaming service likely won’t notice a thing. That’s bad news, especially when the next real emergency happens. According to recent Nielsen data, U.S. consumers are already spending half their TV viewing time with digital video platforms like YouTube and Amazon Prime. In other words: Half of America’s TV viewers are missing out on emergency alerts because they’re watching online instead. “It is vital that emergency alert systems adapt to changes in consumer technologies,” says University of Colorado Denver communications professor Hamilton Bean, an expert in public alert and warning systems. “Whether through streaming services, mobile devices, or IoT [Internet of Things], emergency alerts work best when they reach people where they are—at home, at work, or in public settings.” The federal government first began testing emergency alerts in the 1950s to warn citizens of a possible Soviet nuclear attack. Federal alert systems have been modernized multiple times since those early days, including an expansion to mobile phones in 2012. But in recent years, regulators and emergency management officials have struggled to keep up with rapidly changing media consumption habits and shifts in the TV business. This has led to confusing gaps in the Emergency Alert System. One example: Consumers who have switched their TV subscriptions from a cable company to an internet-based TV service like YouTube TV, Fubo, or Hulu + Live TV may also miss out on alerts. These so-called “virtual” pay TV operators don’t participate in the EAS, which means they don’t interrupt their programming to carry such warnings. But if a YouTube TV subscriber happens to be tuned into a local broadcast network like ABC or Fox, they may see the alert after all. Those channels are frequently ingested from local broadcast TV affiliates, which in turn do work with FEMA. In other words: YouTube TV subscribers who watch Dancing With the Stars on ABC during an emergency may get a warning, while those tuned into Bravo’s Southern Charm may be blissfully unaware of any impending danger. “Regardless of the other aspects of regulation, when it comes to public safety concerns, [traditional and internet-based pay TV services] should be on equal footing,” says John Bergmayer, legal director of the nonprofit technology advocacy group Public Knowledge. Virtual pay TV services already need to know a subscriber’s location to serve up local broadcast channels, which should help them target consumers with the right alerts. “And like cable, they have the technical capacity to both interrupt a program or to add some sort of crawl along the bottom of the screen,” Bergmayer says. Streaming services and their media company owners have generally resisted the idea of being forced to carry emergency alerts. In a 2021 regulatory filing, the Motion Picture Association, which counts Netflix, Disney, and Skydance among its members, declared that it would be “enormously technically difficult, if not entirely impracticable” to expand emergency alerts to streaming. One problem the industry association pointed to is the federated nature of America’s Emergency Alert System. While Tuesday’s test alert goes out nationwide, real warnings about wildfires or flooding are necessarily local. Requiring a streaming service like Netflix to relay those alerts would mean building out extensive monitoring infrastructure in every state. Some hope that the fresh Advanced Television Systems Committee (ATSC) 3.0 broadcast standard, which brings modern technologies to antenna TV, will come to the rescue. In theory, modern TVs equipped with ATSC 3.0 tuners could interrupt a Netflix stream as soon as they receive an emergency alert via antenna. In practice, there’s no regulation in place to require this yet. Critics also fear that ATSC 3.0’s content protection technologies could hamper emergency warnings. In the end, the lesson from Tuesday’s test may be that emergency alerts can’t rely on just one technology. “There is no silver bullet,” says Art Botterell, author of To Warn Is Human: A Cultural History of Public Warning. Instead of trying to find a tech fix, he’d prefer that we invest in civic infrastructure and strengthen the bonds between neighbors so they can alert and help one another. “We need to facilitate that person-to-person sharing,” Botterell says. That, in turn, may also help people who happen to tune into the wrong TV show at the wrong moment.

Most overdue invoices settle within a month past due, so funds arrive roughly two months post-billing. The same survey notes US enterprises often lose 1% to 2% of B2B invoices to bad debt. Software that shortens this window performs four main functions:.

What invoice-to-cash software does not handle is core billing operations. Billing schedules, revenue recognition, and GL accounting remain within the ERP. Contract-first platforms initiate workflows from signed agreements and map customer billing prior to collection efforts; invoice-first applications pick up after ERP invoice generation.

Most finance stacks have four layers: the ERP that creates the invoice and holds the books, a payments network, a reminders tool, and an AR automation layer working the steps in between.

The ERP covers the last row, and a reminders tool covers timing. The rows in between depend on reading what a customer or a portal sent, which is AR automation work. That share keeps growing. Paper checks fell to 26% of B2B payments in 2025, per the AFP 2025 Digital Payments Survey as reported by Nacha, and FedNow settled about 2.5 times as many payments in Q3 2026 as a year earlier, per Federal Reserve FedNow statistics. Heading into 2027, more money arrives over electronic rails while its remittance detail lands somewhere else.

Layer: AI-native AR automation, for Series A to Fortune 500 finance teams.

Published pricing: Pricing scales with business volume and isn't a percentage of collections.

Leak it closes: Unapplied cash first, then stalled replies and portal rejections.

Layer: AR automation with built-in payments, sold as Invoiced by Flywire.

Published pricing: Not published.

Leak it closes: Cash application, where CashMatch AI handles wires that pay several invoices at once and payments that arrive without remittance.

Layer: Payments network and AR suite.

Published pricing: Not published.

Leak it closes: Invoice delivery into buyer portals, through 260+ AP portal integrations run from one interface.

Layer: AR automation layer with AI agents, on the ERP.

Published pricing: Not published.

Leak it closes: Customer replies that carry a promise-to-pay date or a dispute.

Layer: Payments network with customer portal.

Published pricing: Not published.

Leak it closes: Payment acceptance, through a customer portal for paying and disputing invoices online.

Layer: Reminders tool with AI reply drafts, on Xero and QuickBooks.

Published pricing: Essentials $69 a month; Pro $99 to $799 a month; Custom from $999 a month.

Leak it closes: Replies that sit unanswered at small and midsize companies.

Published pricing: US $259, $779 or $1,169 a month by annual revenue band; annual billing saves 10%.

Leak it closes: Follow-up timing, with reminders sent from your own email address on a schedule that escalates.

On Xero or QuickBooks with customers paying from the emailed link, the leak tends to be timing, and a reminders tool covers it. Once W-9 requests and payment questions fill your team's week, the replies need a different layer.

Portal rejections and lump-sum wires put the leak in the table's middle rows, where an AR automation layer on the ERP fits. In a demo, we'd ask each vendor to show how fast its software flagged a rejected portal invoice, then to apply a multi-invoice wire with a blank memo live.

If your team still keys card numbers or chases ACH details, start with the payments layer. A payments network with a customer portal gives buyers stored methods and autopay. Unless the vendor notes otherwise, it won't read replies or file into buyer portals, so plan an AR layer for those stages.

Whichever of the best accounts receivable software platforms you pick, it sits on top of the ERP. Four steps keep the books intact:.

#23609. The young rebel alliance trying to get people to love technology again

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 37m • 📚 Deep Dive (7468 w)
