General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

The young rebel alliance trying to get people to love technology again

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 37 min read (7468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~37 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a spare and cavernous former eyewear emporium near the luxury stores of San Francisco’s Union Square, a motley group of tech devices is spread out across display counters and pedestals.
  • In a spare and cavernous former eyewear emporium near the luxury stores of San Francisco’s Union Square, a motley group of tech devices is spread out across display counters and pedestals.
  • The space is like some bizarro Apple Store, but instead of offering futuristic devices you didn’t know you needed, it’s a showcase of devices you didn’t know could even exist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a spare and cavernous former eyewear emporium near the luxury stores of San Francisco’s Union Square, a motley group of tech devices is spread out across display counters and pedestals. One is a desktop computer shaped like a cartoon frog. Another is an e-ink laptop controlled by buttons made of felt. Nearby, there’s an AI assistant hidden inside a fuzzy parrot meant to perch on a user’s shoulder. The space is like some bizarro Apple Store, but instead of offering futuristic devices you didn’t know you needed, it’s a showcase of devices you didn’t know could even exist. Devices on display at TIAT’s latest group exhibition, Every Thing Computer. [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Manufacturer] This store is not a store, but a three-year-old gallery called the Intersection of Art and Technology, or TIAT, which hosts a near-constant stream of events, meetups, and exhibitions focused on experimentation among self-described creative technologists. The devices are part of TIAT’s latest group exhibition, Every Thing Computer, which explores “playful computing” and experimental interfaces. Some are clearly one-off art projects (see the punchable oversize keyboard escape button and the computer mouse shaped like female genitalia), but others are more earnest and commercial attempts to reimagine what we want our devices to be. Signature by NOCELLCOVERAGE, 2026, (custom Gameboys, custom software). [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] Many of the people showing at TIAT, who consider themselves both artists and technologists, are building these devices as physical proof that an alternative to the current Silicon Valley ecosystem is possible. They are part of a growing community in San Francisco and beyond reconsidering how technology can bring people more joy—or at least give them more agency over the devices they use. “We like to call this the rebel alliance of creatives that are trying to go out and have better ideas for what the future can be,” claims Liz Dorman, whose San Francisco-based startup, Era, sponsored the exhibition at TIAT. Her company is building a platform for customizable AI devices, putting her near the center of the creative technologist ecosystem. Thanks to AI tools, more nimble factories, and the motivation of a generation who grew up with smartphones in their hands, the prospect of developing new kinds of devices is more possible, and desirable, than ever before. Amy Wibowo with Froggy Computer, 2020, (computer: acrylic, acrylic cement, Raspberry Pi; desk mat: cloth, rubber). [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company “We’ve had so much lock-in and walled-garden effects because of the App Store and because of how hard it is to make hardware,” Dorman says. “That now is finally changing.” But taking down Big Tech is beside the point for many of the people in the creative technology community. Instead of competing at the same massive scale as the tech giants, these ambitious, and predominantly young, tech people are trying to build new hardware that both serves a niche audience and broadens the spectrum of consumer technology. The more commercial among these devices are just now starting to ship, and they’re meeting the market in a moment of highly anticipated AI hardware coming from companies with trillion-dollar valuations. “That’s precisely why we need artists to provide perspectives on all this new technology,” says Ash Herr, TIAT’s founder. A DIY resurgence Aly B’s Tallygotchi, 2026, (TPU 3D print covered in leather). [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] While there are no hard numbers on how big this scene is, there are emerging and established creative technology groups and meetups from San Francisco to New York, including TIAT, Physical Futures, Fidget Camp, Gray Area, the School for Poetic Computation, the New Museum’s New Inc., the Resonant Computing Lab, and more. Many have academic roots in vaunted computing and human-computer interface labs like Carnegie Mellon’s Human-Computer Interaction Institute, New York University’s Interactive Telecommunications Program, and several labs at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “There are a lot of students who are kind of tired of computers,” says Marcelo Coelho, director of MIT’s Design Intelligence Lab. “In many ways, their response is to invent their own computer.” People exploring these concepts often self-describe as creative technologists, but some see their work more broadly as indie hardware, while others find it to be closer to fashion hardware or even bespoke “couture computing.” The through line is a desire to break out of the winner-takes-all mindset that’s fueled the Big Tech companies in recent years. “Pretty much the story of San Francisco right now is all these people with egos being like, ‘I know what the future is. Let me tell you what the future is.’ And you can’t edit or change anything,” Dorman says. “A lot of the underlying stuff that’s happening in creative tech is coming from those feelings of we actually want to take ownership over our technology.” Liz Dorman, cofounder, Era. [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] Dorman describes this as a shift to “couture technology,” where a more open ecosystem would allow people to customize hardware to their own specific needs. “It’s like you can sew your own shirt, or you can buy it from your favorite creative, or you can get it mass-produced,” Dorman says. Doing it yourself is nothing new for the modern tech world, of course. Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak built the earliest version of what would become an Apple computer in a bedroom. And it’s an ethos that’s carried through the years, according to Barry Threw, executive director of Gray Area, the San Francisco-based art and technology nonprofit that’s been leading tech-centered events, education, and research programs since 2008. “Open hardware and people wanting to have some agency and access to these kinds of tools is always a trend that’s going on,” Threw says. He points to the mid-2010s, when there was a lot of interest in DIY hardware, through events like Maker Faire, and open-source software, printed circuit boards, and microcontrollers from Arduino and Raspberry Pi. Inês Lucas’s, Source Knowledge Nodes, 2026, (leather, PLA, electronics, brass). [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] AI has opened new opportunities for this mode of creation, with vibe coding making it vastly easier to create digital tools and applications. “It makes it more attainable for folks who start doing interesting hardware and software DIY things because the software side of it doesn’t become such a burden,” Threw says. But AI has also spurred a related backlash, as the leading AI labs and companies pursue advancements at a pace that has even some of its own executives worried for the future of humanity. As those few big companies appear to be guiding the direction of AI’s development, nearly three-quarters of people are concerned about what they are creating. “When people have less confidence in the direction of their public services and institutions, not just in tech but in general, I find this DIY ethos happening,” Threw says. “They go back to trying to take some agency into their own hands and build their own tools.” Visitor interacting with Louis Chavey’s (P)rose Garden,  2026, (topsoil and “your thoughts”). [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] In San Francisco and other tech hubs, the concern is also personal. Software engineers, once the backbone of Silicon Valley and the tech world at large, are finding themselves replaced by the very technology they once created, sparking existential crises about what, if anything, they can do next. Creative technology is proving to be one alternative. “Across the technology spectrum, people are searching for where meaning and value and creativity lie when it’s not possible just to be a software engineer anymore because that stuff’s getting automated,” Threw says. “As the creativity around software development has been taken over by these AI tools, hardware is kind of the next frontier.” Creating a new creative practice Kelin Zhang holds up a camera and takes a photo of my face on her computer screen. We’re on a video call, the pandemic-cemented default meeting mode mediated through phones or laptops with built-in cameras. The camera she’s holding, though, is not some add-on element of another device. It’s a stand-alone camera meant for taking photos. But there’s a twist: Instead of actually producing a photo, the camera uses its lens to capture and process an image and then, for reasons that are not immediately apparent, uses AI to write and print a poem about it. Poetry Camera is Zhang’s pet project turned consumer product. Conceived on a whim with her friend Ryan Mather back in January 2023, it was willed into being through a combination of online tutorials, AI vibe coding, open-source printed circuit boards, and 3D printers. After a weekend of poking around, they built a working prototype. [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] “I was like, wow, it’s a lot easier to get started in hardware than I thought,” she says. Zhang wasn’t starting from scratch. She has a bachelor’s degree in computer science from MIT, and had spent nearly a decade working in digital product design. When she had the idea for Poetry Camera, she had just left her job as staff product designer at Twitter, which had recently been acquired by Elon Musk. “I got a front-row seat to everything and I thought, You know what? I’m kind of done with corporate tech,” she says. ChatGPT had been released publicly just a few months earlier, and Zhang had the sense that big changes were coming to the tech world. She decided to take a year to explore what it could look like to create an AI-first digital design practice. Poetry Camera was the first thing she prototyped. “With AI, it’s only going to get easier and easier,” Zhang says. “If you’re motivated to work on a project, it lowers the barrier by so much.” Almost four years later, Poetry Camera is a $349 consumer product that’s garnered fans in both the tech and poetry worlds. Anthropic, a longtime supporter, put in a rush order last winter for a batch to hand out at a Super Bowl party. Poetry Camera’s success has buoyed Zhang to start a physical product studio called Tenderworld. “People are excited and delighted by form factors that aren’t just apps trapped behind the screen of a phone or a computer,” she says. Zhang picks up the Poetry Camera she used to take my photo and rips out the receipt-like thermal paper printed with the poem it created. But instead of focusing on my face on Zhang’s screen, the camera was looking past her laptop at a shelf of other Poetry Cameras in boxes. The poem it wrote was about itself. ‘Well, I want to change it’ Like a stall at a seedy flea market, there’s a table in a storefront window near San Francisco’s Transamerica Pyramid that’s covered with dozens of random consumer technology gadgets. Spanning the past five decades, they include a Macintosh Newton tablet, several varieties of early-2000s flip phones, an alien-esque cassette tape player, an AM/FM radio shaped like a peanut M&M, and multiple garish wristwatches with built-in cameras. Nestled among these are newer devices, like the Humane AI Pin and the Rabbit R1. This display is part of the office of Era, the startup Dorman cofounded to build a software platform and hardware for customizable AI devices. None of the items on the table are for sale—this being San Francisco, people do pop in and ask—but rather they’re a nostalgia-tickling reminder that tech devices used to look a lot different from the rectangular phones in our pockets today. The display is a subtle prod at the bland landscape of modern hardware. Why can’t tech look like this again? “It hasn’t felt very optimistic recently, especially with all the releases happening by Big Tech companies,” Dorman says inside Era’s office, two 3D printers humming in the background. “It feels like these companies are not only out of touch with people, but they’re forcing technology onto people that they don’t actually want.” Era, which has raised more than $11 million in funding, was founded to offer people the chance to decide what they want their tech to look like and how it can function, starting with the development of a puck-like AI core that it sees as the open-source basis of highly customizable devices. Calling itself “a small Gen Z team raised with smartphones,” the company is mostly twentysomethings who were still in grade school when the first iPhone was released. Dorman, who grew up in New Jersey jailbreaking the early iPhone models, was dismayed when Apple made that kind of custom hacking impossible. Later, after an internship at Apple, she got her own job in Big Tech working for Humane, the company cofounded by former Apple executive Imran Chaudhri that raised more than $230 million to create a post-iPhone screenless AI device. That device, the AI Pin, flopped, and Dorman was not surprised. The fact that its form factor so closely resembled a police officer’s body-worn camera was one major issue, but so were more aesthetic concerns. Dorman, for one, thought there should be more variety than the single black-and-white color palette, and more of an embrace of the flexibility AI offers. “I hated the voice and personality we chose for the device. It was the equivalent of giving everyone an iPhone and being like, you can’t change the wallpaper. And I was like, ‘Well, I want to change it,’” she says. And she did, hacking her AI Pin to use the voice of the blogger-narrator from the television teen drama Gossip Girl. She started showing off the device to her friends, and using it much more often than before. “That is very much the feeling that we’re chasing at Era.” Dorman cofounded Era in 2025, teaming up with two other young AI-leaning technologists who were similarly concerned about the direction Big Tech and AI companies were heading. “I think something that’s really true across the consumer landscape is everybody feels left behind by AI,” Era cofounder Megan Gole says. She previously worked at venture capital firm Sutter Hill Ventures, which was involved in OpenAI’s acquisition of former Apple design chief Jony Ive’s AI hardware startup Io in 2025. Seeing how the tech establishment envisioned AI’s rollout into mainstream culture struck her as too limited. “Our options right now are join or die. Keep up with the AI bus or be a Luddite and get off your phone,” Gole says. Era offered a third way, built more from the ground up. “We want people’s feedback, and we want to create this new world that you guys are the center of,” she says. Dehong Hao’s Publisher, 2026, (vintage rotary telephone, microcomputer, inkjet printer, paper, custom software). [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] Era’s intent is to provide the building blocks that make it easier for people to harness AI in their own specific and bespoke ways, breaking free from reliance on a phone to mediate its usage. The company’s puck device is envisioned as the computer inside whatever device a user wants to make, with the ability to access more than 15 different AI models and an interface that can adapt it to whatever task a user might imagine. “Your tools can feel more retro in the sense that you know what each one is for, you use it, each interaction is meant to end, and you put it away,” Gole says. In the AI-enabled future Era’s cofounders envision, people get to determine what, precisely, their devices are supposed to do, whether it’s a fridge magnet that delivers French cooking lessons or an e-ink display that reacts to the double-tap of a button to display the current time in Canberra, Australia. “It enables people’s individuality to exist within an AI world that makes a very smooth median of everyone,” Gole adds. Make hardware weird again Joel Simon’s LIFEFORM, 2026, (ceramic, Mac Mini, laser projector, Qwen 3.8). [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] A few blocks away from Era’s quirky gadget collection, a different kind of AI hardware is taking shape. The much-hyped AI device from OpenAI and Io is taking final form inside the studio of LoveFrom, Ive’s closely guarded design firm. My recently planned visit to the studio was scuttled because OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was stopping by later in the day, and “everything is out,” someone at the company told me. With Ive’s Apple design prestige and OpenAI’s market-driving muscle, many believe the forthcoming device could be the zeitgeisty iPhone of the AI age. People have reportedly taken to flying drones over LoveFrom’s studios hoping to catch a glimpse of whatever it is through now-shaded skylights. Others are skeptical there will be a next dominant device form factor like the iPhone, or that consumers even want one to emerge. Sebastian Bidegain and Harry Isaac‘s company, Noware, is betting there will be a market—or many markets—for much more niche tech devices. Their first product is a 128-gigabyte USB data stick, but one encased in a jewelry-inspired enclosure and glammed out with a tiny screen for customizable low-res animations. Designed to be worn as a necklace or attached as a bag charm, it’s an unexpected and flamboyant take on the banal task of carrying and sharing digital files. “We wanted some of the electronics in our lives to be more expressive and playful and just weird,” Isaac says. Noware garnered enough in presales to fund production of the first batch of the device, named Puff, and its founders have managed to climb the learning curve of working with tech and jewelry manufacturers in China to actually get it built. “It’s difficult to manufacture. And that is maybe part of the reason why another bigger company hasn’t done something like this,” Bidegain says. “But I think that’s part of what makes it really cool.” Bidegain and Isaac see barriers lowering all around, from the technology they use to design and prototype devices to the factories’ increasing ability to manufacture smaller batches of products. “For most other products there’s a range of options, and I think technology is going to be the same,” Isaac says. “I just think that the field is opening up more now that it’s becoming more accessible, and we want to be one of those options.” Mina Fahmi also sees potential in niche tech devices. His startup, Sandbar, is building a wearable AI ring for note-taking, which sounds not all that different from the AI pins, pendants, and charms coming out from companies like Meta, Plaud, and Friend. But Sandbar’s ring, called Stream, isn’t trying to record everything. Instead, Stream is intended to be used to record specific thoughts from its wearer, who pushes a small integrated button and then whispers those thoughts directly into the ring. “A lot of people want to remember things without pulling out their phone,” Fahmi says. On a recent video call, he brings his Stream ring up to his mouth and begins whispering. It’s so quiet I can’t hear him through his computer’s microphone, yet the ring picks up every word he says. It’s a way of reducing what Fahmi calls the friction of using voice to interact with technology, especially for personal thoughts or sensitive subjects. Stream, with its highly attuned microphone, is meant specifically for people to promptly record what they have in mind as easily as possible. It’s a use case that Fahmi admits is on the fringe. There are plenty of other AI tools for capturing and summarizing conversations and work meetings, he concedes, but says not enough of them are built to help people record their own thoughts, ideas, and reflections. “We started Sandbar because we believed we would need new interfaces to fully realize the potential of AI for expanding human expression,” he says. “We’re not out here trying to sell a million units in year one,” Fahmi adds. “What’s been clear to us is that it’s more key to create a thing that people really get value out of than to litter the earth with electronics.” Tech gets personal [Photo: Alexa Trevino for Fast Company] Back at TIAT’s exhibition opening, where a harpist is putting away her instrument and a DJ is setting up her decks, the crowd is thickening. Ken Kocienda stands out, and not just because he’s multiple decades older than most of the people in the room. Kocienda is arguably a member of the tech establishment that many in the exhibition are trying to rebel against. As a principal software engineer at Apple, he helped make the first iPhones, and is credited with creating its infamous keyboard autocorrect. He was also the head of product engineering at Humane. Kocienda’s at the exhibition to see what some of the younger generations are trying to do with their technology. As someone who’s been coding since the 1980s, he’s forever curious about where software and hardware will go next, and he’s working on his own project to improve AI-assisted software development. He sees AI as opening up the potential for new forms of technology, especially special-purpose devices that run counter to the indispensable multitool approach of the iPhone. “I think the more personal we make technology, the more willing people are going to be to integrate it into their lives,” he says. But that doesn’t mean Kocienda is abandoning his iPhone. “Computing paradigms don’t go away,” he says, arguing that major developments in technology build on each other while also changing the role of previous innovations. He sees a time when personally specific devices are what we primarily use, while our phones stay mostly tucked in pockets or bags, more utility than tool. “Even mainframes are still in use today,” he says. MIT’s Coelho, who has a few students with projects in the TIAT show, says this moment of technological advancement is opening the doors to a wide range of new products and companies. “I think there’s an opportunity for thousands of startups to come up in this space,” he says. The form these new devices will take is hard to predict, but there may be some seeds of that future in the TIAT exhibition. For TIAT founder Ash Herr, the purpose of the space is to expose more people to these emerging ideas, and to have people from across the technology and arts spectrums cross-pollinate. “I want people who are all in on their full-time tech jobs and people who are more feral to come together, learn, laugh, and ideate,” she says. What, if anything, comes out of that is unclear. But for the creative technologists in this growing movement, the time seems ripe for offering up something new, and the tools are in their hands.

In a spare and cavernous former eyewear emporium near the luxury stores of San Francisco’s Union Square, a motley group of tech devices is spread out across display counters and pedestals. One is a desktop computer shaped like a cartoon frog. Another is an e-ink laptop controlled by buttons made of felt. Nearby, there’s an AI assistant hidden inside a fuzzy parrot meant to perch on a user’s shoulder.

The space is like some bizarro Apple Store, but instead of offering futuristic devices you didn’t know you needed, it’s a showcase of devices you didn’t know could even exist.

Sources indicate that this store is not a store, but a three-year-old gallery called the Intersection of Art and Technology, or TIAT, which hosts a near-constant stream of events, meetups, and exhibitions focused on experimentation among self-described creative technologists. The devices are part of TIAT’s latest group exhibition, Every Thing Computer, which explores “playful computing” and experimental interfaces.

Some are clearly one-off art projects (see the punchable oversize keyboard escape button and the computer mouse shaped like female genitalia), but others are more earnest and commercial attempts to reimagine what we want our devices to be.

Sources indicate that many of the people showing at TIAT, who consider themselves both artists and technologists, are building these devices as physical proof that an alternative to the current Silicon Valley ecosystem is possible. They are part of a growing community in San Francisco and beyond reconsidering how technology can bring people more joy—or at least give them more agency over the devices they use.

Industry observers note that “We like to call this the rebel alliance of creatives that are trying to go out and have better ideas for what the future can be,” notes Liz Dorman, whose San Francisco-based startup, Era, sponsored the exhibition at TIAT. Her tech giant is building a platform for customizable AI devices, putting her near the center of the creative technologist ecosystem.

Thanks to AI tools, more nimble factories, and the motivation of a generation who grew up with smartphones in their hands, the prospect of developing new kinds of devices is more possible, and desirable, than ever before.

“We’ve had so much lock-in and walled-garden effects because of the App Store and because of how hard it is to make hardware,” Dorman states. “That now is finally changing.”.

But taking down Major Tech is beside the point for many of the people in the creative technology community. Instead of competing at the same massive scale as the tech giants, these ambitious, and predominantly young, tech people are trying to build fresh hardware that both serves a niche audience and broadens the spectrum of consumer technology. The more commercial among these devices are just now starting to ship, and they’re meeting the market in a moment of highly anticipated AI hardware coming from companies with trillion-dollar valuations.

“That’s precisely why we need artists to provide perspectives on all this new technology,” indicates Ash Herr, TIAT’s founder.

Industry observers note that while there are no hard numbers on how significant this scene is, there are emerging and established creative technology groups and meetups from San Francisco to Latest York, including TIAT, Physical Futures, Fidget Camp, Gray Area, the School for Poetic Computation, the New Museum’s New Inc., the Resonant Computing Lab, and more. Many have academic roots in vaunted computing and human-computer interface labs like Carnegie Mellon’s Human-Computer Interaction Institute, New York University’s Interactive Telecommunications Program, and several labs at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

In a recent development, “There are a lot of students who are kind of tired of computers,” says Marcelo Coelho, director of MIT’s Design Intelligence Lab. “In many ways, their response is to invent their own computer.”.

People exploring these concepts often self-describe as creative technologists, but some see their work more broadly as indie hardware, while others find it to be closer to fashion hardware or even bespoke “couture computing.” The through line is a desire to break out of the winner-takes-all mindset that’s fueled the Big Tech companies in recent years.

“Pretty much the story of San Francisco right now is all these people with egos being like, ‘I know what the future is. Let me tell you what the future is.’ And you can’t edit or change anything,” Dorman says. “A lot of the underlying stuff that’s happening in creative tech is coming from those feelings of we actually want to take ownership over our technology.”.

Sources indicate that dorman describes this as a shift to “couture technology,” where a more open ecosystem would allow people to customize hardware to their own specific needs. “It’s like you can sew your own shirt, or you can buy it from your favorite creative, or you can get it mass-produced,” Dorman states.

Recent findings suggest that doing it yourself is nothing new for the modern tech world, of course. Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak built the earliest version of what would become an Apple computer in a bedroom. And it’s an ethos that’s carried through the years, according to Barry Threw, executive director of Gray Area, the San Francisco-based art and technology nonprofit that’s been leading tech-centered events, education, and research programs since 2008.

“Open hardware and people wanting to have some agency and access to these kinds of tools is always a trend that’s going on,” Threw claims. He points to the mid-2010s, when there was a lot of interest in DIY hardware, through events like Maker Faire, and open-source software, printed circuit boards, and microcontrollers from Arduino and Raspberry Pi.

It has been revealed that AI has opened latest opportunities for this mode of creation, with vibe coding making it vastly easier to create digital tools and applications. “It makes it more attainable for folks who start doing interesting hardware and software DIY things because the software side of it doesn’t become such a burden,” Threw says.

It has been revealed that but AI has also spurred a related backlash, as the leading AI labs and companies pursue advancements at a pace that has even some of its own executives worried for the future of humanity. As those few big companies appear to be guiding the direction of AI’s development, nearly three-quarters of people are concerned about what they are creating.

Recent findings suggest that “When people have less confidence in the direction of their public services and institutions, not just in tech but in general, I find this DIY ethos happening,” Threw claims. “They go back to trying to take some agency into their own hands and build their own tools.”.

Sources indicate that in San Francisco and other tech hubs, the concern is also personal. Software engineers, once the backbone of Silicon Valley and the tech world at large, are finding themselves replaced by the very technology they once created, sparking existential crises about what, if anything, they can do next. Creative technology is proving to be one alternative.

In a recent development, “Across the technology spectrum, people are searching for where meaning and value and creativity lie when it’s not possible just to be a software engineer anymore because that stuff’s getting automated,” Threw says. “As the creativity around software development has been taken over by these AI tools, hardware is kind of the next frontier.”.

Kelin Zhang holds up a camera and takes a photo of my face on her computer screen. We’re on a video call, the pandemic-cemented default meeting mode mediated through phones or laptops with built-in cameras. The camera she’s holding, though, is not some add-on element of another device. It’s a stand-alone camera meant for taking photos. But there’s a twist: Instead of actually producing a photo, the camera uses its lens to capture and process an image and then, for reasons that are not immediately apparent, uses AI to write and print a poem about it.

In a recent development, poetry Camera is Zhang’s pet project turned consumer product. Conceived on a whim with her friend Ryan Mather back in January 2023, it was willed into being through a combination of online tutorials, AI vibe coding, open-source printed circuit boards, and 3D printers. After a weekend of poking around, they built a working prototype.

“I was like, wow, it’s a lot easier to get started in hardware than I thought,” she indicates.

It has been revealed that zhang wasn’t starting from scratch. She has a bachelor’s degree in computer science from MIT, and had spent nearly a decade working in digital product design. When she had the idea for Poetry Camera, she had just left her job as staff product designer at Twitter, which had recently been acquired by Elon Musk. “I got a front-row seat to everything and I thought, You know what? I’m kind of done with corporate tech,” she says.

Industry observers note that chatGPT had been released publicly just a few months earlier, and Zhang had the sense that big changes were coming to the tech world. She decided to take a year to explore what it could look like to create an AI-first digital design practice. Poetry Camera was the first thing she prototyped.

“With AI, it’s only going to get easier and easier,” Zhang states. “If you’re motivated to work on a project, it lowers the barrier by so much.”.

Almost four years later, Poetry Camera is a $349 consumer product that’s garnered fans in both the tech and poetry worlds. Anthropic, a longtime supporter, put in a rush order last winter for a batch to hand out at a Super Bowl party. Poetry Camera’s success has buoyed Zhang to start a physical product studio called Tenderworld. “People are excited and delighted by form factors that aren’t just apps trapped behind the screen of a phone or a computer,” she states.

Zhang picks up the Poetry Camera she used to take my photo and rips out the receipt-like thermal paper printed with the poem it created. But instead of focusing on my face on Zhang’s screen, the camera was looking past her laptop at a shelf of other Poetry Cameras in boxes. The poem it wrote was about itself.

Like a stall at a seedy flea market, there’s a table in a storefront window near San Francisco’s Transamerica Pyramid that’s covered with dozens of random consumer technology gadgets. Spanning the past five decades, they include a Macintosh Newton tablet, several varieties of early-2000s flip phones, an alien-esque cassette tape player, an AM/FM radio shaped like a peanut M&M, and multiple garish wristwatches with built-in cameras. Nestled among these are newer devices, like the Humane AI Pin and the Rabbit R1.

Sources indicate that this display is part of the office of Era, the startup Dorman cofounded to build a software platform and hardware for customizable AI devices. None of the items on the table are for sale—this being San Francisco, people do pop in and ask—but rather they’re a nostalgia-tickling reminder that tech devices used to look a lot different from the rectangular phones in our pockets today. The display is a subtle prod at the bland landscape of modern hardware.

Why can’t tech look like this again?

Industry observers note that “It hasn’t felt very optimistic recently, especially with all the releases happening by Big Tech companies,” Dorman states inside Era’s office, two 3D printers humming in the background. “It feels like these companies are not only out of touch with people, but they’re forcing technology onto people that they don’t actually want.”.

Sources indicate that era, which has raised more than $11 million in funding, was founded to offer people the chance to decide what they want their tech to look like and how it can function, starting with the development of a puck-like AI core that it sees as the open-source basis of highly customizable devices. Calling itself “a small Gen Z team raised with smartphones,” the manufacturer is mostly twentysomethings who were still in grade school when the first iPhone was released. Dorman, who grew up in New Jersey jailbreaking the early iPhone models, was dismayed when Apple made that kind of custom hacking impossible.

Industry observers note that later, after an internship at Apple, she got her own job in Big Tech working for Humane, the company cofounded by former Apple executive Imran Chaudhri that raised more than $230 million to create a post-iPhone screenless AI device. That device, the AI Pin, flopped, and Dorman was not surprised. The fact that its form factor so closely resembled a police officer’s body-worn camera was one major problem, but so were more aesthetic concerns. Dorman, for one, thought there should be more variety than the single black-and-white color palette, and more of an embrace of the flexibility AI offers.

“I hated the voice and personality we chose for the device. It was the equivalent of giving everyone an iPhone and being like, you can’t change the wallpaper. And I was like, ‘Well, I want to change it,’” she says. And she did, hacking her AI Pin to use the voice of the blogger-narrator from the television teen drama Gossip Girl. She started showing off the device to her friends, and using it much more often than before. “That is very much the feeling that we’re chasing at Era.”.

Dorman cofounded Era in 2025, teaming up with two other young AI-leaning technologists who were similarly concerned about the direction Substantial Tech and AI companies were heading.

Recent findings suggest that “I think something that’s really true across the consumer landscape is everybody feels left behind by AI,” Era cofounder Megan Gole says. She previously worked at venture capital firm Sutter Hill Ventures, which was involved in OpenAI’s acquisition of former Apple design chief Jony Ive’s AI hardware startup Io in 2025. Seeing how the tech establishment envisioned AI’s rollout into mainstream culture struck her as too limited.

“Our options right now are join or die. Keep up with the AI bus or be a Luddite and get off your phone,” Gole says. Era offered a third way, built more from the ground up. “We want people’s feedback, and we want to create this upcoming world that you guys are the center of,” she says.

Era’s intent is to provide the building blocks that make it easier for people to harness AI in their own specific and bespoke ways, breaking free from reliance on a phone to mediate its usage. The tech giant’s puck device is envisioned as the computer inside whatever device a user wants to make, with the ability to access more than 15 different AI models and an interface that can adapt it to whatever task a user might imagine.

“Your tools can feel more retro in the sense that you know what each one is for, you use it, each interaction is meant to end, and you put it away,” Gole notes.

In the AI-enabled future Era’s cofounders envision, people get to determine what, precisely, their devices are supposed to do, whether it’s a fridge magnet that delivers French cooking lessons or an e-ink display that reacts to the double-tap of a button to display the current time in Canberra, Australia.

“It enables people’s individuality to exist within an AI world that makes a very smooth median of everyone,” Gole adds.

In a recent development, A few blocks away from Era’s quirky gadget collection, a different kind of AI hardware is taking shape. The much-hyped AI device from OpenAI and Io is taking final form inside the studio of LoveFrom, Ive’s closely guarded design firm. My recently planned visit to the studio was scuttled because OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was stopping by later in the day, and “everything is out,” someone at the tech giant told me.

With Ive’s Apple design prestige and OpenAI’s market-driving muscle, many believe the forthcoming device could be the zeitgeisty iPhone of the AI age. People have reportedly taken to flying drones over LoveFrom’s studios hoping to catch a glimpse of whatever it is through now-shaded skylights.

Others are skeptical there will be a next dominant device form factor like the iPhone, or that consumers even want one to emerge.

Recent findings suggest that sebastian Bidegain and Harry Isaac‘s firm, Noware, is betting there will be a market—or many markets—for much more niche tech devices. Their first product is a 128-gigabyte USB data stick, but one encased in a jewelry-inspired enclosure and glammed out with a tiny screen for customizable low-res animations. Designed to be worn as a necklace or attached as a bag charm, it’s an unexpected and flamboyant take on the banal task of carrying and sharing digital files.

“We wanted some of the electronics in our lives to be more expressive and playful and just weird,” Isaac says.

Recent findings suggest that noware garnered enough in presales to fund production of the first batch of the device, named Puff, and its founders have managed to climb the learning curve of working with tech and jewelry manufacturers in China to actually get it built. “It’s difficult to manufacture. And that is maybe part of the reason why another bigger firm hasn’t done something like this,” Bidegain says. “But I think that’s part of what makes it really cool.”.

In a recent development, bidegain and Isaac see barriers lowering all around, from the technology they use to design and prototype devices to the factories’ increasing ability to manufacture smaller batches of products. “For most other products there’s a range of options, and I think technology is going to be the same,” Isaac says. “I just think that the field is opening up more now that it’s becoming more accessible, and we want to be one of those options.”.

Mina Fahmi also sees potential in niche tech devices. His startup, Sandbar, is building a wearable AI ring for note-taking, which sounds not all that different from the AI pins, pendants, and charms coming out from companies like Meta, Plaud, and Friend. But Sandbar’s ring, called Stream, isn’t trying to record everything. Instead, Stream is intended to be used to record specific thoughts from its wearer, who pushes a small integrated button and then whispers those thoughts directly into the ring.

“A lot of people want to remember things without pulling out their phone,” Fahmi states.

On a recent video call, he brings his Stream ring up to his mouth and begins whispering. It’s so quiet I can’t hear him through his computer’s microphone, yet the ring picks up every word he notes. It’s a way of reducing what Fahmi calls the friction of using voice to interact with technology, especially for personal thoughts or sensitive subjects. Stream, with its highly attuned microphone, is meant specifically for people to promptly record what they have in mind as easily as possible.

According to recent reports, it’s a use case that Fahmi admits is on the fringe. There are plenty of other AI tools for capturing and summarizing conversations and work meetings, he concedes, but says not enough of them are built to help people record their own thoughts, ideas, and reflections. “We started Sandbar because we believed we would need newly introduced interfaces to fully realize the potential of AI for expanding human expression,” he says.

“We’re not out here trying to sell a million units in year one,” Fahmi adds. “What’s been clear to us is that it’s more important to create a thing that people really get value out of than to litter the earth with electronics.”.

Why Portugal’s No. 7 jersey will forever look different

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Portuguese Football Federation can’t retire superstar soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo’s No.
  • The Portuguese Football Federation can’t retire superstar soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo’s No.
  • It has been revealed that portugal’s Saturday game against Denmark was the team’s first since Ronaldo retired earlier this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Portuguese Football Federation can’t retire superstar soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo’s No. 7 due to strict FIFA rules around player numbers. Instead, the team got creative and used a different font. A No. 7 with a cross stroke through it will be used on kits for players who wear the number from here on out. Portugal’s Saturday game against Denmark was the team’s first since Ronaldo retired earlier this month. The entire team came out in “Ronaldo 7” jerseys with the old-style number before the match to pay tribute to the player who captained the team for 19 years. Then during the match, player Carlos Forbs wore the new cross-stroke 7 for the Portuguese national team. “This is yet another way to immortalize the meaning of such a special number and honor the legacy it represents,” the team said in a statement. [Photos: Octavio Passos/Getty Images, Joao Bravo/Sports Press Photo/Getty Images] Other professional teams and leagues retire numbers to honor legendary players. In 1997, MLB retired the No. 42 for Jackie Robinson, the league’s first Black player and a former National League MVP. The NHL retired 99 in 2000 for Wayne Gretzky, who still holds the league’s record for most career points. The NBA’s Chicago Bulls will never again have a 4, 10, 23, or 33 after retiring them for Jerry Sloan, Bob Love, Michael Jordan, and Scottie Pippen, respectively. The international football body doesn’t give teams or players as much freedom with numbers during its tournaments, as each team has to use all consecutive numbers from 1 to 26 for their 26-person rosters. That meant that when Lionel Messi retired in October, the Argentine Football Association didn’t retire his No. 10, despite the fact that Claudio Tapia, AFA’s president, said in 2024 it would be retired. Portugal’s solution is a clever, unconventional work-around. If you can’t change the number, at least change how the number looks. Fonts with alternative characters, or characters with multiple design variations, give designers flexibility to add optional elements like swashes, flairs, or cross strokes on characters like 7 and Z. By adding a cross stroke to their 7, Portugal figured out how to honor a retired legend with a number they technically can’t retire.

The Portuguese Football Federation can’t retire superstar soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo’s No. 7 due to strict FIFA rules around player numbers. Instead, the team got creative and used a different font. A No. 7 with a cross stroke through it will be used on kits for players who wear the number from here on out.

It has been revealed that portugal’s Saturday game against Denmark was the team’s first since Ronaldo retired earlier this month. The entire team came out in “Ronaldo 7” jerseys with the old-style number before the match to pay tribute to the player who captained the team for 19 years. Then during the match, player Carlos Forbs wore the upcoming cross-stroke 7 for the Portuguese national team.

“This is yet another way to immortalize the meaning of such a special number and honor the legacy it represents,” the team noted in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that other professional teams and leagues retire numbers to honor legendary players. In 1997, MLB retired the No. 42 for Jackie Robinson, the league’s first Black player and a former National League MVP. The NHL retired 99 in 2000 for Wayne Gretzky, who still holds the league’s record for most career points. The NBA’s Chicago Bulls will never again have a 4, 10, 23, or 33 after retiring them for Jerry Sloan, Bob Love, Michael Jordan, and Scottie Pippen, respectively.

Sources indicate that the international football body doesn’t give teams or players as much freedom with numbers during its tournaments, as each team has to use all consecutive numbers from 1 to 26 for their 26-person rosters. That meant that when Lionel Messi retired in October, the Argentine Football Association didn’t retire his No. 10, despite the fact that Claudio Tapia, AFA’s president, said in 2024 it would be retired.

Portugal’s solution is a clever, unconventional work-around. If you can’t change the number, at least change how the number looks. Fonts with alternative characters, or characters with multiple design variations, give designers flexibility to add optional elements like swashes, flairs, or cross strokes on characters like 7 and Z.

By adding a cross stroke to their 7, Portugal figured out how to honor a retired legend with a number they technically can’t retire.

According to recent reports, picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that proposal. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide shows how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

Industry observers note that wooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Industry observers note that medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company states you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Industry observers note that saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you want one of the U.S. Mint’s $1 coins featuring President Donald Trump’s portrait, you might need to purchase in bulk. The Mint unveiled its new limited-edition $1 Trump coins will be available beginning November 19 in 1,000-coin bags. The 1,000-coin bags weigh about 20 pounds, and due to shipping weight constraints, there’s a maximum of two units per order, although there’s no household order limit. One bag costs $1,365 including shipping. The Mint first released the $1 Trump coins in September, but the $65 25-coin roll and $154.50 100-coin bag formats that they were once available in are no longer in stock. [Photo: U.S. Mint] That means those looking to buy them will either have to purchase the 1,000-coin bag, or buy a 24-karat gold proof coin that comes in a clamshell case (the latter option will also be available November 19, though the Mint hasn’t noted how much it will cost). The Mint states its mintage limit for the bags is 15,100, and 75,000 for the gold proof coin. All told, that’s a lot of coins with a living president’s face on them for a country that traditionally doesn’t put living presidents on its money. Trump is the first to do it in a century (Calvin Coolidge was the last). U.S. law has prohibited the country’s currency from depicting living presidents since 2005, but the Trump administration treated a 2020 law allowing for commemorative coins for the country’s 250th anniversary this year as a work-around to design a Trump coin. [Photo: U.S. Mint] Joseph Menna, chief engraver of the U.S. Mint, designed the coin. It shows Trump’s scowling face from his second-term official portrait taken by chief White House photographer Daniel Torok on the heads side along with the inscriptions for “Liberty,” “In God We Trust,” and “1776-2026.” The tails side shows the presidential seal. The coins are legal tender, though the Mint promotes them as commemorative collectibles. A pair of Senate Democrats introduced the Change Corruption Act earlier this year, which would have prohibited the coin from being minted, but it was never brought up for a vote under the Republican-controlled Senate. Under Democratic control, Trump could have a harder time putting his face on U.S. money going forward. With time running out, the Mint is putting out its Trump coins in bulk and at a discount. While the 1,000-coin bag is a bigger up-front payment, it’s also the cheapest these coins have been sold for. The 25-coin roll was sold at a 160% markup, and the 100-coin bag was sold at a 54.5% markup, while the 1,000-coin bag is being sold at a 36.5% markup. In the case of Trump’s coin, it costs money to spend money.

China engineers behind J-35 fighter jet pioneer 3D-printed load-bearing structures in military aircraft

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, the developers of China’s J-35 fighter jet platform, used metal 3D printing to create large primary load-bearing structures for military aircraft applications.
  • Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, a research organization under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), has been working on 3D-printed aircraft components since 2003.
  • The engineers are no strangers to large 3D-printed components: in 2005, they achieved secondary load-bearing structures; then, in 2012, large primary load-bearing titanium alloy structures, earning additive manufacturing expert Wang Huaming and his team China’s National Technological Invention Award.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, the developers of China’s J-35 fighter jet platform, used metal 3D printing to create large primary load-bearing structures for military aircraft applications. Global Times reports the structure is over 16.4 feet (five meters) in length, using segmented printing and fusion techniques.

Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, a research organization under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), has been working on 3D-printed aircraft components since 2003. The impressively large 3D-printed components are the culmination of decades of research and development of various metal additive manufacturing techniques.

The engineers are no strangers to large 3D-printed components: in 2005, they achieved secondary load-bearing structures; then, in 2012, large primary load-bearing titanium alloy structures, earning additive manufacturing expert Wang Huaming and his team China’s National Technological Invention Award.

Recently, however, the team created a primary load-bearing structure even larger, at over 16.4 feet. The massive component is not printed in one piece, as printing such a large structure faces warping and cracking problems, as stated in Progress and Challenges of Laser Direct Manufacturing of Large Titanium Structural Components, published in the Chinese Journal of Lasers. To avoid these problems, two techniques were employed: Segmented Additive Manufacturing (SAM) and additive fusion joining. It sounds like fancy words to say it was printed separately and welded, and it technically wouldn’t be wrong — but the key distinction is that it is part of the whole workflow; basically, metal 3D printing into the intentionally designed gaps between the components and creating one whole printed piece.

Additive manufacturing eliminates the need for expensive molds and multi-part construction. Titanium alloys are notoriously difficult to machine, cast components are usually weak, and joining parts using bolts and screws is additional labor — metal 3D printing solves all of this by creating a strong printed part in the desired shape in one large piece, minimizing the need for additional fasteners. By eliminating molds, the team can iterate much faster and create more complex structures that would otherwise not be possible with traditional manufacturing techniques.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, homebuilders aren’t slashing prices on new homes, but they’ve found another way to entice buyers—they’re slashing mortgage rates. Because affordability remains a key reason why many would-be homebuyers remain on the sidelines, builders are offering reduced mortgage rates to get people over the threshold. Americans who bought a new home paid an average starting mortgage rate of 5.01% in the third quarter, compared with a 6.15% rate for buyers of existing homes, according to a report released Tuesday by Realtor.com. Such incentives aren’t new. Many builders have long leveraged their relationships with lenders or have offered mortgage rate buydowns to help buyers during periods of high interest rates. And even if the incentives are temporary, they can add up meaningfully: Austin-based Realtor.com estimates that homebuyers could save nearly $3,100 in interest on the purchase of a $400,000 home with a 10% down payment in the first year of homeownership compared with someone buying the same-priced existing home at the average starter rates. Though these sorts of adjustments aren’t reflected in the listing price, it highlights how builders are adapting to the affordability challenges in the housing market, according to Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. “Reduced mortgage rates can help make a new home more affordable for buyers while allowing builders to hold asking prices relatively steady,” he remarked in a statement. #23600. Tech Report: The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2469 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2469 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory.
  • Even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM.
  • But expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory. Part of the company’s occasional (and all-but-dead) dip into hardware products, the Shield Tablet — and its revitalized K1 follow-up, which I also owned through a recall program on the original — carried me through the back half of college, frequently keeping my Chromebook in my backpack in lieu of a mini Bluetooth keyboard or the Shield Tablet’s built-in stylus. Its front-firing speakers made it great for movie-watching, and while I’m not much of a mobile gamer, I did find it to be a great device for emulation, especially when paired with an external controller.

Even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM. And considering the market for Android tablets in general, it’s not all too surprising to see very few companies trying to make headway into offering a miniature, gaming-focused tablet that can easily be thrown in a backpack. Lenovo, however, has managed to fill its spot quite well. 9to5Google’s own Ben Schoon found himself smitten with the Gen 3 model nearly two years ago, and now, its Gen 5 successor has found its way into my nostalgic hands.

But expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016. Whether the Legion Tab Gen 5 can win over your heart really depends on your patience with some old-school Android jank — and whether your wallet can withstand an exceptionally-high asking price. Still, with recent advancements in PC emulation, it’s hard to say Lenovo isn’t onto something.

Industry observers note that considering the decade between their respective releases, I’m actually quite surprised just how much this tablet reminds me of the original Shield Tablet. Its 8.8-inch 16:10 LCD panel combined with a boxy matte-black design and a near-identical weight meant that I immediately felt at home holding this thing in my hands. You lose out on a couple of clutch features — most notably the built-in stylus — but largely speaking, this feels like the correct size and shape for a miniature gaming tablet.

Still, it’s not all perfect. Take, for example, the completely unnecessary camera bump that prevents this slate from properly laying flat on a desk. No one is buying this thing to use the camera, and judging by my very limited experience trying it out, I’m fairly confident whatever potato sensor is shoved in here would fit fine flush with the chassis. I’m pretty fed up with OEMs leaning on camera bumps to make any device look or feel more premium than it actually is, and that goes double quadruple for tablets like this.

Just like its predecessor, this thing still picks up smudges and fingerprints at an unreasonable level, its matte-black finish unable to hide anything. 360 grams is also a little heavier than I’d expect for a slate of this size, though to be fair, it’s much more noticeable in portrait than landscape. Holding the tablet with two hands to watch a movie or make my way through another round of Balatro made its top-heaviness much less noticeable.

According to recent reports, this display is sharp and fast — with one minor caveat — and reasonably bright in all circumstances except direct sunlight thanks to its 600 nits of brightness (and 800 in HBM). Really, it’s the LCD of it all that gets me here; this thing is nearly $1,000, and the lack of OLED alone makes it difficult to recommend at this price. It’s not an outright bad panel, but I found its contrast levels to be pretty lacking, with most blacks only ever showing up as dark grays on-screen.

It has been revealed that oh, and that caveat: On two different occasions, I caught the tablet stuck in 60Hz mode, regardless of what refresh rate option I selected in settings. Switching back and forth between modes a few times eventually unstuck it, but it’s definitely a bug worth being aware of.

I think I’d feel a lot better about recommending this to someone looking for a content consumption device if this screen looked a little more premium. Your mileage may vary though — if you can get your hands on a demo unit before buying one, if only to see the display, I’d recommend it. For everyone else, this price tag might have you waiting for the OLED panel rumored to be arriving on next year’s successor.

At $900 — or potentially more, considering this tablet actually launched at $850 — the Legion Tablet’s hardware leaves something to be desired. Biometrics are the most obvious weak spot; camera-based face unlock is the only biometric option provided here, without a fingerprint scanner in sight. I wouldn’t blame some if they saw this as a dealbreaker, because even if you’re willing to put up with the security concerns that a basic front-facing camera brings to the table, I can promise you you’ll be typing the code in all the time. Whether you’re trying to unlock in a darker environment or it’s just been four hours since you last unlocked the slate, make sure you have your pin memorized.

It has been revealed that if you’re primarily buying this as a content consumption machine, I think you’ll mostly have a great time. Lenovo built stereo sound into this slate, but did so in one of the smartest ways I’ve ever seen, ensuring all speakers are located to the right side along the bottom and top of the device. This might sound a little unbalanced in portrait mode, but in landscape, it guarantees you’re never actually covering up the speakers while holding the slate in your hands, something practically every other equivalent tablet is guilty of. No headphone jack here, unfortunately, something I would’ve liked to have seen on a gaming-focused device.

Sources indicate that I find battery life genuinely difficult to judge on tablets, especially if you don’t pick it up every single hour of every single day, but I’ve been impressed overall with the Legion Tab’s longevity. Some weekend YouTube binge watching sessions at relatively high brightness settings left me with plenty of juice in the tank, and its standby time between sessions has been excellent. Obviously, if you’re really pushing your graphical limits on this thing — or if you’re emulating non-native software through something like DroidDeck — you’re going to see a bit of a dip, but combined with fast charging and two USB-C ports for both portrait and landscape access, battery life gets a substantial thumbs-up from me.

Recent findings suggest that lenovo’s packed a couple of accessories in the box with this thing, but I wouldn’t get too excited. While it’s nice to see a 68W charger included for those aforementioned fast top-offs, the included folio case is just awful. Not only does the triangle-shaped flap barely stick together to form a proper stand, but one of the corners of my case was loose enough to frequently flex back and forth. Holding the tablet while wrapped in its case just felt bad, in the way that so many bundled cases often feel, and a quick look at Amazon shows that basically no recognizable brand — or unrecognizable, for that matter — has stepped up to offer something better.

The Legion Tablet also includes a screen protector in the box, if that’s how you roll.

Unsurprisingly, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in here can handle effectively anything you dare to throw at it. While my mobile games might be limited to more casual, indie fare like Balatro — and, by the by, if you’re still enjoying Balatro a couple of years later, the size and shape of this device makes it perfect — graphically-intense games played fine. Asphalt Legends or the HoYoverse games might not be my cup of tea, but they perform excellently on this device, and compared to the 12-inch tablets companies like Samsung and Amazon have become obsessed with, the display size here actually feels perfect.

It has been revealed that we definitely have to talk about emulation, though, because it’s increasingly becoming the main focus of mobile gamers everywhere, and this feels like a tablet perfectly designed for something like DroidDeck. Getting Steam emulation — complete with the Deck’s usual Substantial Picture mode UI — available as an application on the Legion Tab Gen 5 takes all of two minutes and a handful of taps on your display, and I have to say, I’m pretty shocked at just how impressive the overall experience is right now.

DroidDeck gave me the option to bring my mini gaming tablet experience full-circle. While my Steam library has no shortage of games I think could run without stressing this slate, I wanted to push the envelope a little bit. Persona 3 Reload felt like as good a candidate as any: a modern title that doesn’t necessarily require quick response times and fits virtual controls quite nicely. Plus, most of my gaming time on Nvidia’s tablet a decade ago was spent working through Persona 3 Portable; like poetry, it rhymes. I installed the game, ran it on the Legion Tab, and to my surprise and delight, it was absolutely in a playable state.

It has been revealed that now, there are some caveats here. I did drop the game’s graphics preset to low, and even still, there were some occasional hiccups while running around an early dungeon. The game’s initial intros and disclaimers actually gave the impression the title wouldn’t run at all, but I was able to sneak up on a shadow, use a slash attack to begin the battle — basically the only thing in P3R that remotely requires accurate timing — and issue commands to my player character and party mates.

In a recent development, obviously, your experience emulating Steam titles on the Legion Tab will vary on what you want to play, and with such wide variables between experiences, I probably wouldn’t push most gamers to run out and pick one up right away. It might be early days for DroidDeck, but considering how we’ve already seen it progress, I wouldn’t be surprised to see some buyers picking this up as a Valve-esque take on a gaming tablet.

With all of that power under the hood, though, it’s Lenovo’s take on Android that leaves a lot to be desired. It’s not just that this feels like a rough-and-ready take on AOSP, an unrefined package that would feel more in line with devices from a decade ago, though, yes, that’s half the struggle here. But at its worst, the Legion Tab Gen 5 simply feels unoptimized in daily use.

Scrolling through web pages or various apps often felt sluggish and heavy, like the UI elements on screen never actually match the movement of my finger, and it’s unclear how much of that was due to the refresh rate bug I described above. Auto-rotate was both super finnicky and super sluggish, alternating back and forth between one state or the other, and the auto-rotate button that pops up when it’s disabled would frequently fail to appear. Occasionally, I’d run into app concerns, such as choppy playback on a 1440p YouTube video that got so bad — regardless of what resolution I selected — that I had to fully force close the app in settings to fix it. Even getting the slate to reliably wake up (or not wake up) when picking it up was annoying, as it’s simultaneously sensitive enough to frequently turn on when I don’t want it to, or to stay asleep when I’m trying to unlock it. Inevitably, I turned that setting off.

Sources indicate that you might think that shelling out $900 for an Android tablet would buy you an out from pre-installed bloatware; you’d be wrong. During setup, the Legion Tab attempts to install a whole host of apps and games, including Perplexity, TikTok, Temu, several match-three games that I’ve truly never heard of, and no less than two mahjong and solitaire titles each. In fact, there might actually be three solitaire titles depending on what “Jigsawcard Solitaire Puzzle” is, but I unchecked all of these apps during setup and didn’t deem the title worthy of bothering to check.

While Lenovo has been trying to improve its software upgrade policies on some recent devices, this slate isn’t among that group. To my knowledge, there is no official update schedule for this device, but based on past performance, I’d expect somewhere around 2 OS upgrades and 4 years of security patches, give or take.

Recent findings suggest that I would’ve loved nothing more than to recommend this year’s Legion Tab to small tablet fans and gamers everywhere, but when this thing is $200 more than Apple’s latest iPad Mini — which in and of itself is absolutely overpriced — and $100 more than the base OLED Steam Deck post-price hike, I just have a hard time telling anyone to buy it. Really, its Steam performance was one of the few areas that made me feel truly excited by this thing, but it’s simply too unpredictable an experience at this point (and price) for me to recommend.

Even setting aside the price, there’s simply too much here that feels unfinished or rough around the edges for my liking. A handful of bug fixes and a couple of additional optimization passes could fix a lot of my more minor quibbles, but despite what I just said, you can only ignore the $900 price tag for so long before it bites you in the ass.

We have seen a post-iPad Mini discount bringing this slate to an Apple-matching $700 ahead of the holidays, but even that price is $150 more than its predecessor was at launch without a whole lot to show for it. If you’re looking for a gamer-friendly tiny tablet, I do think Legion is a brand worth keeping your eye on, especially as DroidDeck and other Steam emulation apps continue to evolve. But at this point — and for this price — your best bet is waiting for whatever model follows this one. It might still be stupid expensive, but at least you’ll be getting OLED.

Sources indicate that A decade ago, Nvidia’s Shield Tablet felt like a no-brainer addition to my everyday carry. But in this economy, gamers and tablet fans alike are simply better off dropping $900 elsewhere.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A Harvard-led study estimates that 403 hyperscale U.S.
  • According to recent reports, hyperscale data centers, in this case, refer to sites run by a hyperscale cloud or content provider, or a colocation operator who serves one, with a capacity in the tens of megawatts.
  • Nobody officially counts what the data centers actually draw from the grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A Harvard-led study estimates that 403 hyperscale U.S. data center sites consumed about 82 TWh of electricity in a year, 1.8% of the country’s total, with more than half coming from gas and coal sources, Wired reports. This compares to the entire state of Michigan selling 99 TWh in 2024. The data centers’ pull also put out an estimated 25.7 million metric tons (Mt) of CO2, which is two to three times a 2018 estimate.

According to recent reports, hyperscale data centers, in this case, refer to sites run by a hyperscale cloud or content provider, or a colocation operator who serves one, with a capacity in the tens of megawatts. The 675 candidate sites came from data vendor Baxtel, with 403 confirmed with satellite imagery and building-footprint maps, at an average capacity of 39.9 MW and a median of 36 MW.

Nobody officially counts what the data centers actually draw from the grid. Instead, the electricity is estimated by multiplying each site’s maximum capacity by the hours in a year and an estimate of how hard the data centers run. For CO2 and the source mix, each site is placed in its grid region, of 23 total in the study, with a regional average mix from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). These are then multiplied and added up for the total number. Such estimation methods may reduce the strength of arguments against data center buildouts.

In a recent development, the power is also not evenly laid out, with 142 of the sites located in Virginia alone, taking 21.4 TWh, or about a quarter. PJM, a grid operator for 13 states, including Virginia, and D.C., or America’s largest grid, covers 32.8 TWh, or about 40%, more than any other region. Notably for Virginia, its power draw is actually just a bit below the 22.85 TWh estimate for all U.S. hyperscale sites from 2018. See the table for more details.

Recent findings suggest that not all power is equal — renewables, for example, can be perceived more favorably — and 53.9% of the estimated draw comes from fossil fuels, 38.2% of the total from gas and 15.2% from coal. Renewables cover 25.3% while nuclear handles the remaining 20.9%. Estimates put this in the 21–31 Mt range for CO2 output, versus the 10.5 Mt estimate from 2018.

In a recent development, estimated carbon intensity, though, is lower than the average, at 314 g of CO2 per kWh versus 348 for the entire U.S. grid, or about 10% lower. Admittedly, almost a quarter of the load is in regions dirtier than the U.S. average. The likely reason it’s lower is that the biggest loads lie in PJM territory, which is nuclear-heavy, while Oregon, for its part, is hydro-heavy. The estimates, in this case, use 2023 plant data, and the method does not trace which plant feeds which site and also leaves out clean-power contracts and credits.

Recent findings suggest that the study’s results also lag reality as the window ended in April 2025 and, with how much development there has been for AI, among other things, the footprint “could already be substantially larger now in 2026,” lead author Gianluca Guidi said in a statement. Another concern is that the median site capacity in the study is relatively small compared to upcoming buildouts, with many campuses now planned in the hundreds or thousands of megawatts. On-site power, such as gas plants, also may not show up in grid data.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Official numbers may be forthcoming, though, as the Energy Information Administration’s pilot surveys of data center energy use are complete, and the agency is using them to design a survey of the sector, a spokesperson told Wired. The first pilots, which debuted in March, relied on web surveys and in-person interviews, with 196 companies asked about energy sources, electricity use, plus servers and cooling, although not covering all states. Gauging the direct human impact is next in the chain, with Francesca Dominici, the study’s corresponding author, saying that quantifying health effects is an crucial next step.

  • Despite having closed dozens of restaurants in the last year, Noodles & Company has seen sales at remaining restaurants grow.
