📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, despite having closed dozens of restaurants in the last year, Noodles & Tech giant has seen sales at remaining restaurants grow. Executives at the fast-casual restaurant chain have pointed to a variety of reasons for the improvement. These include more customers dining at nearby locations after store closures; the addition of new, innovative dishes; and improved marketing and restaurant operations. How many Noodles & Company stores are closing? In its third-quarter earnings release, the Colorado-based company remarked it now expects to close between 34 and 36 company-owned and seven to eight franchised restaurants this year, for a total of 41 to 44. (By comparison, Noodles & Company closed 33 company-owned restaurants in 2025.) At the same time, it reported that system-wide comparable sales rose 9.5% in the third quarter. “We continue to see a meaningful improvement in our restaurant-level economics related to our portfolio optimization project,” CFO Mike Hynes said on a November 13 earnings call. Hynes said that during the third quarter, the company closed 12 company-owned restaurants and two franchised locations, and opened one new franchised restaurant. Are more closures happening in 2027? Hynes said the company doesn’t have firm numbers for 2027 closures, but its “best thinking right now would be 10-15 closures next year,” some of which would be natural lease expirations. Overall, the fast-casual chain’s footprint has gotten smaller, third-quarter numbers reveal: As of September 29, the company had 383 restaurants: 306 company-owned and 77 franchised. That’s down about 12% from 435 (349 company-owned and 86 franchised) a year earlier. What Noodles & Company is doing to turn things around Noodles & Company has enjoyed success with its ramen offerings. Its limited-time Chili Garlic Ramen dish attracted new and existing customers. In October, the company made ramen a permanent menu category, adding Gochujang Carbonara Ramen Noodles, Sweet Sesame Steak Ramen Noodles, and Spicy Korean Steak Ramen Noodles. The fast-casual eatery plans to rotate new ramen dishes to the lineup over time. As of Monday’s market close, shares of Noodles & Company (Nasdaq: NDLS) were up an impressive 60.4% year to date. However, the stock is down more than 30% over the last five days since its most recent earnings report.

What is Model Routing in AI?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • In a recent development, "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages.
  • A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

In a recent development, "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages. Most AI apps send both to the same large model and pay large-model prices for each one.

Model routing fixes that. A router looks at each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it, and keeps the expensive model for the requests that need it.

In this guide we'll cover what model routing is, how routers decide, and what it saves. Then we'll build a small router in about 60 lines of JavaScript and run it over 200 customer messages. At one setting it matched a large model's accuracy for about a third of the cost. At another it came within a point and a half for 89% less.

It has been revealed that model routing in AI is the practice of sending each request to the model best suited to it, instead of sending every request to one model. A router sits between your app and a pool of models, reads each request, and picks a model based on what you care about: cost, speed, or quality.

You'll also see it called AI model routing, LLM routing, or LLM model routing. They all mean the same thing. The pool might be a small and a large model from one provider, or models from several providers behind one API.

According to recent reports, the idea rests on one observation: most requests are easy. A small model answers them as well as a large one, in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the price. The router's whole job is finding the hard ones.

The diagram below demonstrates a typical AI model routing architecture.

It has been revealed that model routing works in three steps: the router reads the request, decides which model should answer it, and forwards the request to that model. The middle step is where routers differ. Routing tools decide which model to use in one of four ways.

Rule-based routing uses rules you write by hand. Requests from free-initiative customers go to a small model. Anything tagged as code goes to a coding model. Prompts over a certain length go to a model with a bigger context window. It's simple, predictable, and free to run, but the rules only know what you thought of in advance.

Intelligent model routing uses a model to make the decision. A small, fast classifier reads each request and predicts which model in the pool will answer it well. You'll also see it called smart or dynamic model routing.

Industry observers note that two more terms come up here. Task-aware routing picks a model by the kind of job, like summarising, coding, or answering a support question. Context-aware routing also looks at what surrounds the request, like the conversation so far, the user, or the tools available.

The major platforms work this way. Microsoft describes its Foundry model router as "a trained language model" that picks a model for each prompt in real time. Google indicates Gemini Notebook uses its latest Decisions API as a real-time router, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. I've tested the Google Decisions API against Jev on the same messages we'll use below.

It has been revealed that cascade routing tries the cheapest model first and only moves up when the answer isn't good enough. The usual test is confidence: if the cheap model is sure, keep its answer. If it isn't, send the request to a stronger model. It's also called confidence-based routing, and it's what we'll build below.

A cascade needs no separate classifier, because the first model's own confidence does the routing. The trade-off is that escalated requests pay for two models and wait for both.

In a recent development, fallback routing is about staying up, not saving money. If a model times out, hits a rate limit, or its provider has an outage, the router sends the request to the next model on a list. Most production routers combine fallbacks with one of the three methods above.

The main benefits of model routing in AI systems are lower cost, faster responses, and fewer outages, without giving up quality on the hard requests.

We'll build a cascade router for a job every support tool has: sorting customer messages. Each message gets one of ten labels, like atm support or request refund.

It has been revealed that the test set is 200 messages from Banking77, a public set of banking support messages: ten labels, 20 messages each. They're the same 200 messages from my zero shot classification test, which is where the single-model numbers below come from.

Put both keys in a .env file and run the examples with node --env-file=.env. It's the same setup as in my guide to getting a YouTube API key.

It has been revealed that create router.mjs. The first function sends the message to Jev with one multiple-choice question, and returns the label Jev picked along with its confidence:.

It has been revealed that confidence runs from 0 to 1. When nearly all the probability sits on one label, it's close to 1. When Jev is torn between two labels, it drops.

In a recent development, the second function asks Claude Opus 5.5 the same question. The output_config block limits the answer to one of our labels, so there's no free text to parse. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema explains how that works.

The router itself is about a dozen lines:.

If Jev is at least 80% confident, its answer goes straight back. If not, Claude answers instead. And if Claude fails, the router falls back to Jev's answer, because a shaky answer beats an error page.

Try it on an easy message and a harder one:.

Industry observers note that jev was sure about the lost card. On the ATM question it leaned towards card acceptance with a confidence of 0.64, so the router asked Claude, which got it right.

Because cheap, strong, and threshold are options, the same function routes between any two models.

It has been revealed that model routing reduces AI costs by keeping easy requests on a cheap model and paying for the expensive one only when it's needed. Here's what that looked like on our 200 messages, starting with each model on its own:.

Opus gets six more messages right out of 200, and costs more than 120 times as much.

Now the router, at four confidence thresholds:.

Sources indicate that speed improved too. At the 0.8 threshold, the messages Jev kept came back in a median of 227 ms. The ones that escalated took about 2.1 seconds, because they waited for both models.

A note on method: I ran every message through both models once and saved the answers, then replayed the router over them at each threshold. That's how you compare thresholds without paying for the same test four times.

Then I ran the router live to check. At 0.95 it scored the same 95.0% and sent 61 messages to Opus. At 0.8 it scored 93.5% and sent 20, a point under the replay. Two answers moved: one of Jev's confidence scores landed at 0.82 instead of 0.78, just over the line, and Opus changed its answer on one message. Scores near the threshold shift a little between runs, so leave yourself a margin.

According to recent reports, the choice of cheap model matters less than you'd think. With Google's Gemini Decision 1 in first place instead of Jev, a 0.7 threshold reached the same 95% for US$0.28 per 1,000 messages.

Model routing can cost a little quality, and the threshold decides how much. In our test the gap to Opus ranged from nothing at 0.95 to two points at 0.7.

In a recent development, the loss comes from one place: answers the cheap model got wrong while feeling sure. At the 0.8 threshold, Jev kept five wrong answers because its confidence was above the line. Opus got four of those five wrong as well, so only one was a real loss: "Do all ATMs take this card?", which Jev filed under card acceptance with a confidence of 0.91.

Escalating isn't risk-free either. On one message, Jev had the right label with a confidence of 0.44, and Opus overruled it with the wrong one.

Industry observers note that to optimize costs using AI model routing, measure first, route second, and keep measuring. These six steps cover LLM model routing cost optimization for any pair of models:.

In a recent development, the return is easy to estimate once you know the split. If nine in ten requests stay on a model that costs 1% as much, the bill drops by about 89%, which is what we measured.

In a recent development, several inference providers have multi-model routing built in, and most AI gateway platforms support model routing too, so you don't have to write your own. As of November 2026, these are the top model routing solutions for AI apps. Each name links to the tool's model routing docs:.

Hosted model routing platforms for large language models decide for you, which is the fastest way to start. A hand-built router like ours takes more work, but you choose the signal and you can see why every request went where it did.

An LLM router is the component that does model routing for large language models. It can be a function in your own code, like the one in this guide, a hosted model such as Microsoft Foundry's model router, or a feature of an AI gateway.

Industry observers note that smart model routing is another name for intelligent model routing: a model, not a hand-written rule, decides where each request goes. Dynamic model routing means the same thing.

According to recent reports, the ROI of AI model routing depends on how much of your traffic a cheaper model can handle. In our test, a 0.8 threshold kept 89.5% of messages on the cheap model and cut the cost per 1,000 messages from US$1.96 to US$0.22, for about a point of accuracy. The build was about 60 lines of code.

In a recent development, openRouter's auto model routing works through its Auto Router. You set the model to openrouter/auto, and a decision model picks a model and a reasoning effort for each request. You pay the standard rate of whichever model it selects, with no extra fee.

OpenClaw model routing is a primary model plus an ordered list of fallbacks. In the OpenClaw model routing configuration you set agents.defaults.model.primary and agents.defaults.model.fallbacks, and an agent can override the fallback list. When a model fails, OpenClaw first rotates auth profiles on the same provider, then moves to the next model on the list, as its model failover docs describe. That makes it fallback routing, not cost-based routing.

An AI gateway simplifies model routing by putting every model behind one API, one set of keys, and one place for logs. Your app calls the gateway, and the routing rules live in config instead of code, so changing a model doesn't need a deploy.

Sources indicate that mid-stream failover is when a router switches models after a streamed response has already started, because the first model failed partway through. It's the hardest kind of failover, because the user has already seen part of an answer. Many routers only fail over before the first token arrives and return an error after that, so check what your gateway does.

On Monday, I unboxed the iPhone Duo I pre-ordered back in October and experienced a disarming sense of déjà vu. It’s beautiful hardware married to a messy, often painful software onboarding experience atypical of Apple’s usual polish. It reminds me of the Galaxy Fold’s early years.

In a recent development, I was most looking forward to the combination of a foldable form factor and Apple’s superior app ecosystem, but even the apps that have been updated to support the upcoming aspect ratio, on both the front and back, feel ungainly and buggy. In moving UI elements from the bottom to the right, even with the display open, the Duo forces a rebuilding of essential muscle memory that’s prevailed across mobile platforms, including Android foldables, for 20 years.

In a recent development, the front display, in particular, is a massive test of one’s patience: apps, even ones ostensibly optimized for its stout dimensions, often feel unusable, with UI elements that would be prominent on the iPhone 18 Pro hidden behind overflow menus on the Duo. It’s exasperating and, frankly, boggling.

But what’s interesting is the enthusiasm with which developers are approaching the latest form factor. Reddit threads reveal dozens of Duo-optimized app recommendations that feel novel and, if not polished, then propulsive. There’s a fascinating delta between waiting for my bank, or Starbucks, or Kobo, to get its act together to support the Duo and seeking out net-new opportunities and experiences.

I spent most of the summer using the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and I didn’t expect going back to it to feel so stately and predictable: the showcase of a platform with fewer highs but none of the Duo’s current lows.

According to recent reports, I’m not sure if I’m going to keep the Duo and wait out its colicky infancy. But I do know that until now I hadn’t given Samsung enough credit for the amount of work it did to make foldable software feel ordinary, and that’s the highest compliment I can pay.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the 1870s, tailors in London and Paris raced to redesign the most fundamental garment in a man’s wardrobe: the shirt. Until then, men pulled shirts over their heads, with fabric that billowed down to their waist. But innovative shirt makers in Paris and London—like Charvet and Brown, Davis & Co.—realized that men wanted closer-fitting shirts. The breakthrough came when they sewed buttons down the front, along with darted seams and shoulder yokes, creating a flattering fit. As a final flourish, they added a stylish collar with pointed tips. And so the button-up shirt came into the world. Over the next century, it would become one of the most iconic garments of our time. It conveyed good taste, but, perhaps more importantly, social status. A crisp, spotless shirt made it clear that the man wearing it didn’t work with his hands. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All available 3D movies are included with your Disney+ subscription and come with extras you can only experience in VR.

While 3D movies on a VR headset are uniquely amazing (much more convincing than 3D TV ever was), the most exciting part of the Meta Quest experience is the immersive environments. Disney and Meta worked together to create a fully unique movie-watching experience that gives movies more than just the depth that 3D movies typically have; you’ll also be watching the movies in an environment that’s unique and changes throughout the movie.

Meta states you can “Catch Star Wars: A Fresh Hope (Episode IV) from a comfy spot on Tatooine, see the Avengers battle Loki from atop Avengers Tower, settle in for a Pixar movie night on the Monsters, Inc. Scare Floor, and more.” Some of these immersive environments were shown off at Meta Connect in September when Meta VR Glasses were revealed, but it’s a bit surprising to see so many of them launch months ahead of VR Glasses’ retail debut.

Industry observers note that disney also highlights IMAX experiences, which are also available in the Disney+ app on Meta Quest headsets. These movies mimic the full IMAX experience in VR by putting you in a virtual theater with a massive screen, all at the correct IMAX aspect ratio. Rumor also has it that Meta will include other 3D movies with its Meta VR+ subscription service.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Walt Disney Firm (NYSE: DIS) announced its fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results today, and it exceeded investor expectations.
  • The Walt Disney Company (NYSE: DIS) announced its fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results today, and it exceeded investor expectations.
  • But while shareholders may be buoyed by the news, Disney’s employees are likely feeling less cheerful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Walt Disney Firm (NYSE: DIS) announced its fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results today, and it exceeded investor expectations. But while shareholders may be buoyed by the news, Disney’s employees are likely feeling less cheerful. That’s because the company, which has already laid off thousands this year, claims more job cuts are on the way. Here’s what you need to know. Disney’s Q4 beats on revenue and EPS Today, Disney announced its Q4 2026 results for the period that ended on October 3. Overall, the results were positive for the company, which saw double-digit growth in several key areas: Revenue: $25.9 billion (up 16% from the same quarter a year earlier) Income: $3.5 billion (up 71%) Total segment operating income: $5 billion (up 43%) Entertainment operating income: $1.3 billion (up 92%) Sports operating income: $1.3 billion (up 53%) Experiences operating income: $2.2 billion (up 20%) Adjusted earnings per share came in at $1.77, up from $1.11 in the same quarter a year earlier. Disney’s Q4 results this year were helped by a 53rd week in the company’s fiscal calendar. To put some of those numbers into perspective, the company exceeded analysts’ expectations on revenue and adjusted EPS. Analysts had expected revenue of $25.1 billion and an adjusted EPS of $1.67, notes CNBC. Experiences, which include Disney’s popular theme parks, were one of the highlights for both Disney’s Q4 and full year fiscal 2026, with the company’s Q4 Experiences revenue increasing 15% and its full fiscal year 2026 Experience revenue up 9%. “Our continued growth in both guests and guest spending at Experiences once again highlights the differentiated strength of our diversified global portfolio,” Disney’s CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston wrote in its shareholder’s letter. Other areas of strength for Disney in Q4 included 22% subscription revenue growth and 12% consumer product growth. Shares of The Walt Disney Company were down roughly 1.6% in premarket trading on Monday after the report. The stock is up 6.12% year to date. Disney talks AI… Artificial intelligence is top of mind for the business world, so it’s no surprise that Disney touched on the topic in its most recent earnings announcement. The company stated that its customers at its parks are “increasingly using AI-powered tools to discover, plan, and book their travel,” and Disney, in turn, is “exploring several new ways to meet them where they are.” Disney said it wants its experiences “to appear as a vacation option within the AI tools guests use for inspiration and planning,” likely referring to AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini. To achieve this, the company said it is integrating its “offerings directly into those tools so guests can book more efficiently.” …and says more layoffs are coming In its Q4 results, Disney also touched on cost-cutting efforts, including layoffs. During 2026, Disney has initiated several rounds of job cuts, including 1,000 in April at its television and movie division, more than 100 at Pixar in July, and hundreds in HR and technology roles in September. Then, just this month, CNBC reported that Disney plans to lay off several thousand employees in an effort to reduce costs by up to 20%. Unfortunately, Disney seems to have confirmed that report today. Disney says it is planning about $3 billion in cost-cutting efforts by fiscal 2029 and CFO Johnston told CNBC that part of those efforts will include more layoffs. “We do expect more layoffs,” Johnston said. Fast Company reached out to Disney for comment. We will update this story if we hear back. The job cuts will reportedly help fund Disney’s content spend for fiscal 2027, which is projected to reach $26 billion, up 9% from the year before. Disney has not yet stated which divisions the job cuts will affect, or how many employees will lose their jobs.

Adjusted earnings per share came in at $1.77, up from $1.11 in the same quarter a year earlier. Disney’s Q4 results this year were helped by a 53rd week in the firm’s fiscal calendar.

Recent findings suggest that to put some of those numbers into perspective, the company exceeded analysts’ expectations on revenue and adjusted EPS. Analysts had expected revenue of $25.1 billion and an adjusted EPS of $1.67, notes CNBC.

Experiences, which include Disney’s popular theme parks, were one of the highlights for both Disney’s Q4 and full year fiscal 2026, with the firm’s Q4 Experiences revenue increasing 15% and its full fiscal year 2026 Experience revenue up 9%.

“Our continued growth in both guests and guest spending at Experiences once again highlights the differentiated strength of our diversified global portfolio,” Disney’s CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston wrote in its shareholder’s letter.

Other areas of strength for Disney in Q4 included 22% subscription revenue growth and 12% consumer product growth.

Shares of The Walt Disney Company were down roughly 1.6% in premarket trading on Monday after the report. The stock is up 6.12% year to date.

Artificial intelligence is top of mind for the business world, so it’s no surprise that Disney touched on the topic in its most recent earnings announcement.

The tech giant remarked that its customers at its parks are “increasingly using AI-powered tools to discover, blueprint, and book their travel,” and Disney, in turn, is “exploring several new ways to meet them where they are.”.

Disney said it wants its experiences “to appear as a vacation option within the AI tools guests use for inspiration and planning,” likely referring to AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini.

To achieve this, the manufacturer said it is integrating its “offerings directly into those tools so guests can book more efficiently.”.

In its Q4 results, Disney also touched on cost-cutting efforts, including layoffs.

During 2026, Disney has initiated several rounds of job cuts, including 1,000 in April at its television and movie division, more than 100 at Pixar in July, and hundreds in HR and technology roles in September.

Then, just this month, CNBC reported that Disney plans to lay off several thousand employees in an effort to reduce costs by up to 20%.

Unfortunately, Disney seems to have confirmed that report today. Disney says it is planning about $3 billion in cost-cutting efforts by fiscal 2029 and CFO Johnston told CNBC that part of those efforts will include more layoffs.

“We do expect more layoffs,” Johnston said.

Recent findings suggest that fast Company reached out to Disney for comment. We will revision this story if we hear back.

The job cuts will reportedly help fund Disney’s content spend for fiscal 2027, which is projected to reach $26 billion, up 9% from the year before.

Disney has not yet stated which divisions the job cuts will affect, or how many employees will lose their jobs.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • American Express is giving cardholders another reason to make their dinner reservations through Resy.
  • The firm is launching Resy Rewards Tuesday, a new loyalty program that lets eligible Amex cardholders earn four additional Membership Rewards points per dollar they spend at participating restaurants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that american Express is giving cardholders another reason to make their dinner reservations through Resy. The manufacturer is launching Resy Rewards Tuesday, a new loyalty program that lets eligible Amex cardholders earn four additional Membership Rewards points per dollar they spend at participating restaurants. Those points are in addition to whatever rewards their credit card already earns, so that means some diners could earn as much as 8X points on a single meal. The program marks the first time American Express has brought its Membership Rewards program directly into the Resy app, bringing together two of the company’s biggest offerings as competition for restaurant loyalty heats up. How Resy Rewards works Resy Rewards will initially be available in New York City, with looks to expand to additional U.S. markets in 2027. Eligible American Express cardholders can enroll their cards in the program through the Resy iOS app (Android support is coming soon). Once enrolled, you’ll find a new Rewards tab where you can browse participating restaurants and make reservations. To earn the bonus points, diners need to book through that Rewards tab, complete their reservation, and pay for their meal using their enrolled American Express card. They’ll then earn four additional Membership Rewards points for every eligible dollar spent, on top of the points their card would normally earn. For American Express Gold Card members, for instance, who already earn 4X points on qualifying restaurant purchases, that means earning up to 8X points per dollar spent. That means a $200 dinner that would normally earn 800 points could earn 1,600 points through Resy Rewards. Eligible American Express Business Gold Card members can also earn the additional points. However, the card’s existing 4X restaurant rewards depend on restaurant spending being among the cardholder’s top two eligible spending categories during the billing cycle. A points cap also applies. At launch, Resy Rewards will be available at a selection of New York City restaurants, including Carne Mare, Colonia Verde, Hearth, Kiko, OPTO and Le Pavillon. The company plans to expand the program to additional U.S. cities in 2027, when select restaurants on Tock, another reservation platform owned by American Express, will also become eligible to participate. Why American Express is betting on restaurant rewards Restaurant loyalty has traditionally been a difficult business. Diners want flexibility in where they eat, while restaurants need to balance the cost of offering incentives against the additional business those programs generate. American Express has an advantage because it doesn’t need to create an entirely new rewards system. Instead, Resy Rewards uses Membership Rewards, an established points currency that millions of American Express cardholders already collect through everyday purchases. “For the first time, we’re bringing American Express’s industry-leading Rewards program into the Resy iOS app and connecting two things our Card Members value deeply: great dining experiences and meaningful rewards,” mentioned Pablo Rivero, CEO of Resy and senior vice president of American Express Global Dining. “As we’ve seen with the success of the Resy Credit, rewarding diners while driving demand and revenue to Resy restaurants is a win on both sides of the table.” American Express points to the success of its existing Resy Credit as evidence that dining incentives can influence consumer spending. According to the company, spending on Resy Credit-eligible American Express card products increased 33% at U.S. Resy restaurants following the credit’s introduction. The credit has also been redeemed at 98% of U.S. Resy restaurants.

Lab-grown chicken is finally becoming affordable. Will consumers bite?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something upcoming on the menu at Epic Steak, an upscale restaurant across the street from Google in San Francisco: “Cultivated” chicken, made partly from chicken cells grown in bioreactors, is now offered to diners right alongside staples like porterhouse and Wagyu.
  • There’s something upcoming on the menu at Epic Steak, an upscale restaurant across the street from Google in San Francisco: “Cultivated” chicken, made partly from chicken cells grown in bioreactors, is now offered to diners right alongside staples like porterhouse and Wagyu.
  • Epic is one of eight California restaurants that serves the food, along with some corporate and college campuses, including Stanford University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something upcoming on the menu at Epic Steak, an upscale restaurant across the street from Google in San Francisco: “Cultivated” chicken, made partly from chicken cells grown in bioreactors, is now offered to diners right alongside staples like porterhouse and Wagyu. Epic is one of eight California restaurants that serves the food, along with some corporate and college campuses, including Stanford University. The Bay Area startup behind the cultivated chicken, Upside Foods, claims it has reached a new milestone in scaling up its production—and that has helped bring the price down in the range of premium farm-raised chicken. Its new product includes a blend of cultivated chicken and plant-based ingredients like soy and olive oil. [Photo: Upside Foods] At Epic, “Southern Fried Upside Chicken” with kimchi slaw and hot honey aioli sells for $12. Waterbar, a neighboring seafood spot with the same chef as owner, sells a five-spice version of Upside chicken for $15. At Chimmelier and Jilli, popular Korean fried chicken restaurants in Los Angeles and San Francisco, K-Pop Chicken made from the new meat sells for $19. “We can put it at a price point on the menu where it can be available for everybody,” says Parke Ulrich, executive chef and owner at Epic and Waterbar. Two of his other Bay Area restaurants, Mersea and Hurrica, will also serve dishes made with Upside chicken. Upside, which launched in 2015 and has raised around $600 million, has spent years on R&D for its cultivated meat—meat produced without raising animals or using slaughterhouses, using real animal cells that grow in tanks the tech giant calls cultivators. The company was originally called Memphis Meats, but rebranded in 2021 with a name that it saw as more consumer-friendly. It’s one of more than 140 companies working in the space of cultivated meat. A handful are selling products on the market, including Vow, which sells cultivated quail and fois gras in Australia, and Wildtype, which sells cultivated salmon at a few U.S. restaurants. In theory, producing meat this way could help reduce the enormous environmental footprint of animal agriculture, though that depends on how it’s made, including how much energy is used. The space has been slow to take off, and some other companies have faced difficulties. Good Meat, another Bay Area-based cultivated meat brand, stopped commercial production in the U.S. in 2024. Two other startups, Meatable and Believer Foods, folded late last year. Over the last several years, “the biggest challenge was the external skepticism that this would have worked,” says Dr. Uma Valeti, cofounder and CEO of Upside Foods. The company first unveiled a commercial facility in 2021, though it didn’t initially use its large-scale bioreactors. (Wired reported that it struggled to use the equipment; the company says that its early R&D challenges have been fully addressed.) In 2022, when the company got regulatory approval of an earlier version of its chicken, it was produced at a small scale. Customers had to make reservations for the dish, available only in limited quantities, at a restaurant that sold it temporarily, or find it at one-off events. [Photo: Upside Foods] Now the company says large-scale production is underway. Upside has built a much larger production line, with 20,000-liter tanks in addition to its earlier equipment. Valeti says the two-story-tall tanks “are the largest of their kind in the world,” including anything ever used in the pharmaceutical industry. (The company had previously planned to build a factory in Illinois, but retrofitted its Emeryville headquarters with the giant equipment instead.) In a year, it claims that it has the capacity to produce more than a million pounds of Upside Chicken on less than half an acre of land. One cultivator produces 1,500 to 2,000 pounds of meat a day; the next “harvest” will begin later this week. Inspectors from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Food and Drug Administration work on-site, using a new regulatory process that was developed for this type of food. [Photo: Upside Foods] Scale helps bring down cost. The company makes a key ingredient for its cell feed, something that was expensive to source previously. The chicken itself has also been redeveloped and now includes some plant-based ingredients. That helps improve the texture and nutrition of the food, Valeti says, but also reduces cost. The company declined to comment on the percentage of the food that’s made from cultivated chicken cells versus plant-based ingredients, saying only that cultivated chicken is the second ingredient after water. [Photo: Upside Foods] For restaurants and cafeterias, the chicken comes in whole cuts, cubed, or shredded varieties. Ulrich, who has been developing recipes for his restaurants with Upside Foods over the last several months—experimenting with everything from soup to a barbecue chicken sandwich—says the chicken flavor is subtle, since the product is a blend. But the texture is “fantastic,” he says. It “peels apart like a chicken breast would. It has those strands. And it’s just very silky in texture.” [Photo: Upside Foods] Upside wants to show demand at the restaurants and cafeterias it works with now, and then will scale up production more and potentially begin retail sales. With more scale, and production facilities built outside the expensive Bay Area, the cost will come down even further. The major question: How many consumers will be willing to eat it? The market for alternative meat has been struggling for a few years. Plant-based meat sales in the U.S. are roughly half of what they were in 2021. As consumers increasingly look for “clean” ingredients—simple, recognizable, and natural—cultivated meat’s production methods are a harder sell. Even as the taste gets closer to conventional chicken, the food is still likely to be perceived as different. Texture is key, chef Ulrich says: “My focus has been trying to get the texture there, because I think people eat with their eyes, and it’s almost more important sometimes than how they taste it. Because if it doesn’t look like chicken, if the look isn’t there, their taste buds automatically go somewhere else.”.

The Frankenstein Table

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything.
  • Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?
  • According to recent reports, for example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Something wicked this way comes.”.

Sources indicate that it was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything. The workings might be different under the hood, depending on the reference boxes, but the syntax and expected outcomes would be same: push to one edge, keep at the center, spread around evenly, etc.

Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?

According to recent reports, for example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid. In other words, it reads like a table, but acts like a grid, allowing me to use grid properties. Believe it or not, some form of this was used in the past to make tables responsive.

In a recent development, before I kill off a table in this article though: there are a lot of advantages to straight-up tables. They provide a clean semantic layout that browsers perfectly understand and translate for assistive technology when needed. There’s even a element.

In a recent development, on the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than a week after Jensen Huang resigned from the firm, Nvidia's board has created its own National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. According to its announcement, the newly introduced standing committee will provide high-level oversight of Nvidia’s “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” with its National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team reporting directly to the group and to interim CEO Colette Kress.

Industry observers note that “Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security,” Nvidia chairperson Harvey Jones remarked. “As the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation.”.

The rumors of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, have thrown the firm into turmoil, especially after his admission and subsequent apology. People have begun digging into details about Ms. Huang, revealing that she was at the center of a tangled web of companies and was reportedly instrumental in importing around $7.5 billion of banned Nvidia chips into China. A deeper investigation also revealed that her husband, Kang Wei, was behind her rise to prominence and seemingly accepted her relationship with the billionaire. It remains unclear if the couple made these shrewd business moves purely for profit or if they were under the control of a hidden third party, but it has certainly exposed the company to additional scrutiny.

According to recent reports, the chairpersons of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence have since invited Jensen to a closed-door briefing to discuss Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage,” while President Donald Trump mentioned that the FBI is looking into Jensen Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang. The U.S. first applied export controls to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, the A100 and H100, in 2022, forcing the manufacturer to create the China-market A800 and H800 GPUs that complied with Washington’s performance limitations.

However, the White House lowered the bar once more in 2023, which resulted in the even more watered-down H20, which, nonetheless, remained in high demand. Even though the Trump administration did not implement Biden’s AI diffusion rule, which threatened to outright ban several countries from buying Nvidia AI chips, the president eventually banned the export of H20 chips to China from April to June 2025.

Even before Trump’s total Nvidia AI GPU ban, there have already been multiple reports of smuggling, with one semiconductor analysis firm tracking more than 1.5 gigawatts of banned AI chips exported to China and estimating that up to 1.5 million Nvidia GPUs were smuggled in recent years. Despite that, the former Nvidia chief has always denied the allegations, saying that “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” Whether the allegations are true or not, it seems that the organization is taking the situation seriously and taking steps to plug any leaks. As for Jensen Huang, he may be out of the company, but he still has to face Congress and all ongoing investigations.

In a recent development, elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

It has been revealed that page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

According to recent reports, the data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

My reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having stated that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor upgrade is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

Recent findings suggest that this guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:.

It's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

You can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:.

Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real consumers.

Export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Industry observers note that elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:.

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:.

Industry observers note that on the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

Industry observers note that work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Recent findings suggest that copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the upcoming site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:.

For page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

And the same heading as a block:.

Industry observers note that newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

It has been revealed that the code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then patch the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the upcoming copy, not both at once.

Sources indicate that leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

According to recent reports, run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

In my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

In a recent development, moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

Corporate networking hours can be painfully awkward. Picture it: dozens of professionals clutching lukewarm drinks, trading similar elevator pitches, and desperately scanning badges to find someone worth talking to. “You have a name tag, a drink in your hand, and no guidance,” Tyler Dean Kempf, creative director of Second City Works, told Fast Company. “It’s up to you to engage people in conversations that are usually focused entirely on work.” Marriott International thinks it has a fix—and it involves pulling a move straight out of the comedy playbook. On Tuesday, the hotel giant announced Unscripted Networking: The Second City Takeover, a upcoming program developed exclusively with Chicago’s 65-year-old improv comedy institution, the Second City. The program is rolling out across more than 125 properties in Marriott Bonvoy’s Convention & Resort Network throughout North America and the Caribbean. It offers a 45- to 60-minute experience that swaps traditional small talk for structured, improv-inspired group play. [Photo: Courtesy of VEA Newport Beach, A Marriott Resort & Spa] A different kind of workplace networking event Rather than putting individuals on the spot for solo stand-up bits, the program pairs two professional Second City hosts with a live music director who formats the session like an interactive variety show. The events are designed for groups of 50 to 750 attendees; the hosts lead rapid-fire transitions through low-stakes exercises by asking participants to debate topics like coffee versus tea, or window versus aisle seats, rather than their resume highlights. In one drill, Kempf noted, attendees act as “corporate wingmen,” learning about a partner before introducing them to another pair in the room to expand their circle. Kempf emphasized that while pitching improv to corporate professionals might send introverts running for the exit, the structure explicitly removes the fear of performance. “When we say the word improv, people get scared because our minds go to being vulnerable, having no script, or performing on stage,” Kempf said. “There’s no performance in this. Our hosts demonstrate vulnerability first from the stage, which signals that it’s safe for people to drop their guard down on the floor.” [Photo: Courtesy of Marriott Bonvoy Convention & Resort Network] Let’s get together Amanda Cox, vice president of Sales, Convention & Resort Hotels, East Region for Marriott International, said as hybrid work environments reduce daily office interactions, live events are bearing an unprecedented burden. “In recent years, there’s less gathering around the proverbial water cooler,” Cox said. “Live meetings and events are being looked upon to be torchbearers of an organization’s culture—and that’s a lot of pressure on event planners.” That pressure is compounded by the challenge of bringing together a multi-generational workforce with different communication norms. Cox noted that in customer insight sessions with event organizers, Marriott found planners struggling to get younger hires and veteran executives on the same page. “It is amazing the barriers that break down when you’re immediately in a place of creative collaboration,” Cox said. Yes, and… Marriott ran nine internal engagements with Second City over the past year to test the concept before scaling it across its resort portfolio. Cox said that incorporating the program at the opening reception of a typical three-day conference can result in deeper engagement throughout the rest of the event. “When you start with that genuine connection, you see the return on investment grow throughout the entire meeting,” Cox said. “You’re getting deeper much quicker because you’ve stepped away from small talk into substantial connection.” By bringing comedy-backed behavioral science into the ballroom, Marriott and Second City are making a clear bet: The fastest way to get corporate professionals to drop their guard isn’t another open bar—it’s getting them to play along.

Industry observers note that corporate networking hours can be painfully awkward. Picture it: dozens of professionals clutching lukewarm drinks, trading similar elevator pitches, and desperately scanning badges to find someone worth talking to.

“When you start with that genuine connection, you see the return on investment grow throughout the entire meeting,” Cox stated. “You’re getting deeper much quicker because you’ve stepped away from small talk into substantial connection.”.

By bringing comedy-backed behavioral science into the ballroom, Marriott and Second City are making a clear bet: The fastest way to get corporate professionals to drop their guard isn’t another open bar—it’s getting them to play along.

#23582. Breaking: The Moat Isn't The Agentic Data; It's Knowing What The Data Means

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (861 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The Moat Isn't The Agentic Data; It's Knowing What The Data Means

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Siddhartha Rao is a VP & Distinguished Engineer at Oracle.
  • Nearly every serious conversation about enterprise AI now includes the same four words: “Context is the moat.” Then everyone nods.
  • But ask what context actually is, and the room goes quiet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Siddhartha Rao is a VP & Distinguished Engineer at Oracle. He has been working on AI and machine learning for the last decade.

Nearly every serious conversation about enterprise AI now includes the same four words: “Context is the moat.” Then everyone nods.

But ask what context actually is, and the room goes quiet. That silence is expensive. Companies are funding agents to “chat with their data” without being able to say what those agents need to know.

I lead generative AI services for Oracle’s AI Data Platform, so I’m not a neutral observer. Still, I’ve watched enough pilots stall to have opinions about why. Here are six of those opinions:.

Recent findings suggest that the fashionable answer to the question of context is data gravity. Bring the models to where the data already lives.

Fine. Do it. But a model sitting next to a petabyte it doesn’t understand is like a tourist outside of a library in a language they can’t read.

The advantage belongs to whomever understands the data (like which of three revenue tables finance actually trusts) and knows which instrument fits which question, whether that means forecasting for demand, Bayesian estimates for risk or deterministic rules for eligibility.

The language model’s job, working out what the data means, is narrower than the hype suggests.

Context includes metadata, the workflows a business actually runs, an ontology of the concepts it reasons in, and an understanding of how its structured and unstructured data relate.

Recent findings suggest that context is not raw rows stuffed into a prompt. Size is not meaning, and we should stop pretending otherwise.

The piece most teams miss is the tool description. An agent never reads your data model. It reads the descriptions of the tools it’s allowed to call. A generic “run SQL” tool tells it nothing. A tool described in the business’s own language, scoped to what that agent should see, tells it how to think.

According to recent reports, prompt engineering was about how you ask. Context engineering is about what the model is told the world contains.

In a recent development, should context live in one platform or stay spread across lakehouses, databases and applications? It’s a false choice. No CIO wants yet another copy of everything, with permissions that drift from the source. Leave the data where it lives and query it in place.

Sources indicate that what has to consolidate is meaning; one semantic layer that bounds the model, orchestrates its tools and decides what each user may touch. That layer, not storage, is the control point.

According to recent reports, gartner predicted in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing costs, unclear value and inadequate risk controls. But read that list again. Nowhere does it say the model wasn’t smart enough.

Pilots run on curated data for a few users who can see everything. Production runs on thousands of users with row-level, column-level and role-based permissions. Agents make it harder by creating data the access model never anticipated, such as summaries, memories or knowledge graphs.

If an agent tells one user what it learned from another’s query, then all you’ve done is build a very polite data leak.

Recent findings suggest that will better reasoning models make proprietary context obsolete? No. The frontier has moved from capability to cost. A model that rediscovers your schema on every question burns tokens, takes a different path each time and returns an answer nobody can trace. That’s a brilliant latest hire with amnesia, billing by the hour.

Sources indicate that context is amortized reasoning. You pay once to understand the business, and every later question inherits it. That math changes only when inference is nearly free, reproducible and able to audit itself back to source rows. I wouldn’t bet the roadmap on all three.

In a recent development, when an agent acts on stale or over-permissioned context, who owns the failure? Juvenal asked the governance question nearly 2,000 years ago: Who watches the watchmen? If you can’t reconstruct what the agent saw, how old it was and whose permissions applied, the answer is the CIO.

Sources indicate that so, build governance in. Citations should trace to the business concept the agent thought it was answering and to the exact rows it used. Memory should point back to source data with a freshness timestamp. A stale finding presented as current is the most dangerous kind of wrong, because it’s plausibly right.

If you fund one thing on Monday morning, make it the expertise, in-house or through a partner, to build an ontology, semantic models and progressive disclosure. Give the model the map first, then reveal detail only as each question demands. It’s cheaper, more accurate and easier to govern because every disclosure becomes a checkpoint for permissions, freshness and lineage.

Industry observers note that before you sign with any vendor, put these six problems on the table. Their answers will tell you more than their demos.

According to recent reports, forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the argument for school cellphone bans is simple: Phones offer endless distraction. Take them away and students can focus on classwork, engage with peers and, ultimately, learn more.But the reality is more complicated, as emerging research demonstrates. Schools can lock phones away in pouches or banish them to backpacks, but they can’t shut out the digital world.In the past few years, more than 40 U.S. states have passed laws that restrict cellphones at schools, according to the Phone Free Schools State Report Card, which tracks state phone legislation. But those laws vary widely and often let schools design their own policies, resulting in a patchwork of rules and enforcement across the country.A large-scale study published Tuesday found strict cellphone restrictions — ones that require students to put phones in locked pouches for the entire school day — result in small academic gains. But, the researchers remarked, the gains can add up if schools continue banning phones. Phone bans appear to help, to a point The study, led by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, found the schools with strict phone restrictions saw “modest” improvements in academic growth, compared with students in similar schools without those restrictions. The study, which analyzed test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools nationally, estimates the academic gains were equivalent to about an additional week or two of learning over a school year.Student achievement has been falling globally since 2013, which is roughly when social media-enabled smartphones took off. The researchers sought to determine if the decline is being reversed now that schools have started taking phones away, said Harvard professor Thomas Kane, one of the study’s authors.“Our answer is yes, phone bans do have a positive effect on growth. But it’s not a panacea,” Kane said. Learning loss was gradual over a decade, he notes, and it’s not surprising that gains would also be gradual. The study used math and reading test data for grades four through 10 from the past five academic years.“While schools should not expect large boosts in achievement immediately, storing students’ phones seems to be a cost-effective way to add 1-2 weeks of instruction each year, which could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” the study indicates.The boost is equal to about half the annual decline in test scores since smartphones became mainstream, the study said. Academic gains are overall ‘disappointing,’ one researcher says Still, the connection between phones and learning is not clear-cut.A different study published in May concluded strict school phone bans had “close to zero” effect on test scores. It compared schools with bans with tens of thousands of other schools.The National Bureau of Economic Research study looked at a different set of standardized test scores than Harvard’s study, as well as GPS phone activity, teacher surveys and data from Yondr, the leading provider of lockable phone pouches, at 4,600 schools that use the pouches.The study had found “modest positive effects” in high school test scores over three years, particularly in math. But the report’s authors, researchers at Stanford, the University of Michigan, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania, were hesitant to conclude overall learning benefits from the bans.Both studies point to a similar conclusion, said Stanford education economist Thomas Dee, an author of the NBER study. “The early results from school phone bans are largely disappointing and raise unresolved questions,” Dee said.Noting that the Harvard study demonstrated learning gains may accumulate over time, Dee said: “I hope they’re right. However, I’m not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.”The reasons, Dee said, could be that students are still distracted on other devices at school. Or, he said, “it may be that we see these disappointing results because out-of-school phone use is harming child development.” Phones aren’t the only tech distracting teens Just because schools or states have phone bans does not mean they’re being enforced, said Jean Twenge, a psychologist at San Diego State University and author of “10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World.”Ask any teacher — or teenager — and they’ll tell you that some phone bans are largely cosmetic. Teens come up with creative workarounds, including stowing burner phones or even phone-shaped rocks in their locked pouches. At schools that rely on students to keep phones in backpacks, adherence to the ban can be spotty.“It happens pretty often that there’s a policy of no phones during the school day, bell-to-bell, and you go into the school and phones are everywhere,” Twenge said.Even without phones, “Do they have laptops at school? Are they just doing social media on laptops instead?” Twenge said.Phone use outside of school affects academics too, Twenge said. “If they have that phone available when they’re studying, how much are they really taking in?”Kane, of the Harvard study, agrees the effect of cellphone use outside of school is “the massive question.” But researchers have not been able to investigate parents and educators’ suspicions that late-night binges on YouTube and other platforms are costly for students.“I find it astonishing that social media companies know how much time kids spend on their platforms, but that data has never been linked to student outcomes,” Kane said. “We can’t provide answers until the social media companies share data.” The Associated Press’ education coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron form unlikely alliance to standardize robot charging as chipmakers push toward unmanned fabs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron are reportedly working together to develop common charging standards for mobile robots used in semiconductor fabrication plants, according to a fresh report.
  • Sources indicate that according to a report by Seoul Economic Daily, the initiative aims to establish common technical specifications that would allow robots from different manufacturers to share charging equipment, reducing the cost and complexity of deploying large robotic fleets across semiconductor manufacturing facilities.
  • Recent findings suggest that so why are three of the world's biggest memory manufacturers, who are also competitors, coming together to establish standards for the robotics industry?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron are reportedly working together to develop common charging standards for mobile robots used in semiconductor fabrication plants, according to a fresh report. Representatives from the three companies have reportedly formed an early-stage consultative body to lead standardization efforts, alongside major industry stakeholders such as the Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International (SEMI) industry association.

Sources indicate that according to a report by Seoul Economic Daily, the initiative aims to establish common technical specifications that would allow robots from different manufacturers to share charging equipment, reducing the cost and complexity of deploying large robotic fleets across semiconductor manufacturing facilities. The broader goal is to accelerate factory automation, particularly in older fabs, while laying the groundwork for fully autonomous semiconductor manufacturing.

Recent findings suggest that so why are three of the world's biggest memory manufacturers, who are also competitors, coming together to establish standards for the robotics industry? What exactly does the collaboration involve? And what are the implications of something as seemingly minor as robot charging for the broader semiconductor and robotics industries?

Sources indicate that soaring demand for semiconductor memory chips used in AI infrastructure has driven manufacturers to automate as many production processes as possible to optimize manufacturing speed and capacity in existing facilities to increase output, while they build additional fabs. Modern semiconductor fabs already have extensive automation systems. However, even these facilities still require human workers for certain operations, such as moving materials between floors and unpacking products, that existing automation systems cannot perform. The issue is even more pronounced in older fabs, which generally have fewer automated material-handling systems and still rely on workers to move wafer containers using manual carts.

In a recent development, one potential solution is to hand these remaining manual operations over to mobile robots, allowing manufacturers to automate tasks without undertaking extensive renovations or installing complex fixed transport systems. These could include autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) that transport materials around the factory, mobile manipulators that combine robotic arms with moving platforms, and humanoid robots capable of performing more complicated handling tasks.

In a recent development, the problem, however, is that these robots come in different builds and configurations, often with their own batteries and accompanying charging infrastructure. A semiconductor fab deploying multiple robot models from different manufacturers could consequently end up requiring separate charging stations for each model. In addition to increasing equipment and maintenance costs, these installations consume valuable factory floor space.

The proposed initiative seeks to address this problem by establishing common charging specifications that different robot manufacturers can adopt. Standardized charging infrastructure would allow multiple types of robots to use compatible charging stations, reducing the need for separate installations and making it easier for semiconductor manufacturers to expand their robotic fleets without adding operational inefficiencies.

The alliance is considering standards covering battery specifications for different mobile robots, charging-station equipment and communication protocols, charging connectors, and battery management systems (BMS). Together, these specifications would establish common requirements for the physical and electronic interfaces involved in charging robots inside semiconductor fabs.

The initial objective is to achieve charging compatibility across different robot models. In addition to letting a fab deploy robots from several manufacturers without having to install a separate charging system for every model, this would also give manufacturers greater flexibility when purchasing new robots, since their choice of supplier would no longer be as heavily influenced by the charging infrastructure already installed in the facility.

It has been revealed that A subsequent step would involve integrating robot charging data with the fab's manufacturing execution system (MES), the software that coordinates and monitors manufacturing operations. With access to information such as battery charge levels, robot availability, and production schedules, the system could coordinate when individual robots operate and when they return for charging. For example, robots could be scheduled to recharge during periods of lower demand or while other robots handle critical material transfers, minimizing interruptions to production. This integration would become increasingly important as manufacturers deploy larger fleets of robots across the hundreds of individual processes involved in semiconductor fabrication.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, the three chipmakers leading the standardization efforts are primarily customers of industrial robotics manufacturers, not manufacturers of the robots themselves, except for Samsung, which has an established robotics business. The objective is to develop specifications that robotics manufacturers and charging-equipment suppliers can incorporate into their products.

On the other hand, the three companies are not independently creating specifications and dictating them to suppliers. The initiative would likely follow an industry standardization process in which robotics manufacturers, equipment suppliers, and other stakeholders contribute to developing and validating the technical requirements. For now, the project remains in its early stages, with participants still determining which components and interfaces should be standardized and consulting robotics and smart-factory specialists.

Recent findings suggest that according to DigiTimes, semiconductor industry participants first explored establishing common robotics standards roughly a decade ago, but discussions made little progress until recently. The renewed momentum is largely attributed to the ongoing semiconductor boom, which has coincided with rapid advancements in industrial robotics.

Unprecedented demand for AI-related memory products, along with record financial performance, has given semiconductor manufacturers both the incentive and the financial resources to invest more aggressively in factory automation. While manufacturers are expanding production capacity to meet demand, latest fabs take years to construct and bring online. As a result, they are simultaneously looking to squeeze out as much capacity as possible from existing facilities by increasing automation and improving productivity.

It has been revealed that as for why Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron are collaborating despite their intense rivalry, the answer likely comes down to shared commercial interests. Incompatible robot charging infrastructure is an industry-wide problem, and all three companies stand to benefit from a common solution. The AI boom has already encouraged numerous partnerships across the semiconductor supply chain, including between companies that are considered fierce rivals, as manufacturers look for ways to overcome common production and infrastructure constraints.

The involvement of these particular companies also gives the initiative considerable weight. Together, Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron control almost the entire global DRAM market. They also operate extensive semiconductor manufacturing networks and represent a substantial potential market for fab-specific robotic equipment. A common set of specifications backed by all three would therefore provide robotics manufacturers with a strong commercial incentive to develop compatible products, potentially shortening development cycles and accelerating adoption.

Recent findings suggest that although the current collaboration focuses on a relatively small aspect of factory automation, it is a significant step for broader standardization across the semiconductor manufacturing and industrial robotics industries. Common charging infrastructure would make it easier to deploy and manage mixed robotic fleets, while future integration with production management systems could bring fabs closer to operating with minimal human intervention. This longer-term ambition of completely autonomous facilities is already taking shape. Both SK hynix and Samsung have outlined looks to develop an autonomous semiconductor fab by 2030.
